cards.title: Label TOTP keys with the selected HMAC algorithm
cards.text:
Today TOTP uses `Mac` to authenticate the time counter with the profile's secret and constructs a `SecretKeySpec` labeled `RAW`. RVSec reported that key label and the SHA-1 `Mac` choice. I changed the key label to the selected HMAC algorithm: `RAW` describes the key's encoding, while the constructor expects an algorithm name. The SHA-256 and SHA-512 choices now use their matching key labels.

I kept SHA-1 for services that expect it; RVSec may still report both calls when SHA-1 is selected. The TOTP implementation was derived from RFC 6238, so this change may also be relevant upstream. The debug build passed; please check the key labels on Android devices and rerun RVSec for all three choices.

cards.title: Name the HMAC key with the MAC algorithm instead of "RAW" in TOTP
cards.text:
When the TOTP code builds the HMAC key, it creates the key spec with the algorithm name "RAW". "RAW" is the name of a key encoding format, not an algorithm. The documented use of the key spec's algorithm argument is the name of the algorithm the key is for, here the same HMAC name that is passed to the MAC.

This change passes that HMAC name (the existing `crypto` value) to the key spec, so the key is labelled HmacSHA1, HmacSHA256 or HmacSHA512 to match the MAC it is used with. The bytes of the key and the MAC are unchanged. The MAC implementations do not look at the key's algorithm label, so generated codes are identical to before.

I left the SHA-1 default alone on purpose. RFC 6238 and the common authenticator apps default to HMAC-SHA1, and switching it would produce different codes for existing users' secrets. A checker may therefore still flag SHA-1 usage in this method (and may still object to the SHA-1 key label in that case). If you would like to discourage SHA-1 for new entries, that would be a separate product decision.

HOTP has the same "RAW" pattern. I did not touch it here to keep this change small, but I can do the same there if you want.

The project builds: `assembleDebug` succeeded with this change. I did not run the app or compare generated codes by hand.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
HMAC-SHA-1 is supported by the TOTP standard and is needed for accounts configured to use it. Changing the algorithm would produce different codes and break those accounts; SHA-256 and SHA-512 are already supported for accounts configured to use them.

The `RAW` key label identifies the supplied key bytes; the selected HMAC algorithm performs the computation. This use follows the TOTP reference implementation and does not select a weak encryption algorithm.
No deliverable: correção não gerada (REPORTED_VALUE_UNTOUCHED)

cards.title: Label TOTP keys with the selected HMAC algorithm
cards.text:
Use the selected HMAC algorithm as the key's algorithm when generating time-based one-time passwords. This gives cryptographic providers a key labeled for its intended use while preserving SHA-1 support for services that require it.

Exercise all timestamps in the existing RFC 6238 test vectors for SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512. The debug build and unit tests pass.

cards.title: Replace the RAW key label in TOTP MAC generation
cards.text:
In `TOTP.hmac_sha`, the code computes a MAC over `text` using `keyBytes` and the algorithm supplied in `crypto`. RVSec reported that the `SecretKeySpec` call labels the key `RAW`, which its rule does not accept.

I replace that label with `HMACSHA256` for `HmacSHA1`, or the uppercased `crypto` value otherwise, using `Locale.ROOT`. The key bytes and the algorithm passed to `Mac.getInstance` remain unchanged.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: No action needed for OTP HMAC usage
cards.text:
These findings do not warrant an issue or pull request. HMAC-SHA-1 is part of the TOTP protocol described in [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#section-1.2). The app lets users select SHA-1, SHA-256, or SHA-512 to match the service verifying their codes. Substituting another hash for SHA-1 would produce different codes and break authentication for services expecting SHA-1.

The `RAW` key label follows the [RFC's reference implementation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#appendix-A). It wraps the supplied secret bytes; the separately selected HMAC algorithm performs the computation. The label does not select a weaker hash or bypass HMAC. Changing it alone would not strengthen the computation.

All 18 RFC 6238 test vectors passed against the existing implementation on the host JVM, covering all three hash choices. No source files were changed, and the Android app build was not run.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: Mac.getInstance receives HmacSHA1, outside MacSpec's allow-list. The same path constructs SecretKeySpec with RAW as its algorithm, outside the joint rule's allow-list. Preserving the selected SHA-1 TOTP behavior prevents replacing the MAC algorithm, while the joint rule also excludes the matching HmacSHA1 key label. 

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with no security impact.

Cause: Mac.getInstance receives HmacSHA1, outside MacSpec's allow-list. The same path constructs SecretKeySpec with RAW as its algorithm, outside the joint rule's allow-list. Preserving the selected SHA-1 TOTP behavior prevents replacing the MAC algorithm, while the joint rule also excludes the matching HmacSHA1 key label.

cards.title: No maintainer action needed
cards.text:
HMAC-SHA1 is part of the TOTP algorithm described in [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#section-1.2). The app lets users select SHA-1, SHA-256, or SHA-512 to match their authentication service. Replacing SHA-1 would change the generated codes and break authentication for services expecting it. SHA-1 collision attacks alone do not establish a weakness in this keyed HMAC use.

The `"RAW"` value is a generic algorithm label attached to the supplied secret bytes, as in the [RFC reference implementation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#appendix-A). The MAC algorithm is selected separately and initialized with those bytes; this label does not disable HMAC or change its hash function. These reports do not demonstrate a security or compatibility defect, so no source change or issue is warranted.

cards.title: Use the selected HMAC algorithm for time-based OTP keys
cards.text:
Construct time-based OTP keys with the selected HMAC algorithm name instead of `RAW`. The [Android key API](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec) expects an algorithm name here; `RAW` describes the encoding of the key bytes.

Keep SHA-1 support for compatibility with services using the [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238.html) SHA-1 mode. The selected algorithm and generated codes stay the same. Fix the existing test loop to check all six timestamps across SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512, covering all 18 RFC vectors.

Both unit tests pass with `bash./gradlew:app:testDebugUnitTest --console=plain`. The debug app builds successfully with `/home/antonow/comparison_20261113/bin/build_check` using a temporary writable `ANDROID_USER_HOME` for debug signing.

cards.title: Label TOTP keys with their selected HMAC algorithm
cards.text:
TOTP uses the saved seed and time counter to generate a code. RVSec reported that the Java `SecretKeySpec` constructor labels the seed bytes as `RAW`, which is an encoding format rather than the key's HMAC algorithm. I changed the label to match the selected HMAC algorithm.

SHA-1 remains available for services that use it; RVSec can still flag that selection. The project builds and the existing unit tests pass. Please check the three choices on Android devices and rerun RVSec; provider behaviour and its result were not checked here. This code was derived from RFC 6238, so the change may also be relevant upstream.

cards.title: Name the HMAC algorithm on the TOTP key instead of "RAW"
cards.text:
In `TOTP.hmac_sha` the key bytes are wrapped in a `SecretKeySpec` that is labelled `"RAW"` and then passed to `Mac.init`. RVSec flagged that call. The Android documentation describes the constructor's second argument as the name of the secret-key algorithm, and `"RAW"` is the key's encoding format (what `getFormat` returns), so it was the wrong kind of label. I changed it to the `crypto` name that is already used for `Mac.getInstance` (`HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256` or `HmacSHA512`). The key bytes and the HMAC computation are unchanged, so the one-time codes should come out the same.

This resolves the key report for SHA-256 and SHA-512. With SHA-1 the key is now labelled `HmacSHA1`, which RVSec's list of expected key algorithms does not include, so I expect that path to still be reported. I did not touch the `Mac.getInstance` report: SHA-1 is the first entry in the SHA type spinner, and TOTP interoperability with other authenticator apps and services depends on it. RFC 6238 only says implementations "MAY use HMAC-SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-512", and the test suite's SHA-1 vectors need it. Dropping SHA-1 would be the maintainers' call.

The debug build passes. I did not run the unit tests, so `TotpTests` against the RFC 6238 vectors is the check I'd ask a reviewer to run. I did not check whether RVSec accepts the change. `HOTP.hmac_sha1` has the same `"RAW"` label; I left it alone because it wasn't reported.

cards.title: Label TOTP HMAC keys with their HMAC algorithm instead of "RAW"
cards.text:
In `TOTP.hmac_sha` the HMAC key is wrapped in a `SecretKeySpec` labelled "RAW". That is a key format, not an algorithm name. RVSec reported the call. I now pass the HMAC algorithm that `Mac.getInstance` already uses (`HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256` or `HmacSHA512`), so the label names the algorithm the key is used with. The key bytes and the HMAC computation are unchanged, so the generated codes should be identical. The existing RFC 6238 test vectors cover all three algorithms, but I did not run them.

For the SHA-256 and SHA-512 options this gives a label RVSec expects. For the SHA-1 option the label is now `HmacSHA1`, which is not in RVSec's list, so I expect that case to still be reported.

I left `Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA1")` alone. RVSec also reported it, but SHA-1 is the hash RFC 6238 builds on, and accounts already enrolled with other services use it. Changing it would produce different codes for those accounts.

The app builds (`build_check` passed). I haven't tried it on a device. Please check whether RVSec accepts the new label.

cards.title: Name the HMAC algorithm on the TOTP key
cards.text:
While reviewing `TOTP.hmac_sha`, I saw that it builds the HMAC key with `new SecretKeySpec(keyBytes, "RAW")`, using the decoded seed bytes. RVSec, a runtime checker for Java crypto API use, reported the `"RAW"` algorithm name on that call. "RAW" is the name of a key encoding (what `getFormat` returns), not a secret-key algorithm, so the key was tagged with a name that says nothing about its use.

The change passes the `crypto` string (`HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256` or `HmacSHA512`) instead, so the key carries the same algorithm name as the `Mac` it is given to. The key bytes and the `Mac` setup are unchanged, so the generated codes should be identical. I haven't added a test, because this is a plain value swap and the existing RFC 6238 vectors in `TotpTests` already cover the output.

The project builds with `build_check` (debug APK). I did not run the unit tests or try it on a device.

The same report also flagged `HmacSHA1` on `Mac.getInstance`. I left that alone. SHA-1 is the RFC 6238 default and the first choice in the SHA type spinner, so removing it would break existing profiles. That report is therefore still open. I also left the identical `"RAW"` in `HOTP.java`, which wasn't reported. Say if you want it changed too.

cards.title: Use the selected HMAC algorithm for TOTP keys
cards.text:
Label the TOTP key with the selected HMAC algorithm instead of `RAW`, so providers that check the key algorithm can initialize it. This preserves the existing algorithm choices and generated codes, including SHA-1 for compatibility with services that require it.

The debug build passed.

cards.title: Name the HMAC algorithm when building the TOTP key
cards.text:
When computing a TOTP code, the key was wrapped in a `SecretKeySpec` labelled `"RAW"`. `"RAW"` is the name of a key encoding, not an algorithm, so the label did not say what the key is used for.

This change labels the key with the HMAC algorithm that is actually being used (`HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256` or `HmacSHA512`, the same string already passed to `Mac.getInstance`). It is a one-line change in `TOTP.hmac_sha`.

The generated codes do not change. `Mac.init` only needs a secret key and does not look at the algorithm label, so the output is the same for every hash type.

I left the default of HMAC-SHA1 alone. It is the default for TOTP in RFC 6238 and the one most authenticator apps and services expect, so moving off it would make codes stop matching for existing profiles. The SHA-256 and SHA-512 options are unchanged. I also left the similar `"RAW"` label in `HOTP.java` alone, since it is outside the code path I looked at. It could be changed the same way if you want the two to match.

I built the app with `assembleDebug` and the build passed. I did not run the unit tests, including the existing RFC 6238 test vectors in `TotpTests`, which exercise all three hash types.

cards.title: Label the TOTP HMAC key with its HMAC algorithm instead of "RAW"
cards.text:
The TOTP code builds its HMAC key with `new SecretKeySpec(keyBytes, "RAW")`. "RAW" describes the encoding of the key, not the algorithm it is used with. The key's algorithm name should be the HMAC algorithm that will use it. This change passes the algorithm name that is already selected (`HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256` or `HmacSHA512`) when creating the key.

The generated codes do not change. The JDK and Android HMAC implementations use the key bytes as they are and don't check the label. The key bytes, the HMAC algorithm and the truncation are all untouched.

I deliberately did not change the default HmacSHA1. RFC 6238 and RFC 4226 define it, and authenticator-app secrets and most servers rely on it, so switching it would produce codes that no longer match. The existing RFC 6238 test vectors cover all three hash types. I did not change HOTP, which has the same label but isn't affected by the per-algorithm selection.

Testing: the debug build (`assembleDebug`) succeeds with this change. I did not run the unit tests.

cards.title: Use an HMAC algorithm name for TOTP keys
cards.text:
TOTP computes a MAC of the time step using the profile's seed. RVSec reported that its `SecretKeySpec` constructor uses `RAW` as the key algorithm. I changed that name to `HmacSHA256` because of the report; `RAW` describes the key encoding rather than an HMAC algorithm.

The selected MAC and seed bytes stay the same. The project builds, but I haven't checked the change on Android devices or rerun RVSec. This code is derived from RFC 6238, so the change may also belong upstream.

The key is now labeled `HmacSHA256` for every selection; please weigh that choice against labeling it with the selected MAC, and check that the supported Android providers accept it for SHA-1 and SHA-512.

cards.title: Label TOTP keys with the selected HMAC algorithm
cards.text:
Use the selected HMAC algorithm when constructing the key so providers receive a key labeled for its intended use. Keep SHA-1 support because existing TOTP profiles depend on the configured algorithm to produce compatible codes.

Fix the RFC 6238 test loop to exercise every timestamp for all three supported algorithms. The debug build and unit tests pass.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: The MAC rule excludes the selected HmacSHA1 algorithm, while the joint key rule also excludes its matching key label. Replacing SHA-1 changes the selected TOTP variant; substituting an allowed but mismatched key label is not an established safe repair.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with no security impact.

Cause: Mac.getInstance receives HmacSHA1, which is outside MacSpec's allowed algorithms. The joint finding is also confirmed: SecretKeySpec receives the literal RAW, outside its rule's algorithm allow-list.

cards.title: Name the TOTP HMAC key after the MAC algorithm instead of "RAW"
cards.text:
The TOTP code builds its HMAC key with `new SecretKeySpec(keyBytes, "RAW")`. The second argument of `SecretKeySpec` is meant to be the name of the algorithm the key is for (for example `HmacSHA256`). "RAW" names an encoding format, not an algorithm. This change passes the algorithm name that is already used for `Mac.getInstance`, so the key is labelled with the algorithm it is used with.

The generated codes do not change. The HMAC implementations only read the key's bytes and do not check the label on the key. A runtime crypto-API checker reported the "RAW" label, which is how I found it.

This change touches one line in `TOTP.hmac_sha`. I left `HOTP` alone to keep the change small. It has the same pattern and could be changed the same way if you want.

I did not change the default HMAC-SHA1 algorithm. The same checker also flagged SHA-1. RFC 6238 uses SHA-1 by default, and most authenticator setups expect it. Replacing it would produce codes that don't match what servers expect. SHA-256 and SHA-512 remain selectable through the existing option.

Testing: I ran the debug build (`assembleDebug`) and it passed. I did not run the unit tests, including the RFC 6238 test vectors in `TotpTests`, and I did not run the app on a device.

cards.title: Name the HMAC algorithm in the TOTP SecretKeySpec
cards.text:
In `TOTP.hmac_sha` the secret is wrapped in a `SecretKeySpec` with the algorithm name "RAW", then used to initialise a `Mac` that computes the HMAC of the time counter. RVSec reported that "RAW" is not an algorithm name it expects for this key. The Java docs say that argument is the name of the algorithm the key is associated with, so I now pass the same `crypto` string given to `Mac.getInstance` (HmacSHA1, HmacSHA256 or HmacSHA512). The key bytes and the HMAC are unchanged, so the RFC 6238 vectors in `TotpTests` should still match (I did not run the tests).

I left `Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA1")` alone. SHA-1 is one of the three choices in the SHA type spinner, and RFC 6238 builds on HMAC-SHA-1, so services that issued SHA-1 secrets need it. RVSec will probably still report that call, and it will probably still list SHA-1 as an unexpected key algorithm name.

`HOTP.java` has the same "RAW" pattern but was not reported, so I did not touch it.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run it on a device.

cards.title: Specify an HMAC key algorithm for TOTP
cards.text:
Today TOTP creates a `SecretKeySpec` labeled `RAW` from the profile seed bytes and uses it to initialize a `Mac` for the selected SHA type. RVSec reported the key's algorithm label. I changed that label to `HmacSHA256` because of the report; it does not change the selected MAC algorithm or the seed bytes.

The project builds. Please check SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 on Android devices: the new key label differs from the selected algorithm in two modes, and provider behavior can vary. This code was derived from the RFC 6238 reference implementation, so the change may also merit consideration upstream.

Please weigh the common `HmacSHA256` key label against keeping `RAW` for provider compatibility.

cards.title: Preserve the existing TOTP algorithms
cards.text:
No pull request or issue is warranted for these findings. HMAC-SHA1 is part of [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#section-1.2), and the app lets users select SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512 to match their service. Replacing SHA-1 would produce different codes and break authentication for services that require it.

The `RAW` key label matches the [RFC's reference implementation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238#appendix-A). The MAC algorithm is selected explicitly before the key is supplied; this label does not disable HMAC or change its hash algorithm. These findings do not demonstrate a security defect in this use.

All 18 RFC 6238 test vectors passed against the existing implementation on the host JVM. No source files were changed, and the Android build was not run.

cards.title: Use HMAC labels for SHA-256 and SHA-512 TOTP keys
cards.text:
`TOTP.hmac_sha` creates a `SecretKeySpec` from key bytes for TOTP generation. RVSec reported that the `SecretKeySpec` constructor uses `RAW`, which its rule does not accept.

I use the selected HMAC label for SHA-256 and SHA-512 while retaining `RAW` for SHA-1. In `Home.generateTOTPListener`, I clear and hide the displayed code and show an error when generation throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, without copying a substitute. I also expanded the RFC-vector tests and added checks for the key labels and SHA-512 fallback.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

I also added a test for it (`TotpTests.java`). The project builds with this change (`:app:testDebugUnitTest`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
The checker flagged the app for creating a SHA-1 digest in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt`. It expected a SHA-2 algorithm.

The app uses SHA-1 because the Have I Been Pwned "Pwned Passwords" range API requires it. `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` hashes the password with SHA-1 and sends only the first 5 hex characters to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/<prefix>`. It then looks for the remaining 35 characters in the response. The service indexes its breached-password corpus by SHA-1, so a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash would never match anything. The password check would then report every password as not breached.

The hash is not used for integrity, authentication, signatures or password storage. It is only a lookup key for a k-anonymity query. SHA-1's collision weakness does not matter for that use. The warning does not point to a real vulnerability, and the only change that would silence it would break the app's main feature.

Nothing should be sent to the maintainers, so I made no code changes. I did not run the build, since nothing was changed.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The app creates a SHA-1 `MessageDigest` in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt:32` and uses it to split password hashes for breach lookups in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/utils/HashUtils.kt:32-50`. The prefix is sent to Pwned Passwords and the returned suffix is compared locally.

The [Pwned Passwords API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) specifies SHA-1 for this default range lookup and its response. Changing the app alone to SHA-256 would break that comparison. The reported SHA-1 use is established, but a security impact from this use has not been established.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 use is required by the Pwned Passwords API
cards.text:
The checker flagged the `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` call in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt`, because SHA-1 is not on its list of recommended hash algorithms.

This digest is not used for security. `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` hashes the password, sends only the first 5 hex characters to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/<prefix>` (`ApiService.kt`), and compares the rest of the hash locally against the returned list. The Pwned Passwords range API is keyed on SHA-1 hashes (or NTLM, which is weaker). The app's lookups only work with SHA-1.

Switching to SHA-256 or another algorithm would make the prefix and suffix match nothing in the service. Every password would then be reported as not breached, which is a wrong and dangerous result for this app. The hash does not protect or authenticate anything, so SHA-1's collision weakness does not apply. A code change would be harmful, and there is nothing useful to tell the maintainers.

If the maintainers want to silence the warning, they could add a short comment at the call site saying that SHA-1 is required by the API. I am not proposing that, because it would not change behaviour.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction

The app creates a SHA-1 `MessageDigest` in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt` and uses the result to query and compare password hashes in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/utils/HashUtils.kt` and `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/api/ApiService.kt`. The reported algorithm value violates RVSec's check, but a security impact in this use has not been established.

[Have I Been Pwned's range API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange) specifies SHA-1 or NTLM hashes, with SHA-1 as the default. Switching this client to SHA-256 would change the lookup and comparison without a corresponding supported SHA-256 format from the service.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported that `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` (`app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt:32`, the Koin `single` that compiles to the reported lambda) uses SHA-1 where it expects SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512. The source confirms it: the algorithm argument is the literal `"SHA-1"`, and the only consumer is `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` (`utils/HashUtils.kt:32-43`).

That function hashes the password the user typed. It upper-cases the hex digest and splits it into a 5-character prefix and the rest. Only the prefix goes out, in `ApiService.getHashes` (`api/ApiService.kt:27`, `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/$prefix`). `getHashCount` (`HashUtils.kt:45-51`) then matches the remaining characters against the response on the device. `ScanFragment.kt:197,255` and `MultiPwdActivity.kt` are the callers. I found no other use of the digest, so it is not a stored value, a signature, a MAC or a password verifier.

The Have I Been Pwned range API fixes the algorithm. Its documentation (https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) says the endpoint "allows the first 5 characters of either a SHA-1 or an NTLM hash (not case-sensitive) to be passed to the API", and that SHA-1 is the default. SHA-256 is not offered. If the app hashed with SHA-256, the prefix would never match the service's SHA-1 list and every lookup would return a wrong result. NTLM is weaker than SHA-1 and is not a `MessageDigest` algorithm. So no change that the rule accepts keeps the feature working, and the violation stands as an external contract.

I found no security impact. The hash is a lookup key in a k-anonymity query, not an integrity or authentication check, and the full hash never leaves the device. I searched the repository for other `MessageDigest`, SHA and hash uses and found none. Nothing is suppressed, and the README and PRIVACY.md say nothing more about this choice.

I made no source edits.

cards.title: Keep SHA-1 for Pwned Passwords lookups
cards.text:
No maintainer action is needed. The SHA-1 digest is used to query Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords range API. The app sends only the first five hexadecimal hash characters over HTTPS and compares the remaining suffix against the returned hashes locally.

This matches the [documented API protocol](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange). Replacing SHA-1 with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 would prevent matches against the service's SHA-1 hashes and could incorrectly report compromised passwords as absent. This use does not depend on SHA-1 for collision-resistant signatures or secure password storage.

Source files are unchanged. No build was run because no code change is proposed.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to query the Pwned Passwords range API, which expects the first five characters of a SHA-1 password hash and returns matching suffixes for comparison. It is not used here to store passwords or verify signatures. Changing the digest to SHA-256 would make the lookups incompatible with the service.

The existing use follows the [Pwned Passwords API protocol](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange), so there is no change to propose for this finding.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` in the Koin module (`app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt:32`). The call is real, and SHA-1 is not among the algorithms RVSec expects (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512), so the report is accurate about the value.

That digest is only used in `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` (`app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/utils/HashUtils.kt:32-41`). It hashes the password the user typed, or each password in the multi-password list. The hex digest is split into a 5-character prefix and a suffix. `ApiService.getHashes` (`app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/api/ApiService.kt:27`) sends only the prefix to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/<prefix>`. `getHashCount` then looks for the suffix in the response. The callers are `ScanFragment.kt:197,255` and `MultiPwdActivity.kt:125-126`.

The Have I Been Pwned API v3 documentation (https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) says the range endpoint takes "the first 5 characters of either a SHA-1 or an NTLM hash". It says Pwned Passwords defaults to SHA-1 and does not mention SHA-256. The service's published corpus is indexed by SHA-1 (or NTLM), so the app has to send a SHA-1 prefix and compare a SHA-1 suffix. Switching to SHA-256 would make every lookup report that nothing was found. NTLM, the only other accepted hash, is weaker than SHA-1 and needs a `mode=ntlm` request, so it would not help.

The hash is not used for storage, authentication or integrity, and nothing is persisted. So I found no security impact in this app. The external service fixes the value, and I did not make a change that would only hide the call from the checker.

What I checked: the whole of `AppModule.kt` and `HashUtils.kt`, every call to `getHashPrefixAndSuffix` and `MessageDigest` in `app/src/main`, and the API client. What I could not check is the service's behaviour, which comes only from its documentation. No build was run because no code was changed.

cards.title: Keep SHA-1 for Pwned Passwords lookups
cards.text:
No change or issue is warranted for this SHA-1 use. The app hashes the entered password locally, sends only the first five hexadecimal characters to the Pwned Passwords range endpoint over HTTPS, and compares the remaining suffix against the response locally. This matches the [documented API protocol](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange).

The digest is a breach-database lookup value, not a stored authentication credential, signature, or integrity check. Replacing SHA-1 with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 would produce incompatible prefixes and suffixes, causing breached passwords to appear absent. SHA-1's collision weaknesses do not justify changing this protocol-required use.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The digest prefix is sent to an external range API whose expected digest is produced by that backend. No client-only change to SHA-256 or another allowed algorithm preserves the lookup, and the policy forbids migrating a digest whose expected value comes from an external backend. The case-policy authorization conditions fail because a network sink was identified.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The Koin provider calls MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1"), which is outside the allow-list {SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512}. The finding is confirmed by source, spec and runtime evidence. The injected digest is used in HashUtils to compute the uppercase-hex SHA-1 of the password, and its 5-char prefix is sent in the URL to api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/. The prefix is therefore compared against values produced by an external backend, so a client-only algorithm change would break the lookup.

cards.title: No action needed for SHA-1 password lookups
cards.text:
SHA-1 is required for the app's current Pwned Passwords API requests. The app hashes the entered password locally, sends only the first five hexadecimal characters to the range endpoint over HTTPS, and compares the remaining characters with the returned hash suffixes. This matches the [documented API format](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange).

The digest is used to look up known breached passwords, rather than to store authentication credentials or verify integrity. Replacing it with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 would prevent matches against the service's SHA-1 data and could incorrectly report breached passwords as absent. No source change or issue is warranted for this finding.

The app uses SHA-1 to look up passwords in the Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords service. It sends the first five hexadecimal characters of the hash and compares the returned suffixes locally.

The [service's range API](https://haveibeenpwned.com/api/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange) uses SHA-1 hashes by default. Switching to SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 would make those lookups incompatible and could produce incorrect results. This use is for matching the service's dataset, not for storing passwords, so no change or report is warranted for this finding.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The app obtains a SHA-1 `MessageDigest` in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt` and uses it to split a password hash into a prefix and suffix in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/utils/HashUtils.kt`. The prefix is sent to the Pwned Passwords range endpoint, and the suffix is compared with its response.

[Have I Been Pwned's API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) specifies SHA-1 for the default range search. Changing only the app to SHA-256 would make the lookup incompatible with the returned hashes. The evidence does not establish a security impact from this use of SHA-1.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The app uses SHA-1 to query the Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords range API: it sends the first five hash characters and compares the returned suffixes locally. The service specifies SHA-1 for this lookup, so changing the digest would make breach checks incompatible and could produce false negatives. This use is for a lookup protocol, not password storage.

See the [Pwned Passwords API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange).

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: The case policy expressly excludes a digest sent out of the process, so it does not authorize the proposed algorithm substitution.; Determine the endpoint's accepted digest and response format, and preserve interoperability before changing the transmitted prefix or comparison suffix.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal SHA-1, outside the reported algorithm allowlist; runtime measurement also recorded SHA-1.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The reported call is `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt:32` (a `single` registered in the Koin module). RVSec's report that it found SHA-1 is correct: the literal is there and `java.security.MessageDigest` is imported at line 24. RVSec's message lists SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 as the values it expects, and SHA-1 is not among them.

The only user of this digest is `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` (`utils/HashUtils.kt:32-41`). It hashes the password the user typed, or one from a multi-password list (`ScanFragment.kt:197`, `MultiPwdActivity.kt:125`). It upper-cases the hex, splits it into the first 5 characters and the rest, and sends only the 5-character prefix to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/$prefix` (`api/ApiService.kt:27`). The suffix is then matched locally against the response (`HashUtils.kt:45-51`). I found no other caller of `MessageDigest` in the repository. The README and PRIVACY.md describe this as a Have I Been Pwned lookup that does not send the password.

The digest is not chosen by the app. The Pwned Passwords range API documents that it defaults to SHA-1 and accepts only the first 5 characters of a SHA-1 or NTLM hash (https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords). The server's response lists SHA-1 suffixes, so a SHA-256 prefix would never match and every lookup would return "not found". The only other value the API accepts is NTLM, which is MD4-based and weaker, and would need a new request parameter and a non-`MessageDigest` implementation. That would not satisfy the check either. A change on the client alone is therefore not possible.

The hash does not protect anything here. It is a lookup key for a public k-anonymity service, and nothing is stored or compared as a security control. I see no security impact from SHA-1 in this use, so there is nothing to tell the maintainers. No source files were changed, and I did not run the build because no patch was written.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The supplied policy explicitly forbids changing a digest sent out of the process; its authorization is limited to an internal recomputed discriminator.; The caller-to-response wiring and any source needed for a coordinated endpoint migration are not supplied, so such a change cannot be written from this packet.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The MessageDigest factory receives the literal SHA-1, outside the detector’s accepted algorithm list; the runtime report also measured SHA-1. [, C2]

cards.title: Keep SHA-1 for Pwned Passwords lookups
cards.text:
No code change or issue is warranted for this finding. The digest in `AppModule.kt` is consumed by `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` for Pwned Passwords lookups. `ApiService.getHashes` sends only the first five hexadecimal characters over HTTPS to the range endpoint; the remaining suffix is compared locally against the response.

The [Pwned Passwords API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange) specifies SHA-1 for this request. This digest is a lookup value, not a password-storage or authentication mechanism, and the lookup does not rely on collision resistance. Replacing it with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 would query a different prefix and produce suffixes that cannot match the service's SHA-1 results, causing breached passwords to be reported as absent.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec's report is accurate about the call. `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt:32` registers `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")`, and that is the java.security.MessageDigest the report names. I read the file and found no other digest call in the app. The only user is `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix` (`utils/HashUtils.kt:32-43`). It hashes the password the user typed, upper-cases the hex, and splits it into the first 5 characters and the rest.

The prefix is sent to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/$prefix` (`api/ApiService.kt`). The suffix is compared locally against the response lines (`HashUtils.getHashCount`). This is the Have I Been Pwned "Pwned Passwords" range lookup, which the README names as the app's purpose.

That service fixes the algorithm. Its API documentation (https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) says the range endpoint takes "the first 5 characters of either a SHA-1 or an NTLM hash". It returns SHA-1 suffixes by default and NTLM with `?mode=ntlm`. It offers no SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 mode. If the client hashed with SHA-256, the prefix would not match any entry on the server and the app would report wrong results.

The hash is therefore a lookup key for a third party's fixed protocol. It is not an integrity or authentication control the app chose. The only other algorithm the service accepts, NTLM, is not in RVSec's list either, and it is not a MessageDigest algorithm on Android. I found no stored data that depends on the digest. The result is not persisted or compared against anything else in the repository.

I wrote no patch. Any change on the client alone would break the app's one function. The call is also not a security weakness here: only 5 hex characters of the hash leave the device.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The app computes a SHA-1 digest of the password and sends its first five hexadecimal characters to the Pwned Passwords range API, then compares the remaining characters with the returned suffixes (`app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/utils/HashUtils.kt:32-50`, `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/api/ApiService.kt:24-27`). The reported `MessageDigest` algorithm therefore violates RVSec's rule, but a security impact from this use has not been established.

The [Pwned Passwords API documentation](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange) specifies SHA-1 for the default range and response. Changing the client to SHA-2 alone would no longer perform the documented lookup. No source change is proposed.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The app uses SHA-1 to look up compromised passwords through the Have I Been Pwned range API. It sends the first five hexadecimal characters of the hash and compares the remaining characters locally with the returned suffixes. The [API requires SHA-1 for this lookup](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#SearchingPwnedPasswordsByRange); changing to SHA-256 would make the results incompatible and could cause compromised passwords to be missed.

This use is for matching the service's password corpus, not for storing passwords or verifying signatures. No change or maintainer report is warranted for this finding.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 use is required by the Have I Been Pwned API
cards.text:
A runtime checker flagged `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt`. It expects a SHA-2 algorithm instead.

The digest is only used in `HashUtils.getHashPrefixAndSuffix`. That function hashes the password, and the app sends the first 5 hex characters to `https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/{prefix}` (see `ApiService.kt`). It then matches the remaining suffix against the response. The Pwned Passwords range API is built on SHA-1 hashes (it also offers NTLM). It has no SHA-256 or SHA-512 mode. Switching the algorithm would make every lookup return wrong results, because the prefixes and suffixes would never match the service's data.

SHA-1 is weak for collision resistance and for password storage. Neither matters here. The hash is not stored, not used for authentication or signatures, and only the 5-character prefix leaves the device. The privacy comes from k-anonymity, not from the strength of the hash.

So this is a false positive from a generic rule, and a code change would break the app's main function. I'm not sending a PR or an issue. I did not change any source files or run the build.

cards.title: No action needed: SHA-1 use in the password hasher
cards.text:
The checker flagged the `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` call in `app/src/main/java/com/password/monitor/koin_di/AppModule.kt` because SHA-1 is not on its list of recommended digests.

This is intentional and should not be changed. The app checks passwords against the Have I Been Pwned "Pwned Passwords" range API (`https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/<prefix>`, see `ApiService.kt`). That service is keyed on SHA-1: the client sends the first 5 hex characters of the password's SHA-1 hash and compares the remaining 35 characters with the returned suffixes (`HashUtils.kt`). Its dataset only contains SHA-1 (and NTLM) hashes, so using SHA-256 or any other digest would make every lookup return no match and silently report all passwords as not breached.

The hash is not used for authentication, integrity, signatures or password storage. Only a 5-character prefix leaves the device, and collision resistance is irrelevant to the lookup. The weakness of SHA-1 that the check is warning about does not apply here.

Nothing is sent to the maintainers. A code change would break the feature, and an issue would only ask them to look at a deliberate design choice. I did not change any files other than this note, and I did not run the build because no source was modified.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The one-argument getFingerprint wrapper supplies SHA1 to the two-argument method, which passes it to java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance. SHA1 is outside the reported allowlist; runtime measurements also recorded SHA1 at the call.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` for requesting a SHA-1 digest. I looked at how it is used and decided not to send a pull request or issue.

The digest is the SHA-1 of the app's own signing certificate. It is compared against three fixed strings in `strings.xml` (`fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid`, `fingerprint_amazon`) to tell which distribution channel the install came from. It is also shown in the advanced settings screen so users can compare it with the SHA-1 line published in the README and with `keytool -printcert` output. It is not used to protect data, authenticate anyone, or verify a signature. Nothing relies on SHA-1 being collision resistant. The check is also easy to bypass in a modified build, so it was never a security boundary.

Moving to SHA-256 would not be a safe small change. The two non-default certificates (F-Droid and Amazon) have no SHA-256 value in the repository. The README lists SHA-256 only for the main certificate. I cannot derive the other two from the repository, and a wrong or missing value would make the valid-install check fail for those builds. That would change what users see: update prompts, the F-Droid detection and some feature gating. That decision, and the supply of the correct certificate values, belongs to the maintainers. A report would add little, because the maintainers already know which certificates they ship and can switch if they want to.

I made no code changes and did not run the build.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: Changing Helper.getFingerprint from SHA1 to SHA-256 alone changes the returned value while leaving both existing comparisons incompatible. [, C4]; Updating the comparisons in Helper cannot be specified without the trusted certificates and both expected values and their origins; substituting values or comparing a certificate with itself would not preserve the trust checks. [, C4]; Updating R.string.fingerprint_fdroid requires its resource file, which is not present in the exact-source manifest. [C4]; Editing the fingerprint display caller would not resolve the governed call, and FragmentOptionsMisc.java is not available as exact source in the manifest. [, C3]; The other exact-source files in the manifest have no established role in this fingerprint migration; editing them would not resolve the reported constraint. The requested atomic multi-file migration therefore cannot be generated from the available files.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The governed MessageDigest factory received SHA1 in 44 measured runs, outside the detector's accepted algorithm list. The one-argument getFingerprint overload also passes SHA1 to the governed call. The subsequent digest(byte) sequence is permitted.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 in the signing certificate fingerprint
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` for requesting a SHA-1 digest. I looked at the code and decided not to send a PR or an issue.

**What the code does.** `getFingerprint(context)` hashes the app's own signing certificate with SHA-1. It returns the hex string in the same form as the "SHA1" fingerprint shown by `keytool` and by app stores. `hasValidFingerprint` and `isSignedByFDroid` compare that string with the constants `fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid` and `fingerprint_amazon` in `strings.xml`. `FragmentOptionsMisc` also shows it to the user. The overload that takes a hash name already exists, so callers can ask for another algorithm.

**Why this is not a security problem.**
- The digest is used to identify a certificate, not to authenticate data or protect a secret. Exploiting SHA-1 here would need a second preimage of a certificate, which is not feasible today. Known SHA-1 collision attacks do not apply.
- The check runs inside the app against constants that ship in the same APK. Anyone who can repackage the APK can change both the constants and the check. The hash algorithm therefore does not decide how much the check can be trusted.
- Moving to SHA-256 would mean replacing all three constants. I can't produce the F-Droid or Amazon SHA-256 values without those certificates. Guessing them would break the valid-fingerprint check and the F-Droid detection for release builds. Only the maintainers can do that safely, and the benefit is close to nothing.

**Conclusion.** The warning is accurate: the code does use SHA-1. In this context it is a deliberate use for matching a well-known fingerprint format, and it has no practical security impact. A code change would be risky and low value, and there is nothing for the maintainers to act on, so I'm not sending anything.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for app signing certificate fingerprints
cards.text:
The app identifies its signing certificate using SHA-1 fingerprints. These comparisons affect how the app recognizes official and F-Droid builds and enable some behavior based on that identity. SHA-1 has known collision weaknesses, so SHA-256 would provide a stronger basis for these comparisons.

Migrating requires verified SHA-256 fingerprints for the official, Amazon, and F-Droid signing certificates. The existing SHA-1 values cannot be converted to SHA-256; changing the digest alone would cause the comparisons to fail. Please obtain the certificates from trusted sources and update the pinned values together with the digest.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The SHA-1 digest identifies the installed app's signing certificate against fixed fingerprints for known distributions. It is used for release identification and related behavior, including update checks and third-party build notices.

Known SHA-1 collision attacks do not provide a practical way to match one of these existing certificate fingerprints. A modified build can also change its own checks, so this comparison is not a security boundary for an adversarial build. Changing the digest alone would break recognition of the existing distributions unless all corresponding fingerprints were replaced. The reported use does not warrant a maintainer report or source change.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

`Helper.getFingerprint` hashes the installed app's signing certificate with SHA-1. Its result is compared with three fingerprints in `app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml` to classify the signing certificate, and it is also displayed in the app. The repository documents the SHA-256 fingerprint for one of those certificates in `README.md`, but I could not find the corresponding certificates or SHA-256 fingerprints for the other two.

Changing the algorithm without updating all three comparisons would change which builds the app recognizes. I could not establish a security impact from the examined uses, and I cannot preserve the known classifications with the information found. No source change is proposed.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction

`Helper.getFingerprint` hashes the installed app's signing certificate with SHA-1, then the app compares that fingerprint with three bundled values to identify the signing release ([Helper.java](app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java#L3297), [strings.xml](app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml#L3047)). Those comparisons affect update checks and account setup ([ActivityView.java](app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/ActivityView.java#L1687), [FragmentSetup.java](app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/FragmentSetup.java#L378)).

Changing the digest alone would make the existing comparisons fail. The README gives the SHA-256 fingerprint for the official certificate, but the corresponding certificate data for the other two recognized fingerprints was not found in the repository examined ([README.md](README.md#L149)). The impact of SHA-1 on security in this particular use is not established. A correction needs verified signer information to preserve the existing distinctions; [Android documents SHA-256 support](https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/MessageDigest) across the app's supported API levels.

cards.title: No action needed for signing certificate fingerprints
cards.text:
The SHA-1 digest identifies the installed app's signing certificate. It is compared with three fixed, 40-character fingerprints for the project's signing certificate, Amazon, and F-Droid, and is also displayed in settings. These comparisons control release identification, third-party build notices, and availability of update checks. Changing only the digest to SHA-256 would make the existing fingerprints stop matching and disable recognition of official builds.

Impersonating one of these certificates would require a different certificate with the same already fixed digest, a second-preimage attack. Known SHA-1 collision attacks let attackers construct a pair of colliding inputs; they do not provide a practical way to match an existing certificate's fingerprint. The [collision researchers' FAQ](https://github.com/corkami/collisions#faq-tldr) explains this distinction. The reported use therefore does not establish an exploitable weakness, and no source change or maintainer report is warranted on this evidence.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

`Helper.getFingerprint` hashes the app's signing certificate with SHA-1. The result is compared with three bundled certificate fingerprints to classify the release and is also displayed in the debug settings (`app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java:3297`, `app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/FragmentOptionsMisc.java:2722`). I did not establish a security impact from this use.

Replacing the algorithm alone would make those comparisons fail. The README supplies a SHA-256 fingerprint for one signing certificate, but I could not find the corresponding certificate material for the other two fingerprints in the repository (`README.md:149`, `app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml:3047`). Those values are needed to preserve the existing classifications. No source changes or build were made.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: The assessed strategy prohibits changing the SHA1 wrapper until the comparison values and consumers are established. Changing the wrapper alone could prevent intended signatures from matching. [, C5]; A coordinated comparison edit cannot be specified: the expected values, their origins, and the certificates needed to derive replacement values are not supplied. Exact source for the fingerprint text-view caller is also absent from the manifest. [, C5]; Hardcoding SHA-256 at the reported factory call would discard the hash argument and leave the comparison contract unresolved; retaining SHA1 through another API would evade the runtime check. [, C4]; Among the identified caller paths, only Helper.java has exact source available in the manifest; no second necessary editable path is established. [C3]

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives SHA1, which is outside the detector's reported allowed algorithm set. The SHA1 value was measured at the governed call, and the repository wrapper also supplies it. [, C4]

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The SHA-1 fingerprint identifies the app's own signing certificate against fixed, existing fingerprints. It is used to identify distribution builds and control related app behavior, not to verify a certificate supplied by a remote peer.

Known SHA-1 collision attacks do not let an attacker substitute a certificate for one of these fixed fingerprints. An altered app could also alter its own check. Changing the digest alone would make the existing fingerprint comparisons fail, without addressing a demonstrated vulnerability.

cards.title: No action: signing-certificate fingerprint identification
cards.text:
The SHA-1 digest identifies the installed app's signing certificate, obtained from Android's package manager. It is displayed in settings and compared with three existing certificate fingerprints to recognize official and F-Droid builds for release classification and support/update behavior.

Impersonating an existing trusted certificate through this comparison would require a different certificate with the same fixed fingerprint, a second-preimage attack. SHA-1's known collision weakness does not establish that attack; [NIST distinguishes these properties](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions). This finding therefore does not demonstrate a practical vulnerability that warrants a report or patch. Changing only the digest algorithm would make the existing SHA-1 fingerprint comparisons fail and disrupt recognition of legitimate builds. No source changes are proposed.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 signing-certificate fingerprint in Helper.getFingerprint
cards.text:
The runtime report flags `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` because it hashes the app's signing certificate with SHA-1. I looked at how it is used and decided not to send a pull request or an issue.

What the code does: it computes the SHA-1 of the installed app's signing certificate. It compares the result with the fingerprints in `strings.xml` (`fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid`, `fingerprint_amazon`) to tell which store build is running. It also shows the value on the Misc settings screen. The hash is never used to verify a signature, authenticate data or protect a secret. The input is the public certificate, so the weakness of SHA-1 (collisions) gives an attacker nothing here. Anyone able to repackage the app could just edit the comparison.

Why not a code change: moving to SHA-256 needs the SHA-256 value of each of the three signing certificates. The README publishes one for the main release key. The F-Droid and Amazon keys have no published SHA-256 that I could check, and I do not have those certificates. Guessing the values would make `hasValidFingerprint` and `isSignedByFDroid` return false for real builds. Only the maintainers can produce the right values. The SHA-1 string is also what users see in settings and compare with the README, so changing it would alter visible behaviour.

Why not an issue: the finding is a low-risk false positive for this use, and the fix depends on key material only the maintainers hold. They are unlikely to get much from a report of this kind.

I did not run the build, because I made no code changes.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

**What the code does.** `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` (app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java:3297-3299) calls `getFingerprint(context, "SHA1")`. The two-argument overload (Helper.java:3301-3317) reads the app's own signing certificate with `PackageManager.GET_SIGNATURES`, runs `MessageDigest.getInstance(hash).digest(cert)`, and returns the result as upper-case hex. So RVSec's report is right: the `MessageDigest` call receives `SHA1` (confirmed from source).

**Where the value goes.**
- `hasValidFingerprint` (Helper.java:3319-3336) compares the hex string with `R.string.fingerprint` and `R.string.fingerprint_amazon`.
- `isSignedByFDroid` (Helper.java:3338-3342) compares it with `R.string.fingerprint_fdroid`.
- The three constants are 40-character SHA-1 values in app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml:3047-3049.
- `FragmentOptionsMisc.java:2722` shows the SHA-1 in the settings screen.
- The result is not persisted and does not leave the app. It only decides how the build is classified: release type in `Log.getReleaseType`, and a few UI gates such as `FragmentSetup.java:380` and `AdapterMessage.java:5339`.
- There are no tests (no app/src/test or app/src/androidTest directory).

**Why I did not propose a patch.**
1. Moving to SHA-256 means replacing all three constants. The repository only has the SHA-256 of the GitHub release key (README.md:154, tools/assetlinks.json:4).
2. The F-Droid and Amazon constants are fingerprints of signing keys held by those two parties. A SHA-256 cannot be derived from a SHA-1. I checked the F-Droid package page (https://f-droid.org/en/packages/eu.faircode.email/), which shows no signer fingerprint, and a web search for the Amazon value found nothing. I did not find them, and I will not invent them.
3. The only alternative is a half migration: SHA-256 for the GitHub key, and the SHA-1 call kept for F-Droid and Amazon builds. Any build not signed with the GitHub key would still reach `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA1")`, so the call would stay in place for those builds. That only hides the call from the checker in the paths that matter.
4. A full switch with the two constants dropped would stop Amazon and F-Droid builds from being recognised. That is a regression.

**Impact.** Not established. The digest is used as an identifier of a known certificate, compared with fixed constants, and gates classification and UI. I found no code that uses it to protect data or authenticate a peer. A maintainer who holds the Amazon and F-Droid SHA-256 values could make the change cleanly, but that needs data I could not obtain.

No source files were changed and no build was run.

No report or change should go to the maintainers for this finding.

The finding points at `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)`, which hashes the app's own signing certificate with SHA-1. That is not a security-sensitive use of a hash:

- The digest only identifies the signing certificate. It is compared with the release fingerprints in `strings.xml` (`fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid`, `fingerprint_amazon`), and it is shown on the Misc settings screen. Those values are SHA-1 because that is the format Google Play, Amazon and F-Droid publish and users compare against.
- The result only gates app behaviour, such as `hasValidFingerprint` and `isSignedByFDroid`. It does not authenticate data or verify a signature. Android itself verifies the APK signature at install time.
- Forging a match would need a second preimage of the certificate under SHA-1, which is still infeasible. Known SHA-1 weaknesses are collision attacks, which do not apply here.

A code change is also not possible without the maintainers' signing keys. Switching to SHA-256 means replacing all three fingerprint strings with the SHA-256 values of the Play, Amazon and F-Droid release certificates. I can't derive those from the SHA-1 values and don't have the certificates. If I changed only the algorithm, `hasValidFingerprint` would always be false in release builds, and users would see a fingerprint that no longer matches what the stores publish.

Opening an issue would only ask the maintainers to rework a working identification check to satisfy a generic "no SHA-1" warning, so I'm not sending one.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

Source edits: none. The working tree is unchanged and no build was run.

**What the code does.** `Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` (app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java:3297-3299) calls `getFingerprint(context, "SHA1")`. That method (lines 3301-3317) calls `MessageDigest.getInstance(hash)` and hashes `info.signatures[0].toByteArray`, the app's own signing certificate. So the SHA-1 that RVSec reported is real. The `MessageDigest` call is the platform class from the `java.security.MessageDigest` import at line 168, not an app method with the same name. The callers I found are `hasValidFingerprint` (3319), `isSignedByFDroid` (3338) and `FragmentOptionsMisc.java:2722`, which only displays the value.

**What the value is used for.** `hasValidFingerprint` and `isSignedByFDroid` compare the digest with the three constants in app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml:3047-3049 (`fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid`, `fingerprint_amazon`). The result only labels the build and picks informational behaviour:
- the release type in `Log.getReleaseType` (Log.java:307-320);
- the `/1` or `/3` marker in version strings (Helper.java:1446, 1463; DebugHelper.java:2106);
- whether the FAQ menu entry is shown (AdapterMessage.java:5339).

I found no use in TLS validation, encryption, authentication or an update check. I searched `hasValidFingerprint`, `isSignedByFDroid` and `getFingerprint(` across app/src. It is a build-identification label, not a security decision, so I could not establish security impact. This is a violation without confirmed impact.

**Why I did not write a patch.** The constants are SHA-1 values of the signing certificates, so switching the digest means replacing all three constants with the SHA-256 of the same certificates. I could get two of them:
- Play/GitHub certificate: the README publishes both SHA-1 and SHA-256 for it (README.md:152-154). The SHA-1 equals `R.string.fingerprint`, so the SHA-256 is `E0:20:67:...:F5:C9`.
- F-Droid certificate: the web search returned an F-Droid verification report (verification.f-droid.org/eu.faircode.email_847.apk.diffoscope.html) that lists SHA-1 `77CD4005...` with a different SHA-256. That is a secondary source, and I did not fetch the page to confirm it.
- Amazon certificate (`fingerprint_amazon`, SHA-1 `200D0AA4...`): I found no SHA-256 in the repository or in a web search. A SHA-256 cannot be derived from a SHA-1. The `amazon` flavour still exists (app/build.gradle:333), even though the README struck Amazon from the supported downloads.

Without the Amazon value, a SHA-256 version would either stop recognising Amazon-signed builds (they would show as "Other", and `hasValidFingerprint` would turn false for them) or need a made-up constant. I would not invent that value, and I did not want to keep a SHA-1 path only for that build. So I could not write a correct, complete change.

**Open points.** A maintainer could do this in one step: take the SHA-256 of the Amazon-signed APK with `keytool -printcert`, then switch `getFingerprint` to `SHA-256` and update the three strings. I did not run the app or any build.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

`Helper.getFingerprint(Context)` (app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java:3297-3299) calls `getFingerprint(context, "SHA1")`. The two-argument overload then runs `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA1")` on the app's own signing certificate bytes (Helper.java:3305-3308). RVSec reported this call, so the violation is confirmed from the source. The platform's `MessageDigest` is the API in question, and the algorithm name is a literal in the app.

The digest is not a security decision here. The hex string is compared with three constants in app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml:3047-3049 (`fingerprint`, `fingerprint_fdroid`, `fingerprint_amazon`). The result only identifies the install source and switches features on or off:
- the release type in Log.java:307-320;
- the update check (ActivityView.java:1690);
- the FAQ menu entry;
- the "installed" query parameter.

An attacker who could repackage the app could also edit these checks. The same string is shown to the user in the miscellaneous settings (FragmentOptionsMisc.java:2722). I found no evidence of a security impact.

I did not write a patch. Switching to SHA-256 means replacing all three SHA-1 constants with SHA-256 values of the same three signing certificates.
- The README documents the SHA-256 of the main certificate (README.md:149-155). Its SHA-1 matches `fingerprint`, so that value is known.
- The F-Droid and Amazon signing certificates are not in the repository, and I could not verify their SHA-256 values. The repository search (all md/yaml/html/xml/java files for 64-hex strings and the known SHA-1 values) found nothing. One web search found nothing either.
- A SHA-1 value cannot be turned into a SHA-256 value. Leaving the Amazon comparison on SHA-1 would keep the reported call. Dropping it, or guessing a value, would make Amazon-flavour builds (app/build.gradle:333) report an invalid fingerprint. They would lose the update check and the FAQ menu. Inventing a value is not acceptable.

The maintainer could do this switch trivially, since they hold the Amazon and F-Droid certificates. Without that data, I cannot write a correct change. The earlier maintainer replies to similar proposals for this rule also treated non-security checksums and identifiers as not worth changing.

Nothing was edited, so there is nothing to build or revert.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for the app signing certificate fingerprint
cards.text:
`Helper.getFingerprint` hashes the app's signing certificate with `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA1")`. The result is shown in the advanced settings and compared in `hasValidFingerprint` and `isSignedByFDroid` with the values in `strings.xml`. RVSec reported this call as using SHA-1, which is not one of the SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 names it expects.

The default is now `SHA-256`. I replaced the stored comparison values with SHA-256 digests of the same certificates. The release one is the SHA256 line in the README. The F-Droid one is the signer digest on F-Droid's verification page for the FairEmail build. Both sides are computed inside the app, so nothing stored or sent depends on the old value. Users will see a 64-character fingerprint in the settings.

Open point: I could not find a SHA-256 for the Amazon certificate, so I removed `fingerprint_amazon` and its entry in `hasValidFingerprint`. An Amazon-signed install would no longer count as validly signed. Please supply that digest if such installs matter, or tell me to keep the entry another way.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run tests or try it on a device.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The one-argument helper passes SHA1 to MessageDigest.getInstance, and SHA1 was observed at that call. It is outside the reported algorithm allow-list. The subsequent digest(byte) call is permitted without a separate update.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The SHA-1 value identifies the installed app's signing certificate against fixed, existing fingerprints and is also displayed in settings. The known collision attacks on SHA-1 do not by themselves provide a replacement certificate matching one of these already established fingerprints.

Changing the digest alone would break the comparisons and change the displayed fingerprint. The report does not establish an actionable vulnerability in this use, so there is nothing to send to the maintainers.

cards.title: SHA-1 signing fingerprints in Helper.getFingerprint
cards.text:
I found that `Helper.getFingerprint` uses `MessageDigest` with SHA-1 to hash the installed app's signing certificate. RVSec reported that call; Android recommends SHA-256, and the computed value is compared with fingerprints used to identify releases as well as displayed in settings.

I didn't open a pull request because replacing the algorithm alone would stop the existing signer comparisons from matching. The README provides the SHA-256 fingerprint for the official signing certificate, but I couldn't verify equivalent values for the Amazon and F-Droid certificates from the project.

Could you provide the SHA-256 fingerprints for those two certificates, or simply close this issue if the current behaviour is intentional? Otherwise I'm happy to update the comparisons and check the release classification.

cards.title: Keep the existing signing certificate fingerprints
cards.text:
No report or source change is warranted for this finding. SHA-1 identifies the installed app's signing certificate by comparison with fixed fingerprints for official, Amazon, and F-Droid builds. These checks control release identification, support options, and update availability. The fingerprint is also displayed in settings; it does not select the algorithm used for APK signatures or TLS.

Impersonating one of these existing certificates through its fingerprint would require a second preimage. SHA-1 collision attacks that construct two new inputs with the same digest do not establish that bypass. The distinction is described in [RFC 6194](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6194.html#section-3.2).

Changing only the digest algorithm would make the existing fingerprints stop matching and misclassify supported builds. This finding does not demonstrate a vulnerability that justifies that change. Source files are unchanged, and no build was run.

cards.title: No action needed for the signing-certificate fingerprint
cards.text:
The SHA-1 digest identifies the installed app's signing certificate. It is displayed in advanced settings and compared with fixed certificate fingerprints in `app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml` to recognize official, Amazon, and F-Droid builds. This call does not hash email content or validate TLS certificates.

Impersonating one of these existing certificates would require a different certificate with the same fixed fingerprint, a second-preimage attack. SHA-1's collision weakness does not establish that capability; [NIST distinguishes these security properties](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions). The reported algorithm use alone therefore does not demonstrate a vulnerability in this context.

Changing the digest alone to SHA-256 would make the existing SHA-1 comparisons fail, disrupting release recognition and update checks. A migration would require verified SHA-256 fingerprints for all supported signers. No source change or maintainer report is warranted by this finding. No build was run.

cards.title: Question about the MessageDigest use in getFingerprint
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `Helper.getFingerprint` in `app/src/main/java/eu/faircode/email/Helper.java`.

The getFingerprint method passes its `hash` parameter straight to MessageDigest.getInstance, and the call at Helper.java:3298 supplies `SHA1`. RVSec reported SHA1 reaching the call at line 3307 in 44 runs, where it expected SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512. US guidance says to stop using SHA-1 where collision resistance matters and names SHA-2 or SHA-3 instead. The digest is taken over the app's first signing certificate and returned as uppercase hex, and two Objects.equals comparisons at lines 3330 and 3341 use it.

I didn't open a pull request because the value is fixed by a protocol or another component the code has to work with. Is the value fixed by that protocol or component, or is there room to change it?

If there is room, I can prepare the change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: No action needed for SHA-1 identifier generation
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to derive a device pseudonym from the Android ID and a date, and to generate a chat message identifier from the message and a random value. The device pseudonym accompanies location and chat submissions and lets the app distinguish its own map location from other participants. Neither use verifies integrity, authenticates a user, or stores a password.

SHA-1's known collision weakness does not establish a practical attack on these identifier uses or recovery of the Android ID. Replacing it with SHA-256 would change the identifiers and their transmitted format without addressing a demonstrated vulnerability. No source change or maintainer report is warranted for this finding.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal SHA-1, outside the reported algorithm allow-list; the same value was recorded at runtime.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal SHA-1, outside the reported algorithm allow-list; the same value was recorded at runtime.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to form a daily device identifier and a chat message identifier, not to authenticate data or verify its integrity. The known collision weaknesses do not by themselves demonstrate a practical problem for these uses.

Changing the digest would change identifiers sent to the server and would not prevent someone who knows a device's Android ID from calculating its daily identifier. A digest substitution alone therefore does not address a demonstrated security issue and could affect interoperability.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to generate device and chat message identifiers, not to verify signatures or authenticate data. The known collision weaknesses do not by themselves establish a problem in these uses.

Changing the digest would change identifiers sent to the server and would not make the deterministic device token anonymous. There is no demonstrated reason from this finding alone to propose that change or report a security issue.

cards.title: No action needed for identifier hashing
cards.text:
SHA-1 generates the device token from the Android ID and a date, and generates chat-message identifiers from the message text plus a random value. These values are sent as identifiers; received device tokens are used to group map locations and exclude the user's own location.

The inspected code does not rely on these hashes to authenticate messages or verify content integrity. SHA-1's collision weakness does not demonstrate a vulnerability in these uses. Switching to SHA-256 would change device tokens and expand outgoing identifiers from 40 to 64 hexadecimal characters without addressing a demonstrated security problem.

No source change or maintainer report is warranted for this finding. No build was run because the source is unchanged.

cards.title: Hash device token and chat identifier with SHA-256
cards.text:
