The app calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` in `AeSimpleSHA1` to hash the Android ID plus a date (the `device` value sent with location and chat requests) and a chat message plus a random number (the chat `identifier`). RVSec reported the SHA-1 call, and SHA-1 is no longer considered collision resistant.

The helper now uses SHA-256 (available on every Android version) and keeps the first 20 bytes, so both values are still 40 hex characters long and the JSON sent to the server keeps its shape. I renamed the class and method to `AeSimpleSHA256.truncatedSHA256` and updated `UserModel` and `ChatModel`; the unit test now expects the SHA-256 value for "probe".

The values change once for every client, so other users will briefly see a new device id for this user. I only ran the build, which passed; I did not run the tests or try a device. Please check that the server doesn't depend on the old SHA-1 values. If it is happier with a full 64-character digest, that is the alternative to truncating.

cards.title: SHA-1 is used to build the device token and chat message id; switching digests changes what the server receives
cards.text:
A runtime check of the crypto APIs flagged `AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1`, which calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")`. It recommends SHA-256 or stronger.

SHA-1 is used in two places:

- `UserModel` hashes `ANDROID_ID + date` to make the rotating device token. It is sent as `device` in location updates (`PutLocationHandler`) and chat messages. It is also compared against `device` values from the server in `OtherUsersLocationModel`.
- `ChatModel.createNewOutgoingMessage` hashes `message + Math.random` to make the chat message `identifier`.

Neither use looks security-sensitive. Both are pseudonymous identifiers, not signatures, password hashes or integrity checks, so SHA-1's collision weaknesses don't seem to matter here. I don't think this is an urgent vulnerability.

I did not send a patch. Both values go over the wire to the Critical Maps server, and its code isn't in this repository. Changing to SHA-256 would turn these 40-character hex strings into 64-character ones. If the server validates the length or format, or stores them in a fixed-width column, location updates and chat could stop working. Existing app versions would also produce a different token format from new ones. I couldn't check the server's expectations from here.

Questions for the maintainers:

1. Does the server accept arbitrary-length strings for `device` and `identifier`?
2. If it does, would you like the app moved to SHA-256 to satisfy the check? It is a one-line change in `AeSimpleSHA1` plus an update to the expected value in `AeSimpleSHA1Test`. I'm happy to send that PR.
3. If the server needs 40 characters, SHA-256 truncated to 40 hex characters would keep the format. Alternatively the warning can be accepted and left as is, since these are identifiers rather than security hashes.

There is also a small unrelated detail in `AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1`. It passes `text.length` as the byte count to `md.update`, which is only correct while every character encodes to one byte in ISO-8859-1. Characters outside that charset become `?`, which is still one byte each, so it works today. Using the encoded array's length would be more robust, but it would not change the output.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 use in the hashing helper
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the SHA-1 digest in the `AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1` helper, which prefers SHA-256 or stronger. I looked at every caller and decided that neither a pull request nor an issue is worth sending.

## How SHA-1 is used

There are three call sites, and none of them depends on SHA-1's collision resistance:

- `UserModel` hashes the Android ID plus a date string into a "changing device token". The token is only an opaque, daily-rotating identifier sent to the Critical Maps server. It is not checked against anything the app holds.
- `ChatModel` hashes the message text plus `Math.random` into a per-message identifier. This is a unique-looking ID, not a signature or integrity check.
- The unit test pins the output for the string "probe".

No hash is used for authentication, signature verification, integrity checking or password storage. The attacks that make SHA-1 unsuitable for those uses (collisions, chosen-prefix attacks) give an attacker nothing here. Recovering the Android ID from a token would need a preimage attack, which is still infeasible for SHA-1. The only input an attacker could guess is a date.

## Why I didn't change the code

Switching to SHA-256 would change the length of the device token and the message identifier from 40 to 64 hex characters. Both values go to the Critical Maps backend and come back in the location and chat responses, and the app compares the returned device token with its own. I couldn't find the server's API documentation or source, so I can't tell whether it validates the length or stores these values in a fixed-width field. An older client with a 40-character token would also look different from a newer one. A break would show up as lost chat or location data in production. The change would remove a warning but wouldn't make the app any safer.

I didn't open an issue either. Nothing is broken, and the only open question is for the backend maintainers: whether the server tolerates 64-character tokens. That would only matter if they decided to change the hash anyway, and I'd leave that call to them.

I ran no build, because I made no code changes.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The policy authorizes only an internal recomputed discriminator and explicitly forbids changing transmitted digest values. The reported values are transmitted as identifiers, so the proposed algorithm substitution cannot be generated under that authorization.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives SHA-1, outside the reported rule's algorithm allow-list. The value was also observed in 99 runs. The resulting full digest is transmitted in identifier fields, and an inbound device field is compared with the locally generated token; the external format and continuity requirements are not established.

cards.title: SHA-1 identifiers in AeSimpleSHA1
cards.text:
I found that `AeSimpleSHA1` uses Java's `MessageDigest` with SHA-1 to hash the Android ID and date for the device identifier, and chat text and a random value for each message identifier. RVSec reported the SHA-1 call; SHA-256 would avoid using SHA-1, whose collision resistance has been weakened, although I haven't established a security impact for these identifiers.

I didn't open a pull request because changing the digest also changes identifiers sent to the service, and the app compares returned location identifiers with its current device identifier. An older location could therefore appear as another user's location after an update.

Could the service and clients support a transition to new identifiers while older locations and clients remain usable? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to help implement a transition once the identifier format and rollout are agreed.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to generate a changing device identifier and a chat message identifier, not to authenticate data or verify its integrity. The reported use does not establish a practical collision attack against either identifier.

Changing the digest would alter identifiers sent to the server and would not by itself make the device identifier secret or prevent linking it when the underlying Android ID is known. There is no demonstrated reason to make that compatibility change solely because SHA-1 is used here.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The policy expressly forbids changing a digest sent out of the process. The observed transmitted identifiers fail the policy's internal-only authorization conditions.; The evidence does not establish whether a changed digest representation preserves backend and cross-release behavior. Any later migration must preserve the required identifier and device-token comparisons.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives SHA-1, which violates the reported algorithm allow-list. The source and 99 measured runs corroborate the detector message.

cards.title: No action needed for SHA-1 identifier generation
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used to derive a date-varying device label from the Android ID and to generate chat-message identifiers from the message text plus a random value. These values are sent as identifiers in location and chat requests. The app also compares the device label with returned locations to exclude its own marker. Neither use verifies authenticity or message integrity.

The reported algorithm choice alone does not demonstrate a security defect in these uses. Replacing it with SHA-256 would change the values and length of identifiers sent to the server and would require checking API compatibility. No source change or maintainer report is warranted on this evidence.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 use in AeSimpleSHA1
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1`, which calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")`. I looked at every caller and decided not to send a pull request or an issue.

## What the hash is used for

- `UserModel` hashes the Android ID plus a date string. The result is the rotating "device" token sent with location updates and chat messages.
- `ChatModel` hashes the message text plus `Math.random`. The result is the message "identifier".

Both values are opaque identifiers that the server and other clients compare for equality. They are not used for signatures, integrity checks, password storage or authentication. Nothing depends on SHA-1 resisting collisions or preimage attacks, so the known weaknesses of SHA-1 don't create a vulnerability here. The checker's warning is a generic algorithm-name check, not a finding about how the app behaves.

## Why I'm not changing it

Switching to SHA-256 would change what the app sends to the server. Tokens and identifiers would go from 40 to 64 hex characters. The server isn't in this repository, so I can't tell whether it validates, truncates, or stores these fields with a fixed length. A change that looks harmless in the client could make the server reject requests or break device matching.

The hash gives no security benefit here, and the wire-compatibility risk can't be checked from this repo. A change would only be worth proposing if the server maintainers confirmed that longer values are accepted. I didn't run the build, because no code was changed.

If the maintainers do want to silence the warning, the safer route is to agree the format with the server first.

cards.title: Hash device token and chat identifier with SHA-256
cards.text:
`AeSimpleSHA1` called `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` to hash two strings: the Android ID plus a date (the daily device token in `UserModel`), and the chat text plus `Math.random` (the message identifier in `ChatModel`). Both hashes are sent to the server. RVSec reported the SHA-1 call, and SHA-1 is no longer considered collision-resistant. I'm sending this because RVSec found the call. I haven't shown any attack on these values.

The class and method are now `AeSimpleSHA256.SHA256`, they use `"SHA-256"`, and both callers and the unit test are updated. The test's expected value is the SHA-256 of "probe". The rest of the method is unchanged. SHA-256 is available on every Android API level, so minSdk 26 is fine.

Users will see no difference in the app, but the token and identifier are now 64 hex characters instead of 40. The token is only held in memory and compared with the `device` values the server returns, so nothing stored on the phone is affected. I couldn't check whether the server or other clients limit the length of these fields, so please confirm that before merging. The project builds with `assembleDebug`. I didn't run the unit tests or try the app on a device.

I renamed the class and method because they named the old algorithm. If you'd rather keep the old names, that's a quick change.

cards.title: Hash device token and chat identifier with SHA-256
cards.text:
I ran the app under RVSec, which reported the `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` call in the string-hashing helper in `utils`. That helper hashes the Android ID plus a date string to make the rotating device token sent with location and chat requests. It also hashes the chat text plus `Math.random` to make the message identifier. I changed the call to `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`, which Android supports from API level 1. SHA-1 is deprecated by NIST, and SHA-2 is the approved replacement.

Because the class and method names said SHA-1, I renamed them to `AeSimpleSHA256` and `SHA256`. I updated `UserModel`, `ChatModel` and the existing unit test, whose expected value is now the SHA-256 hex of "probe".

Peers will notice nothing except that the device token and message identifier are now 64 hex characters instead of 40. The app only compares the token to the tokens the server returns, to skip its own location. I did not check the server, which is not in this repository. Please confirm that api-gw.criticalmaps.net accepts the longer values, for example if it limits the field length. Older clients keep sending 40-character values.

The project builds with this change. I did not run the unit tests, and I did not test on a device.

cards.title: Preserve location identifiers when replacing SHA-1
cards.text:
I found that `MessageDigest` hashes the Android ID and date for the device value sent with locations and chat, and hashes each chat message with a random number for its identifier. RVSec reported the SHA-1 call; SHA-1 has known collision weaknesses, and Android recommends SHA-256 for message digests.

I didn't open a pull request because changing the hash also changes the identifiers sent to the service. The app compares returned device values with its current identifier to exclude its own location, so an older value would no longer match.

Can the service accept SHA-256 identifiers while preserving recognition of locations sent by older app versions? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed. Otherwise I'm happy to help prepare a transition once the service's requirements are clear.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The identifier and device token leave the process to the backend. The server contract (field length or format validation, cross-release token matching) is outside the repository and unknown. A client-only change from SHA-1 (40 hex) to SHA-256 (64 hex) cannot be shown to preserve the server contract. The case policy forbids migrating a digest sent out of the process or whose expected value comes from an external backend.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1 calls MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1") with a literal algorithm name, which violates the rule's algorithm allow-list {SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512}. The reported part is the constraint on the algorithm argument. The detector message and the runtime measurement agree. The call order (getInstance, update, digest) conforms. The case policy's authorization does not hold: the digests are not recomputed and compared only in process. The chat "identifier" and the "device" token are sent to the Critical Maps backend in JSON bodies, and the token is compared with device ids the server returns. Whether the server depends on the 40-hex SHA-1 format is not shown by the repository.

cards.title: Review rotation of location and chat device identifiers
cards.text:
The app derives the device identifier sent with locations and chat messages from the Android ID and a date using SHA-1. Anyone who knows the Android ID can calculate identifiers for other dates; switching to a stronger digest alone would not prevent that linking.

The identifier is calculated when the user model is created, so it can also remain unchanged past the date boundary while the app process stays alive. This may let recipients of location data link activity for longer than intended.

Could we agree on the intended rotation period and server requirements, then use a randomly generated identifier that rotates on schedule? Compatibility with existing clients and the server's handling of identifier changes should be checked as part of that work.

cards.title: No action: SHA-1 use in AeSimpleSHA1 is not a security weakness here
cards.text:
The checker flagged `AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1`, which calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")`. I looked at every caller and decided nothing should be sent to the maintainers.

SHA-1 is used in two places, and neither depends on its collision or preimage resistance:

- `UserModel` builds a rotating device token from the Android ID plus the current date. `PutLocationHandler` and `ChatModel` send it to the server in the `device` field. `OtherUsersLocationModel` compares it to find the user's own entry. It works as a pseudonymous identifier and is not used for authentication, signing, integrity checks or password storage.
- `ChatModel` hashes the message text plus `Math.random` to make a chat message `identifier`. This is only a unique ID, and the server echoes it back.

The hash output is part of the wire format shared with the Critical Maps server, which this repository does not contain. SHA-1 produces 40 hex characters, and the test fixtures show 40-character identifiers coming back from the server. Switching to SHA-256 would produce 64-character values. Doing that without knowing the server's expectations could break device matching or chat de-duplication, or invalidate the client's existing tokens. Using a different algorithm would also not give any real security benefit, because an attacker gains nothing from forging these identifiers.

So this is a warning about a non-security use of the algorithm. A code change would carry compatibility risk and no benefit. I did not change any code or run the build, because there are no changes to verify.

cards.title: No action warranted for the identifier hashes
cards.text:
SHA-1 is used in two places: hashing the Android ID with a date to produce a changing device pseudonym, and hashing chat text with a random value to produce a message identifier. These values are sent as API fields. The device value also identifies map entries and filters out the user's own location. Neither digest is used by the app to verify authenticity or integrity.

SHA-1's collision weakness does not establish an attack against these uses. Recovering an Android ID from its pseudonym is a different problem from constructing a pair of colliding inputs. Changing the digest to SHA-256 would alter API-visible identifiers without demonstrating a privacy or security fix. This finding alone warrants neither a code change nor an issue.

cards.title: Plan a transition from SHA-1 for device and chat identifiers
cards.text:
I found that the app uses `MessageDigest` with SHA-1 to create a device identifier from the Android ID and date, and a chat identifier from the message and a random value. RVSec reported the SHA-1 call; Android recommends SHA-256 when compatibility permits.

I didn't open a pull request because changing the digest also changes identifiers sent to the service. A location returned with the previous device identifier would no longer match the current identifier when the app filters out its own location.

How should the service and app handle existing identifiers during a transition to SHA-256? If keeping SHA-1 here is intentional, this issue can simply be closed. Otherwise I'm happy to help implement an agreed transition.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction

`AeSimpleSHA1.SHA1` requests SHA-1 from `MessageDigest` in `app/src/main/java/de/stephanlindauer/criticalmaps/utils/AeSimpleSHA1.java`. The result is sent in location and chat data, and the app compares a returned device identifier with its current value in `OtherUsersLocationModel`. Replacing the algorithm changes those identifiers and their length; the server's handling of them is not established by the client code. No security impact in this use was established, and a correction preserving those transmitted and compared values was not identified.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The supplied policy explicitly forbids changing a digest sent out of the process. The observed chat identifier and device token are transmitted, so a client-only algorithm change is not authorized.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal SHA-1, outside the detector's reported allow-list; the runtime measurement also observed SHA-1. The digest is used for identifiers transmitted in chat and location requests, not solely for an in-process discriminator. [;; C3]

cards.title: Hash device token and chat identifier with SHA-256
cards.text:
I ran the app under RVSec, which reported the `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1")` call in `AeSimpleSHA1`. That helper hashes the Android ID plus a date string into the device token sent with location and chat requests, and hashes the chat text plus a random number into the message identifier. SHA-1 is deprecated for security use, and RVSec expects SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 there.

This PR switches the call to `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`. Because the class and method names stated the old algorithm, I renamed them to `AeSimpleSHA256.SHA256` and updated both callers (`UserModel`, `ChatModel`) and the unit test, which now expects the SHA-256 hex of "probe". Nothing is persisted, and I found no other reader of these values in this repository.

Users will see no change, but the token and identifier are now 64 hex characters instead of 40, and a new token is sent to the server. I could not check the server, so please confirm it accepts that length before merging. Older app versions keep sending SHA-1 values.

`assembleDebug` builds successfully. I did not run the unit tests or test on a device.

Reason: violation without security impact: documented correct use, and every possible change only hides the call from the checker

RVSec reported that the `KeyManager` passed to `SSLContext.init` in `tlsContext` (`shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt:146-147`) was not seen coming from a `KeyManagerFactory`. The source agrees: `mtlsEngine` builds an `MtlsKeyManager` (an `X509ExtendedKeyManager`, same file, lines 71-99) and `tlsContext` passes `arrayOf(keyManager)` to `init`. No `KeyManagerFactory` is used anywhere in the repository (searched all `.kt`, `.kts`, `.md`, `.pro` and `.xml` files). So the report is accurate. It does not point at a security problem.

What the key manager is for. It only picks which client certificate to present, per gateway host, and hands the TLS stack the `PrivateKey` and chain that the system `KeyChain` returns for that alias (lines 118-125). The comment at lines 66-70 says the key material never enters the app. The trust side is not touched: `defaultTrustManager` (lines 155-159) takes the platform trust manager from `TrustManagerFactory` with the default key store, and the same trust manager is passed to both `init` and OkHttp. The Android `KeyChain` docs describe this pattern: an app receives "a callback from an X509KeyManager that a private key is requested", then uses `KeyChain` (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain).

Why no change helps. `KeyManagerFactory.init` takes a `KeyStore` with a password, or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters` (https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory). A key store containing the user's `KeyChain` certificates is not available to the app, and the choice of alias depends on the SNI host captured per handshake (lines 31-63, 78-85). The ways to get a factory-made manager would be:
- a custom `KeyStoreSpi` or provider over the same `KeyChain` lookups;
- a factory-made manager wrapped around `MtlsKeyManager`;
- copying entries into an in-memory store.

The first two put a new object around the same logic, and the checker would still see the same keys and chain. The third would lose the per-host, per-handshake alias choice and move the key handling into the app. None of them changes what is trusted or presented, so each only hides the call from the checker. I did not write one.

Not examined: the other requirements of the same published rule (the `"TLS"` argument to `getInstance`, and the trust-manager and random arguments). RVSec did not report them at this call. Changing `"TLS"` to a single-version string would also stop the context from negotiating TLS 1.3 on some Android versions, so I left it alone. No source files were changed.

Reason: violation without security impact

The key manager passed to `SSLContext.init` is constructed by the app rather than returned by a `KeyManagerFactory`. It selects a certificate for the gateway host and obtains its key and certificate chain from Android's KeyChain (`shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt:71-98,112-147`).

Passing a custom key manager is supported by the API; the [Java security guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/security-developer-guide.pdf) demonstrates a custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` for alias selection. The reported origin of the manager alone does not establish a security impact. Replacing it with a default factory manager would change the app's per-gateway certificate selection, which is documented in `docs/ROADMAP.md:323`. No equivalent factory-produced manager preserving that selection was identified.

cards.title: No action: the client-certificate key manager is meant to be hand-written
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the TLS context built in `ClientCerts.android.kt`. It saw the key managers passed to `SSLContext.init` and did not see them come from a `KeyManagerFactory`.

That observation is correct, and it is intentional. The key manager here is `MtlsKeyManager`, a small `X509ExtendedKeyManager`. It picks the certificate alias for the host being handshaken. It reads the private key and chain from the system `KeyChain` at handshake time, so the key material never enters the app.

A `KeyManagerFactory` can't do this job. It builds its managers from a `KeyStore` or from key-store builder parameters. The user's key sits behind `KeyChain` and can't be exported into a `KeyStore`, so a factory has nothing to read it from. A factory-built manager also couldn't choose a certificate per gateway host or start presenting a new certificate without a rebuild. A custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` is the approach Android's `KeyChain` documentation and OkHttp's client-certificate examples describe for system-held keys.

The code is otherwise sound:

- The trust side uses `TrustManagerFactory` with the default algorithm and the platform trust store, and nothing is weakened.
- There is no custom hostname verifier and no trust-all manager.
- A host with no matching alias sends no certificate.
- A new context is created on each certificate change, so sessions made with an old certificate are not resumed.

Changing this to satisfy the checker would mean giving up per-host selection or exporting key material, and either is worse. I'm not proposing a code change or opening an issue. The finding looks like a false positive of a rule that assumes every key manager comes from a factory.

Reason: violation without security impact

The key manager passed to `SSLContext.init` is created by the app rather than by a `KeyManagerFactory`, so it does not meet the reported provenance requirement. It selects the certificate for each gateway and retrieves its key and certificate chain from Android's KeyChain ([ClientCerts.android.kt](shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt)).

Android's [KeyChain documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain) describes returning those credentials through `X509KeyManager` callbacks. Replacing this manager with a default factory result would lose the app's per-gateway selection; adding another X509 key manager would not combine their behavior because [SSLContext uses only the first](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext#init(javax.net.ssl.KeyManager%5B%5D,%20javax.net.ssl.TrustManager%5B%5D,%20java.security.SecureRandom)). No security impact from the reported provenance was identified, and no equivalent factory-produced manager was found.

cards.title: Client certificates: keep hostname selection isolated
cards.text:
## What and why

Use the captured hostname to select a client certificate whenever it is available. If that hostname has no certificate, do not fall back to a certificate saved for the server's IP address. This prevents a connection from presenting another gateway's certificate when both resolve to the same address.

## How I tested it

- Tests added: Updated the host test to cover an unmatched hostname with a certificate saved for the socket's IP address.
- The focused Android host tests passed. The Android debug build passed with a writable Android user directory.
- On a device: Not tested.

## Screenshots

Not applicable.

## Checklist

- One feature or fix, and its ROADMAP item is ticked
- Up to date with `master`, and the command under "Tests" in CONTRIBUTING.md passes
- A late answer after a profile, gateway or chat switch is dropped; reconnect, rotation and a second tap work
- Anything cached or stored is keyed by gateway and profile
- Tested with unusual text, if it shows replies or other gateway text: code fences, very long words, CRLF, empty values
- No tokens in URLs, and no fetches of an address on the user's own network that a reply or page links to
- Reuses the app's components, fits at 360 dp in both themes, and icon buttons have content descriptions
- The desktop app builds (`./gradlew:desktopApp:compileKotlinJvm`)
- "Allow edits by maintainers" is on

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
The custom key manager selects the client certificate chosen for the gateway and obtains its private key and certificate chain from Android KeyChain. It is passed directly to the TLS context because certificate selection depends on the gateway host.

Server certificates are verified separately using the platform's default trust manager. The key manager's origin alone does not indicate a TLS security problem, so no change or maintainer report is warranted.

No report or change is needed.

The runtime checker flagged that the key managers passed to `SSLContext.init` in `tlsContext` (in `ClientCerts.android.kt`) did not come from a `KeyManagerFactory`. That is correct, and it is intended.

The app takes the client certificate for each gateway from the system store (`KeyChain`). The certificate is chosen per host, and the private key is never copied into the app. A `KeyManagerFactory` can only wrap a `KeyStore` the app can read, and the keys in `KeyChain` aren't in one. So the app has its own `MtlsKeyManager`, an `X509ExtendedKeyManager`. It picks the alias from the SNI host and hands the store's `PrivateKey` straight to the TLS stack. Passing a custom key manager to `SSLContext.init` is a supported use of the API.

The trust side does use the platform factory (`TrustManagerFactory` with the default algorithm), so server certificate validation is unchanged.

Making the warning go away would mean wrapping `MtlsKeyManager` in a custom `KeyManagerFactory` provider. That adds code and a security-provider registration, with no security gain, only to satisfy the checker. I did not change any code.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Details: The JSSE reference guide documents that KeyManager objects are created either by implementing the interface or by using KeyManagerFactory. The code implements X509ExtendedKeyManager over Android KeyChain, whose private keys cannot be exported to a KeyStore. Any change that satisfies the rule would alter which client key the app presents or would merely wrap the manager to evade the check.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with no security impact.

Cause: The KeyManager passed to SSLContext.init is a directly constructed MtlsKeyManager (an X509ExtendedKeyManager over Android KeyChain), not a KeyManagerFactory output, so generatedKeyManagers[km] does not hold. KeyChain private keys cannot be exported into a KeyStore, so a KeyManagerFactory cannot produce an equivalent manager. The platform-default trust manager is intact, and the "TLS" getInstance literal is not what was reported.

Why the current use can stand: The JSSE reference guide documents that KeyManager objects are created either by implementing the interface or by using KeyManagerFactory. The code implements X509ExtendedKeyManager over Android KeyChain, whose private keys cannot be exported to a KeyStore. Any change that satisfies the rule would alter which client key the app presents or would merely wrap the manager to evade the check.

cards.title: No action: the custom key manager is intended
cards.text:
The checker flagged the function that builds the TLS context for the gateway client. It says the key managers passed to `SSLContext.init` were not seen coming from a `KeyManagerFactory`.

That is true, and it is how the code is meant to work. The client certificate for a gateway (mTLS) lives in the Android system store (`KeyChain`), and the private key never enters the app. `MtlsKeyManager` is an `X509ExtendedKeyManager` that:

- picks the certificate alias for the host being handshaken (the SNI host captured by the socket factory), and
- asks `KeyChain` for the key and chain on the handshake thread.

A `KeyManagerFactory` can't do either of these. The `KeyStore` it wraps needs the key and chain up front and has no per-host choice. The `KeyChain` keys are only reachable through `KeyChain.getPrivateKey` and `KeyChain.getCertificateChain`, not through a loadable `KeyStore`. A gateway with no pick must also present no certificate, which `chooseClientAlias` returning null already does.

The default key manager and `KeyManagerFactory` are for the common case of a keystore the app can load. Here that would mean exporting or copying key material, or losing the per-host selection and the live reload when a certificate changes. Both would be worse than what the code does now.

The trust side is correct: the trust manager comes from `TrustManagerFactory` with the system default. The context is created with `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")`, and nothing weakens certificate or hostname checks. So I don't see a security or correctness problem, and no code change is worth proposing. An issue would only ask the maintainers to look at something that was done on purpose. I didn't build or change anything.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: tlsContext passes a locally constructed array containing the application-defined MtlsKeyManager to SSLContext.init, rather than an array produced by a KeyManagerFactory. The manager performs host-dependent KeyChain credential selection. The reported provenance predicate is therefore violated.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: tlsContext passes a locally constructed array containing the application-defined MtlsKeyManager to SSLContext.init, rather than an array produced by a KeyManagerFactory. The manager performs host-dependent KeyChain credential selection. The reported provenance predicate is therefore violated.

cards.title: No action needed for the client certificate key manager
cards.text:
The Android gateway client intentionally supplies a custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` to select a client certificate by host. Its callbacks retrieve the selected alias's private key and certificate chain through Android's `KeyChain`. This follows the [documented KeyChain integration](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain) with TLS key manager callbacks.

[`SSLContext.init`](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext#init(javax.net.ssl.KeyManager,%20javax.net.ssl.TrustManager,%20java.security.SecureRandom)) accepts key managers directly; they do not have to originate from a `KeyManagerFactory`. Server certificate validation still uses the platform trust manager obtained from `TrustManagerFactory`, and the engine leaves OkHttp's hostname verification enabled. The reported factory provenance alone does not establish a defect, so no code change or issue is warranted.

No source files were changed. No build or tests were run for this assessment.

Reason: violation without security impact: documented correct use, and every possible change would only hide the call from the checker.

RVSec reported that the `KeyManager` passed to `SSLContext.init` in `tlsContext` (`shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt`) did not come from a `KeyManagerFactory`. That is accurate: `tlsContext` is called from `mtlsEngine` with `MtlsKeyManager`, the app's own `X509ExtendedKeyManager`. So the violation is real, but it has no security impact here and I found no change worth sending.

Why the code is the documented use:
- Android's `KeyChain` documentation describes the intended flow as a callback from an `X509KeyManager` that a private key is requested, then `choosePrivateKeyAlias`, then `getPrivateKey` and `getCertificateChain` to return the credentials (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain). `MtlsKeyManager` does this.
- The key stays in the system store. The class comment says the `PrivateKey` is only handed to the TLS stack, and `KeyChain.getPrivateKey` is called from the handshake thread.
- `chooseClientAlias` presents a certificate only when the user picked an alias for the handshake's host. It returns null otherwise, and `chooseServerAlias` returns null.
- The trust side is untouched. The trust managers come from `TrustManagerFactory` with the platform default store, so certificate validation is not weakened.

Why no change helps:
- `KeyManagerFactory.init` takes a `KeyStore` of key material (https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory). The system store's keys are not exposed as one, and the per-host alias choice made from the captured hostname would be lost.
- Wrapping `MtlsKeyManager` in a factory or provider of the app's own, or copying its entries into a store built at run time, would hand the same key manager to the same call. RVSec would see a different call path but the app would trust and present exactly what it does now.

The other checks on this context (the `"TLS"` protocol string, the null `SecureRandom`) were not part of this report. I did not change them, and I did not pin the context to one version, since that would turn off TLS 1.3.

I made no source edits, and the working tree is unchanged. I did not run the build, as there is no change to build.

Reason: violation without security impact: documented correct use, and every change that satisfies the check would either change what the app presents or only hide the call from the checker.

What RVSec reported: in `tlsContext` (`shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt:146-147`), the `KeyManager` given to `SSLContext.init` was not seen coming from a `KeyManagerFactory`. This matches the code (confirmed). The array is `arrayOf(keyManager)`, and `keyManager` is the app's own `MtlsKeyManager` (an `X509ExtendedKeyManager`, same file, line 71), built in `mtlsEngine` at line 112. The trust manager comes from `TrustManagerFactory` with the platform default (line 155-158), so trust and hostname validation are unchanged by this report.

Why it is the documented way to use the system store:
- The Android `KeyChain` documentation describes the flow as a callback from an `X509KeyManager` that a private key is requested, followed by `KeyChain.getPrivateKey` / `getCertificateChain` for the chosen alias (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain). `MtlsKeyManager` does exactly this (lines 118-125). Key material stays in the system store and is only handed to the TLS stack (KDoc, lines 66-70).
- The choice is per host: `chooseClientAlias` (lines 78-85) resolves the alias from the SNI host captured by `SniCapturingSocketFactory`, and from the live saved gateways, with no certificate when nothing matches. Lookups are deliberately not cached (comment at lines 115-117), so a renewed certificate or a revoked grant counts from the next handshake. `MtlsKeyManagerTest` covers these cases.

Why no change is proposed:
- A `KeyManagerFactory` takes its keys from a `KeyStore` loaded up front. KeyChain keys are system-held and opaque to the app, and I did not find a platform `KeyStore` that can hold them (inferred from the API shapes; not tried on a device). The only way I see is a `KeyStore` SPI or a factory written around the same `MtlsKeyManager`. That is the same object and the same behaviour behind a different construction path, so it would only hide the call from the checker.
- Replacing the per-host lookup with a factory-built manager, which chooses by key type and issuer, would drop the host matching. The app could then present a gateway's client certificate to other hosts, and it would lose the live lookup. That changes what the app presents, and the code is already the documented use.
- Creating a `KeyManagerFactory` and discarding it, or wrapping its result in `MtlsKeyManager`, changes nothing the app uses.

Security impact: none established. The custom manager only supplies the client's own certificate. It does not touch server trust, certificate validation or hostname verification, and it presents no certificate when no alias matches the handshake's host.

Other requirements of the same rule, not reported at this call and not part of this unit: the protocol string is `"TLS"` and the `SecureRandom` argument is `null`. `"TLS"` is a negotiating context on Android and pinning it to one version would turn TLS 1.3 off, so I did not change it. These are noted here and not acted on.

Open points: no device run, and no check of whether RVSec would accept any alternative. Search covered the reported file, its common and JVM counterparts, all callers of `mtlsEngine` and `MtlsKeyManager`, the tests under `androidHostTest`, and the README, ROADMAP and CONTRIBUTING. The repository is unchanged (no edits made, no build run).

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction

The key manager passed to `SSLContext.init` is created by the app, rather than by a `KeyManagerFactory` ([ClientCerts.android.kt](shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt)). It selects the certificate for each gateway and retrieves its credentials from Android KeyChain. The reported provenance condition is therefore not met, but its security impact is not established.

[Android's KeyChain documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain) describes returning selected credentials through an `X509KeyManager`. Replacing this manager with a default factory manager would change the app's per-gateway selection; [SSLContext's documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext) says only the first X509 key manager is used. I did not find a safe factory replacement that preserves that behavior.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: tlsContext passes a newly constructed array containing the custom MtlsKeyManager, rather than an array produced by KeyManagerFactory, so the reported generatedKeyManagers predicate is not satisfied. 

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: tlsContext passes a newly constructed array containing the custom MtlsKeyManager, rather than an array produced by KeyManagerFactory, so the reported generatedKeyManagers predicate is not satisfied.
