cards.title: No action needed for client certificate key management
cards.text:
The Android TLS setup deliberately supplies a custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` to `SSLContext.init`. It selects the client certificate alias configured for the gateway host and retrieves its private key and certificate chain through Android's `KeyChain`. This supports the app's per-gateway client certificate selection.

`SSLContext.init` accepts key manager implementations directly; they do not have to come from a `KeyManagerFactory`. Android's [KeyChain documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain) describes returning credentials through key manager callbacks, and the [SSLContext documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext#init(javax.net.ssl.KeyManager,%20javax.net.ssl.TrustManager,%20java.security.SecureRandom)) permits supplying those managers. Server certificate validation still uses the platform default trust manager.

The reported factory provenance does not establish a defect in this setup, so no pull request or issue is warranted. No source files were changed, and no build was run.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: No genuine factory-produced key-manager route is established that preserves the existing host-specific Android KeyChain credential selection.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: tlsContext passes a newly constructed array containing the custom MtlsKeyManager, not an array produced by a KeyManagerFactory. Both resolved callers supply that manager.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The runtime checker's report is that the key managers passed to the TLS context in the gateway engine's client-certificate code (`ClientCerts.android.kt`) did not come from a `KeyManagerFactory`. I read the code, and I don't think the maintainers need a PR or an issue.

The key manager is a custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` (`MtlsKeyManager`). That is on purpose. It has to pick the client certificate per gateway host, and the private key and chain come from Android's system store through `KeyChain`. That store doesn't expose a `KeyStore`, and the key material is non-exportable and never enters the app. A `KeyManagerFactory` can only be built from a `KeyStore` or from a provider's own parameters, so it can't wrap `KeyChain` or choose an alias per host. The usual rule behind this check exists to stop apps from writing weak custom managers that skip validation. This one doesn't do that.

- It only supplies the client's own certificate. It never validates the server's certificate.
- Server validation stays with the platform's default `X509TrustManager`, which comes from `TrustManagerFactory`.
- If no alias matches the host, it presents no certificate, so gateways without client-certificate auth behave as before.

Switching to a factory-built manager would drop the per-host alias selection and the `KeyChain` integration. Those are the whole feature (the "Client certificates (mTLS)" item in `docs/ROADMAP.md`). Adding a code comment just to quiet a checker would also be noise.

So I'm not sending a change. If the maintainers want to see this report, the right fix is to treat the finding as a known false positive for this class.

cards.title: No change needed for client certificate selection
cards.text:
The gateway intentionally supplies a custom key manager that selects the client certificate saved for the destination host and retrieves its private key and certificate chain from Android's KeyChain. Android documents this [KeyChain callback pattern](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain). The [SSLContext initialization API](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext) accepts supplied key managers; they do not have to come from a KeyManagerFactory.

Server certificate verification still uses the platform's default trust manager. The absence of a factory-created client key manager does not establish a security defect, so this finding warrants neither a patch nor an issue.

No source files were changed. Builds and tests were not run.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

The Android gateway code passes its own key manager to `SSLContext.init`. It selects the certificate saved for each gateway and obtains its private key and chain from Android's KeyChain ([ClientCerts.android.kt](shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt)). That manager does not come from a `KeyManagerFactory`.

Android documents using KeyChain credentials in key manager callbacks and remembering a selected alias ([KeyChain documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain)). Replacing the manager with a factory-produced one could change which certificate is presented, and I found no documented factory path that preserves this per-gateway selection. A security impact from the manager's origin was not established, so no change is proposed.

Reason: violation without security impact: documented correct use

RVSec reported that the `KeyManager` passed to `SSLContext.init` in `tlsContext` (`shared/core/src/androidMain/kotlin/dev/hermeskotlin/core/gateway/ClientCerts.android.kt`) did not come from a `KeyManagerFactory`. That is true of the source. The array is `arrayOf(keyManager)`, and `keyManager` is the app's own `MtlsKeyManager`, an `X509ExtendedKeyManager` (`ClientCerts.android.kt:71`, `:112`, `:147`). The trust manager in the same call does come from `TrustManagerFactory` (`:155-158`). The `SecureRandom` argument is `null`, which selects the platform default. RVSec did not report that argument.

The key manager is written by hand because the client certificates live in the system `KeyChain`, and `KeyChain.getPrivateKey` hands the TLS stack a key it does not export. Android's `KeyChain` documentation describes this use: an `X509KeyManager` is asked for a private key, and the app answers from `KeyChain` (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain). `X509ExtendedKeyManager` is documented as the abstract class for applications to extend (https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/X509ExtendedKeyManager).

The manager also does what a `KeyManagerFactory` over a key store cannot do:
- It picks the alias per handshake from the host captured from the socket factory (`:78-85`, `:31-62`).
- It reads the key and chain at handshake time, so a renewed certificate or a revoked grant takes effect on the next connection (`:115-125`).
- It presents no certificate to a host that has no pick, so one gateway's certificate is never sent to another (`:25-30`, `:49-50`).

A factory-built manager would need the key in a `KeyStore` when the context is created. It would then choose by key type and issuer, not by host. The only other route is a factory or provider wrapped around `MtlsKeyManager`, which changes nothing RVSec sees. So every change that satisfies the report would alter which certificate is presented to which gateway, or would only hide the same object.

I found no security impact. Server validation is untouched: the default trust manager is installed through `sslSocketFactory(..., trustManager)` (`:140`). Hostname checking stays with OkHttp. The key manager only supplies a client certificate, and only for hosts the user picked one for. The `TLS` argument to `getInstance` (`:147`) is a negotiating context. Nothing in this report concerns it, so I left it alone.

I made no source edits and ran no build. Outside the repository I only read the two Android documentation pages above. The `KeyChain` page is large and I read only its overview.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: No demonstrated rule-compliant factory route preserves the existing host-specific Android KeyChain credential selection. Wrapping the existing manager in an application-written factory or provider would evade the predicate rather than resolve it.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: SSLContext.init receives an array constructed around an application-defined MtlsKeyManager, not an array observed from KeyManagerFactory, violating the reported generatedKeyManagers requirement. [, C3]

cards.title: No change needed for client certificate key management
cards.text:
The TLS context intentionally uses a custom X509ExtendedKeyManager to select the client certificate saved for a gateway host. Its callbacks retrieve the private key and certificate chain from Android KeyChain using the alias chosen through the system certificate picker. This follows Android's documented [KeyChain integration](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain).

[SSLContext.init](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext#init(javax.net.ssl.KeyManager,%20javax.net.ssl.TrustManager,%20java.security.SecureRandom)) accepts application-supplied key managers; they do not have to come from a KeyManagerFactory. Server certificate validation still uses the platform TrustManagerFactory, and OkHttp's hostname verification is not overridden. The absence of a key manager factory does not establish a defect, so no pull request or issue is warranted.

cards.title: No action: protocol-required MD5 and image cache filenames
cards.text:
Subsonic token authentication requires `MD5(password + salt)`, encoded as lowercase hexadecimal, as specified in the [Subsonic API documentation](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). The request builder follows that format. Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would produce incompatible tokens and break authentication; changing the protocol requires server support.

The remaining callers use the digest to name cached artwork, avatars, and other images, rather than to verify authenticity or integrity. This finding does not establish an actionable defect in those uses. No source change or issue is warranted.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 at md5Hex changes both the transmitted token and persistent filenames, which the current policy expressly forbids; it would also leave the helper's name incorrect. [, C3]; Renaming the helper and updating its Util and FileUtil callers does not remove those policy prohibitions or preserve the established filename derivation. [, C3]; Splitting callers while retaining MD5 for the existing token and filenames leaves the reported runtime violation. Moving the same MD5 computation to another API or helper would conceal rather than resolve it. [, C3]; A compatible coordinated migration cannot be specified from the supplied server and storage evidence, and the current policy does not authorize changing either representation. [, C5]

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: For non-null input, java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal MD5, outside the reported algorithm allow-list. The subsequent digest(byte) call follows the permitted sequence.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

`Util.md5Hex` uses MD5 for both image file names and a token derived from the server password and a salt (`app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java:393-404,1000-1009`; `app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/FileUtil.java:268-296,322-323,349-350`). The [Subsonic REST API authentication specification](https://www.forum.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) specifies MD5 for that token. Changing the shared digest to SHA-256 would change the token sent to the server and break that contract. The report identifies a rule violation, but a security impact in this app was not established.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in `Util.md5Hex` (app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java:1006). The report is real: the call asks for MD5. The code is in this repository's own module, and no suppression or comment marks it as deliberate.

`md5Hex` has two kinds of caller, and I examined all of them (searched `md5Hex` across app/src):

1. Subsonic login token. `Util.getRestUrl` (Util.java:398) sends `s=<random salt>&t=md5Hex(password + salt)` when `ServerInfo.canUseToken` is true (domain/ServerInfo.java:236). The Subsonic API documentation (https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) says: "t: (Since 1.13.0) The authentication token computed as md5(password + salt)". The server computes the same MD5 and compares it. A SHA-2 token would be rejected by the server, so a client-only change cannot be made. The only alternative the code has is the `p=` plain-password parameter (Util.java:407), which is weaker. The salt comes from `SecureRandom` (Util.java:397, 1562).

2. Cover-art cache file names in `FileUtil` (lines 271, 274, 296, 323, 350). The hash only names local `.jpeg` files in the art, avatar and misc directories. No secret or integrity decision depends on it, so there is no security impact there.

Why I am sending nothing: the reported call has to stay MD5 for the token path. Switching only the file-name callers to SHA-256 would leave `md5Hex` and its `getInstance("MD5")` call unchanged for every server login, so the report would still fire. It would also rename every cached cover file, orphaning existing ones and breaking the legacy move from the hashed art file into the album directory (FileUtil.java:279-284), for no gain. Maintainers of other projects have said they would not take that trade for cache-only hashes. I could not check the Subsonic server side, only its published documentation.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

`Util.md5Hex` uses MD5 for a token made from the password and salt in `Util.getRestUrl` ([Util.java:393](app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java#L393), [Util.java:1000](app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java#L1000)). The [Subsonic API authentication specification](https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) requires that MD5 token, so changing the client alone would change the value sent to the server. The same helper also names image files that the app reads back ([FileUtil.java:268](app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/FileUtil.java#L268)).

The reported algorithm is present, but a specific security impact in this app has not been established. No source change is proposed.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The policy authorizes only an internal, in-process discriminator and expressly forbids changing a digest sent out of process or used to name stored data. This helper does both.; The server validation implementation and complete image-path writer and reader inventory are not supplied. A coordinated migration preserving those consumers cannot be written from this packet.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5") violates the reported algorithm allow-list. The helper supplies both a password-derived server token and stored image-file names, so it is not solely an internal discriminator. [, C3]

cards.title: No action needed for MD5 usage
cards.text:
The authentication token is computed from the password followed by a random salt, as required by the [Subsonic API](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would produce tokens that existing servers do not accept. This is a protocol constraint, so an algorithm substitution in the client is not an appropriate fix.

The remaining calls generate filenames for cached artwork, avatars, and other images. These hashes are not used to verify integrity or make authorization decisions. Changing them would change cache filenames without addressing a demonstrated security problem. No code change or issue is warranted for this report.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported that `Util.md5Hex` (app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java:1000-1011) calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. I read the source and the report is correct: the call is `java.security.MessageDigest`, and the algorithm is the literal `"MD5"`, which is not one of the SHA-2 names RVSec listed.

`md5Hex` has two kinds of caller, and one of them cannot change on the client.

1. Server login token. `Util.java:393-401` computes `md5Hex(password + salt)` and sends it as `t=` with the salt as `s=`. This branch runs only when `ServerInfo.canUseToken` is true (stock Subsonic 1.14 or newer and the user has not blocked token use, `ServerInfo.java:236-245`). The Subsonic API defines the token as "md5(password + salt)" ("Since 1.13.0", http://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). The server computes the same value to compare, so a SHA-256 token would be rejected. When the server can't use tokens, the code takes the other branch (`Util.java:405-410`) and does not call `md5Hex`. The reported call therefore has to stay for token login, and the report cannot be cleared by a client-only change.

2. File names for stored images. `FileUtil.java:271, 274, 296, 323, 350` use `md5Hex(...)` to name `.jpeg` files in the app's artwork, avatars and misc directories. The artwork directory is also read by offline-mode code (`OfflineMusicService.java:199, 748`) and by download code. Switching these names to SHA-256 would leave previously stored files unfound and force a re-download. For a user who is offline, that could mean losing artwork they cannot re-fetch. Moving only these callers to a separate SHA-256 helper would also leave `md5Hex` and its MD5 call in place for token login, so RVSec would still report the same call. I considered that and did not draft it.

No security impact is established. The hash does not protect stored data or authenticate anything the app chose. The token algorithm is dictated by the Subsonic protocol, and the file-name use is an identifier, not a security control. I found no tests for `md5Hex` and no project documentation on this point; I did not examine the server side, which is outside this repository.

I made no source changes and did not run the build.

cards.title: Name cached image files with SHA-256 instead of MD5
cards.text:
I reviewed `Util.md5Hex`, which calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. RVSec reported that call. It has two kinds of callers. `FileUtil` uses it to build the `.jpeg` file names for cached playlist, podcast and album art, avatars and misc images. `Util.getRestUrl` uses it for the Subsonic login token.

This change adds `Util.sha256Hex`, which uses `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`, and switches the five `FileUtil` file-name callers to it. The change is made because RVSec reports the call; I found no security impact in how these names are used. Those images can be downloaded again, and nothing else in the app computes or compares the names. Existing files under the old MD5 names are no longer found. The art is fetched again when needed, and the existing cache cleanup and "clear cache" actions remove the old files.

I left `md5Hex` in place for the login token, because the Subsonic API defines it as `md5(password + salt)` (https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). RVSec will therefore still report `md5Hex` whenever a token is built.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I haven't run it on a device. Someone should check how the app behaves offline right after updating. Artwork that was cached only under the old names will show as missing until it is fetched again.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The token digest is built only for stock Subsonic 1.14+ servers and is presumably verified by the server against MD5(password+salt). The evidence does not show that the server accepts any other algorithm, so a client-only switch to SHA-256 would likely break token authentication.; The md5 value names persisted artwork, avatar and misc files in external files directories, and some of those paths are exported by share intent. The case policy forbids changing a digest that names stored data without a migration. No such migration is established, and the files are not a cache directory the platform may clear.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: Util.md5Hex calls MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5") with a literal algorithm that is outside the rule's allow-list of SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. This is a constraint violation on the algorithm argument. The same helper serves two uses that a client-only algorithm change cannot cover. In getRestUrl it builds the token md5(password+salt) sent as &t=, which only a stock Subsonic 1.14+ server verifies, so the algorithm is presumably fixed by that server's token scheme. In FileUtil it names persisted.jpeg artwork, avatar and misc files under getExternalFilesDir, which are read back, renamed and exposed to other apps by share intent. Changing the algorithm would orphan those files and break token authentication. The md5Hex function therefore cannot be made compliant without breaking the server contract.

cards.title: Support stronger server authentication where available
cards.text:
The app authenticates some servers with an MD5 hash of the password and a salt. Anyone who obtains a request's token and salt can attempt to guess the password offline; the token can also be reused to authenticate. HTTPS protects these values in transit, but the app also allows HTTP server URLs.

The [Subsonic API](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) specifies MD5 for this token, so changing the hash on the client alone would break compatibility. Could the app support [OpenSubsonic API key authentication](https://opensubsonic.netlify.app/docs/extensions/apikeyauth/) on servers that offer it, while retaining compatibility with other servers? Encouraging HTTPS would also help protect credentials in transit.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

`Util.md5Hex` uses MD5 both for image filenames and for the password-and-salt token sent by `getRestUrl` ([Util.java](app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java), [FileUtil.java](app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/FileUtil.java)). The [Subsonic API authentication specification](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp#authentication) specifies MD5 for that token, so changing the shared helper to SHA-256 would change the value sent to servers. The code confirms the reported algorithm, but a specific security impact from this use has not been established. No source change is proposed.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in `Util.md5Hex` (`app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java:1006`). I read the whole file. The call is the real `java.security.MessageDigest` (imported at line 79). The algorithm is a literal in the method, so the report is accurate: the method uses MD5.

`md5Hex` has two kinds of caller. I searched the repository for `md5Hex` and `MessageDigest` and found no other callers (confirmed):

1. **Subsonic login token** (`Util.java:398`). `getRestUrl` computes `md5Hex(password + salt)` and sends the result as `t`, with the salt as `s`. The Subsonic API defines this token as `md5(password + salt)`, a 32-character hex string of the MD5 hash, introduced in API 1.13.0 (https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). The server computes the same value to check it. This path is only used when `ServerInfo.canUseToken` is true (`ServerInfo.java:236-246`). A client cannot switch it to SHA-256 on its own, because the server would reject the token.
2. **Artwork file names** (`FileUtil.java:271, 274, 296, 323, 350`). The MD5 hex string names `.jpeg` files in the app's artwork, avatars and misc folders. These folders are under `getExternalFilesDir` (`FileUtil.java:522-523`). The hash is not used for any security decision. It is a file-name key.

**Why I'm sending nothing.** The MD5 in `md5Hex` is fixed by the Subsonic token protocol. A pull request could move only the file-name callers to a SHA-256 helper. Then `md5Hex` would still call `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` for the token, so RVSec would still see the same call and value at the reported method. The change would also orphan the existing artwork files. `getHexAlbumArtFile` (`FileUtil.java:295-297`) is used to find and rename old files by name (`FileUtil.java:279-285`). The maintainers of other apps have declined similar changes for file-name hashes that do no security work.

I found no security impact here. The token is salted and its format is fixed by the protocol. The file names protect nothing. I made no source edits.

Not examined: how non-stock servers handle login. The code sends an obfuscated password instead of a token for those servers (`Util.java:405-410`). That is outside this report.

cards.title: No action: MD5 use in `Util.md5Hex` is intentional
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `Util.md5Hex` for using MD5 instead of a SHA-2 digest. I looked at every caller and decided nothing should be sent to the maintainers.

**Server login token (`Util.java`, around line 398).** The app sends `t = md5(password + salt)` together with the salt `s`. This is the token authentication defined by the Subsonic REST API (1.13.0 and later), and the Subsonic-compatible servers this app talks to (Subsonic, Madsonic, Airsonic and others) check exactly that value. Switching to SHA-256 would make the token fail on every server, so login would break. The client can't change this. A change would have to come from the Subsonic API itself. The app already falls back to the older `enc:` hex password form for servers that can't use tokens, and that fallback is weaker than the token.

**Cache file names (`FileUtil.java`).** The other callers use the digest only to build a stable file name for cached cover art, avatars and similar images. No security property depends on it, because collisions and preimages don't matter for a local cache key. Moving to SHA-256 would change every cache file name. Users would lose their cached artwork and the app would download it again, in exchange for no real benefit.

The finding is a policy-level warning about the algorithm name. In this code MD5 is required by the protocol for one use and harmless for the other. I made no code change and have no issue to file.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

`Util.md5Hex` uses MD5 both for artwork filenames and for the password-and-salt token included in server requests (`app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/Util.java:393-404`, `app/src/main/java/github/paroj/dsub2000/util/FileUtil.java:268-296`). The [Subsonic API authentication specification](https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) defines that token using MD5, so changing the client alone would change the value expected by the server. The security impact of this use in the app is not established. No source change is proposed.

No action: the MD5 use in `Util.md5Hex` is required by the protocol or is non-security, so no issue or PR should go to the maintainers.

`md5Hex` has two kinds of callers.

1. Subsonic token authentication (`Util.java`, around line 398). The Subsonic and Madsonic REST API defines the login token as `md5(password + salt)`. The server computes the same MD5 and compares. Switching this call to SHA-256 would make the token mismatch and break login on every server that supports token auth. The only alternative is the legacy `p=enc:` password parameter, which is worse. The client can't change this without a protocol change on the server side.

2. Cache file names in `FileUtil` (album art, avatars, playlist and podcast covers). The hash only turns a path, title, username or URL into a stable file name. It is not used for integrity or secrecy, so a collision-resistant hash adds nothing. Changing the algorithm would also change every cache file name. Users would re-download all cached cover art, and the old files would be orphaned on disk. That is a real cost for no security benefit.

The checker's complaint is a generic "MD5 is weak" signal. It doesn't apply to either use here. If the project ever wants to quiet it, the least risky route is to keep MD5 for the protocol token and leave the cache naming as it is. That is a judgement call for the maintainers, not a defect to report.

cards.title: No action: MD5 is required for Subsonic compatibility
cards.text:
The authentication code computes MD5(password + salt), as required by the [Subsonic API](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp). Replacing it with SHA-256 would produce tokens that existing servers reject. Changing the authentication algorithm requires a protocol supported by both client and server.

The remaining uses generate filenames for cached artwork, avatars, and other images. These hashes are cache keys, not integrity checks or password storage. Changing them would change existing cache paths without addressing a demonstrated security problem. This finding does not warrant a source change or a maintainer report.

cards.title: No action: MD5 in `Util.md5Hex` is required or harmless
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `Util.md5Hex` because it uses MD5 instead of a SHA-2 digest. I looked at every caller and decided not to send a pull request or an issue.

**Server authentication token (`Util.java`, around line 398).** The Subsonic API's token authentication is defined as `t = md5(password + salt)`, with the random salt sent as `s`. The server computes the same MD5 and compares the two values. If the client used SHA-256, the server would compute a different value, and every login on a token-capable server would fail. The digest algorithm is part of the protocol, so the client cannot change it. When the server doesn't support tokens, the app already uses the older `enc:` hex-encoded password. Moving away from MD5 here would need a change to the Subsonic protocol and to the servers. That is outside this project.

**Cache file names (`FileUtil.java`, the `.jpeg` paths for album art, avatars, playlists and podcasts).** Here MD5 only turns a path, URL or title into a fixed-length file name. It is not used for integrity or secrecy, so a collision-resistant hash adds no security. Switching to SHA-256 would change every cache file name. Every user would lose their cached images and have to download them again, with no benefit.

Because the one security-relevant use is fixed by the protocol and the other uses are harmless, a code change would either break logins or only cause churn. I made no code changes and did not run the build.

Nothing sent: a counterpart outside the repository fixes this value, so the app cannot change it alone.

Details: The configured server implementation and token contract are not identified well enough to write a coordinated compatible change; a client-only SHA-256 substitution is not established as safe.; Existing digest-named image files must remain accessible after an update; changing the shared helper changes their lookup paths.; The supplied policy excludes transmitted digests and digests naming stored data. A change affecting these uses needs separate authorization and a compatible migration strategy.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: Util.md5Hex calls java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5"), outside the detector's accepted SHA-2 algorithm list. The digest is used both for a password-derived server token and for image-file names. [, C4]

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: The supplied policy authorizes only in-process recomputed discriminators and expressly prohibits changing digests used for stored-file keys or sent out of process. Both exclusions apply here.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The governed MessageDigest.getInstance call requests MD5, outside the detector's accepted SHA-2 algorithm list. The same helper also supplies a credential-derived REST token and stored image-file names.

The MD5 digest is required by the Subsonic authentication protocol to compute the token from the password and salt. Replacing it with another digest in the client would cause authentication to fail with compatible servers.

The other uses generate local image-cache filenames, not security checks. Changing those names would invalidate existing cache entries without addressing the protocol requirement. No change is proposed for this report.

cards.title: No action needed for MD5 use
cards.text:
The authentication token is calculated as MD5(password + salt), as required by the [Subsonic API](https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp#authentication). Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would produce incompatible tokens and prevent authentication with supported servers.

The other calls generate filenames for cached artwork, avatars, and miscellaneous images. These hashes are cache keys, not integrity checks or authentication decisions. Changing them would alter existing cache filenames without addressing a demonstrated security problem. No source change or maintainer report is warranted for this finding.

No report or change is needed for the MD5 use in `Util.md5Hex`. It has two callers, and neither is a weakness that switching algorithms would fix.

1. **Subsonic token authentication** (`Util.java`, around line 398). The Subsonic and Madsonic REST API defines the login token as `md5(password + salt)`. Servers verify it with MD5, so a SHA-256 token would be rejected and logins would break on every server that uses token auth. The app can't change this on its own. It is a protocol requirement. It also doesn't let anyone recover a password from the digest alone, because the salt is sent with it and the server can't be asked to use a different hash. The app already falls back to its own legacy password format when the server can't take tokens. A stronger hash would need a new Subsonic API version.

2. **Cache file names** (`FileUtil.java`). The digest names cached album art, avatar and playlist or podcast cover files from a path, title, username or URL. This is a way to get a short, filesystem-safe key and has no security role. Collision resistance doesn't matter here. Moving to SHA-256 would change every cache file name. Users would lose their cached artwork and have to download it again, with no benefit.

So there is no defect to fix and no code change that would be an improvement. The checker flags the algorithm name without knowing what the digest is used for. I didn't change any code or run the build.

cards.title: Support API key authentication for compatible servers
cards.text:
The app authenticates with a token derived from the user's password using MD5. The Subsonic protocol requires this calculation, so replacing the digest would break authentication with existing servers. Captured tokens can be used to test password guesses offline, and the app reuses the same salt and token across requests for the same credentials.

OpenSubsonic supports API key authentication as an alternative that does not depend on the user's password. Please consider adding it for servers that support it, while retaining the existing authentication methods for compatibility. API keys are still credentials and need a protected connection.

References: [Subsonic API](https://www.subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp), [OpenSubsonic API reference](https://opensubsonic.github.io/docs/api-reference/).

cards.title: Support API key authentication for compatible servers
cards.text:
The app authenticates Subsonic requests with an MD5 hash of the password and a salt. Someone who obtains a request URL can test password guesses offline; the app also reuses the same salt and token for subsequent requests. HTTPS protects them in transit, but request URLs can also be exposed in logs.

The [Subsonic API](https://subsonic.org/pages/api.jsp) requires MD5 for its token authentication, so switching the digest alone would break compatibility. Could the app support [OpenSubsonic API key authentication](https://opensubsonic.github.io/docs/api-reference/) where the server offers it, while retaining the existing method for other servers? A separate API key limits password exposure and can be revoked independently.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: The case policy authorizes only an internal recomputed discriminator and forbids changing a digest whose value is exported. The OTP is a truncated digest value placed on the clipboard, and the policy’s review fallback for an internal discriminator does not apply. No authorized client-only change is available under this policy.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The constructor passes the literal MD5 to MessageDigest.getInstance, violating the reported algorithm allow-list. MD5 was also observed at the call in a measured run.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The checker flagged the use of MD5 in `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java`. That class exists only to implement mOTP (`mOTP.java`, which links to the algorithm description at motp.sourceforge.net). The mOTP specification defines the one-time password as the first six hex characters of an MD5 digest, and the secret as the first 16 hex characters of the MD5 of the seed.

The app has to produce the same codes as the server or other mOTP clients, so switching to SHA-256 or another digest would give wrong codes and break every existing mOTP profile. A code change would be a regression, so I did not propose one.

An issue would not help either. The maintainers already chose MD5 on purpose, because the protocol requires it, and the weakness is in the mOTP scheme, not in this app's implementation. Nothing here is specific to this repository that they could act on.

I made no changes to the repository and did not run the build.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec's report is correct about the call. `MD5` in `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java` calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` (line 19) and hashes the string it is given (lines 19-21). It is a literal string, so the report is not a false positive. I searched the repository for every use of the class. It is used only by `mOTP.gen` (`mOTP.java:20,23`) and by the "get secret" dialog in `Profiles.java:250`, and both are the mOTP profile type. HOTP and TOTP do not use it. I found no tests that touch it.

The algorithm is not a free choice of this app. `mOTP.java:13-14` says the code implements the mOTP scheme described at https://motp.sourceforge.net/. That page says the one-time password is made by "hashing the following data with MD5" (time, PIN and the 16-hex-digit init secret), and that the client shows the first 6 digits of the MD5 hash. The user's own mOTP server recomputes the same MD5 value to check the password. That is the code at `mOTP.java:20-24`: MD5 of the seed, its first 16 hex digits, then MD5 of epoch + secret + PIN, first 6 digits. If the client switched to SHA-256, every code it showed would be rejected by existing mOTP servers, and the same goes for the secret shown in the dialog. I did not find a rule-conforming change that servers would still accept. The server side is outside this repository, so I could not check it. The mOTP page does not say how the three inputs are concatenated, so it is silent on that one detail. The code's order follows the project's own implementation, not the page.

I did not find a security stake in this repository's code. The MD5 output is a 6-digit code that is shown, copied to the clipboard (`Home.java:60-66`) and compared by the remote server, and the protocol, not this app, chose MD5. Whether MD5 is weak for that scheme is a question for the mOTP protocol, not for this client.

Nothing is sent to the maintainers and no source files were changed.

cards.title: Preserve mOTP compatibility
cards.text:
No change or issue is warranted for this finding. The [Mobile-OTP algorithm](https://motp.sourceforge.net/#how) specifies MD5 over the time, shared secret and PIN, with the first six hexadecimal characters used as the one-time password. Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would produce codes that existing mOTP servers cannot verify.

The app also derives the shared secret from the seed using MD5 and displays that same secret for server setup. Changing that derivation would invalidate existing enrollments. These uses support mOTP compatibility; the reported algorithm choice alone does not establish an implementation defect. No source changes were made, and no build was run.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The checker flagged the MD5 digest used by the app's mOTP profile type. I don't think this should go to the maintainers, either as a patch or as an issue.

The MD5 helper is used in only two places: `mOTP.gen` and the mOTP secret derivation in `Profiles.java`. The mOTP scheme (https://motp.sourceforge.net/, linked in the code) is defined as the first 6 hex characters of `MD5(epoch + secret + PIN)`, where the secret is the first 16 hex characters of `MD5(seed)`. Existing mOTP tokens and servers all compute this exact value.

Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 or another digest would produce different codes. They would no longer match any mOTP server or other mOTP client, so the feature would stop working for every user. Offering both digests would not help either, because the server decides which one is valid.

The digest is not used for password storage, signatures or integrity checks. It is used only to generate a one-time code in a protocol that fixes MD5. The warning is therefore expected for an interoperable mOTP implementation, and the maintainers already link the specification in `mOTP.java`.

I made no code changes. If the maintainers want to silence this kind of warning, they can add a short comment saying MD5 is required by the mOTP specification. That is a documentation choice for them, and it doesn't need an outside report.

cards.text:
The app uses MD5 to derive the mOTP secret from the seed and to generate mOTP codes. The [Mobile-OTP specification](https://motp.sourceforge.net/#how) requires MD5 for code generation. Replacing it with SHA-2 would produce different codes that existing mOTP servers cannot verify, and changing the seed derivation would change existing secrets.

The finding alone does not establish a vulnerability that can be fixed without changing the protocol or breaking compatibility. No change or issue is warranted on that basis.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The reported call is `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in the `MD5` class (`app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java`, line 19). The RVSec report is correct as far as the code goes: the algorithm is MD5, which is not in the list RVSec expects.

The class has two callers, and both implement the mOTP scheme:

- `mOTP.gen` (`mOTP.java`, lines 20–24) hashes the current time, a secret and the user's PIN with MD5 and shows the first 6 hex characters as the one-time password.
- `Profiles.java` (line 250) shows the same MD5-derived secret to the user.

`mOTP.java` links to the mOTP description (`motp.sourceforge.net`), and the app's info string names "mOTP - http://motp.sf.net" as a reference (`res/values/strings.xml`, line 19). That page says mOTP passwords are produced "by hashing the following data with MD5" and that the first 6 digits of the MD5 hash are the password. The password is checked by a server (or other mOTP verifier) that the user runs. That verifier computes MD5 itself, so a client that used SHA-256 would show codes no mOTP server accepts. The same applies to the secret that the app derives from the seed with MD5: it has to match what the verifier holds.

So the algorithm is fixed by the protocol the app implements, not chosen by the app, and the client cannot change it alone. The spec page does not describe the exact concatenation order, so I relied on it only for the choice of MD5. I did not find a security impact that is specific to this app: the hash is computed over a secret, a PIN and a time value as the protocol defines. The HOTP and TOTP code paths do not use this class.

No code was changed and nothing should be sent to the maintainers. A SHA-256 variant would be a new, incompatible protocol, and the maintainers would have to decide that, not an outside contributor.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in the `MD5` class constructor (`app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java:19`). The call is real and uses the platform `MessageDigest`, so the report is accurate: the algorithm is MD5, not one of the SHA-2 algorithms RVSec expects.

The `MD5` class is used in only two places, and both implement the mOTP algorithm:

- `mOTP.gen` (`mOTP.java:20-24`) computes `md5(epoch + secret + PIN)` and shows its first 6 hex characters as the password. It first derives the 16-character secret as the first 16 hex characters of `md5(seed)`.
- `Profiles.java:250` shows that same derived secret in the "View Secret" dialog. The user then registers it on their mOTP server. The seed notes in `strings.xml:36` say this is the intended flow.

The class comment in `mOTP.java:14` points to the published algorithm at https://motp.sourceforge.net/. That page says the password is made "by hashing the following data with MD5" (time, PIN and the 16-hex-digit Init-Secret). It says the device shows "the first 6 digits of the MD5-hash". It says the server recomputes the value itself. It also states "MD5 is not a limitation". The password is therefore checked by a server that computes the same MD5. The displayed secret is a value the user copies to that server. If the client switched to SHA-256, the passwords would stop matching what any mOTP server computes, and the secrets users have already registered would stop matching too. A client-only change therefore cannot be made safely.

I found no use of MD5 elsewhere in the repository (a search for `MD5` and `MessageDigest` over `app/src` matched only these files). I could not check any server, so the server side rests on the mOTP page alone. The security impact of MD5 here is not established: the hash is part of a fixed external protocol that the app does not choose. I made no source changes and did not run the build.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

The [Mobile-OTP algorithm, “How it's done”](https://motp.sourceforge.net/) specifies MD5 for the one-time password. The app performs that calculation in `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/mOTP.java`; changing it would produce passwords that do not follow the protocol.

The same digest also derives the secret shown to users for enrollment from a saved seed (`mOTP.java` and `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/Profiles.java`). Changing that derivation would change the secret for existing profiles. RVSec correctly reports the MD5 call in `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java`, but a security impact from this particular use has not been established, and a client-only replacement would change values used outside the app.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The constructor calls MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5"), outside the reported SHA-2 allowlist; MD5 was also observed at runtime. The subsequent update-before-digest sequence is separately satisfied.

cards.title: No action: MD5 use is required by the mOTP algorithm
cards.text:
The report flags the `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` call in `app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java`. It wants a SHA-2 digest instead.

The helper has only two callers, and both implement the mOTP algorithm (see `mOTP.java`, which links to the spec at motp.sourceforge.net):

- `mOTP.gen` hashes the seed to get the secret. It then hashes `epoch + secret + PIN` and takes the first 6 hex characters as the one-time password.
- `Profiles` uses the same hash to show the user the derived mOTP secret.

mOTP is defined in terms of MD5. The app has to produce the same codes as the server and as other mOTP clients, which all use MD5. If we replaced MD5 with SHA-256 here, the app would generate codes that no mOTP server accepts, and the secrets shown to users would no longer match their servers. Every existing mOTP profile would stop working.

The app does not use MD5 for anything else. The HOTP and TOTP code paths do not call this helper.

A code change would therefore break the feature, and the use of MD5 here is a protocol requirement, not a mistake in how the API is used. Neither a pull request nor an issue is useful, so I am not sending anything to the maintainers.

Details: The OTP and the derived secret must match what external mOTP verifiers and other mOTP clients compute. Changing MD5 to SHA-256 in the client alone would produce OTPs the server rejects. No repository-side change can fix this without a coordinated change to the verifier.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: MD5.java:19 passes the literal "MD5" to MessageDigest.getInstance, which is outside the allow-list SHA-256/384/512 (constraint violation, confirmed by source, spec and runtime observation). The MD5 class implements the mOTP one-time-password scheme: the seed is hashed, the first 16 hex characters become a secret, and that secret plus epoch and PIN is hashed again, with 6 hex characters returned as the OTP. The displayed 'secret' in Profiles is also derived this way. The digest therefore defines an externally specified output, not an in-process discriminator.

cards.title: No action: MD5 use is required by the mOTP algorithm
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the `MD5` helper because it calls `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` and the checker expects a SHA-2 family digest.

That helper is used only by `mOTP.gen` and by the mOTP profile setup in `Profiles.java`. The mOTP scheme (https://motp.sourceforge.net/, linked from `mOTP.java`) is defined as the first 6 hex characters of `MD5(epoch + MD5(seed)[0:16] + PIN)`. Tokens and servers that implement mOTP all compute exactly this. Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would produce codes that never match the ones from other mOTP clients or from the server, so the mOTP feature would stop working for every existing profile.

MD5 here is a fixed part of a third-party protocol. The app is not choosing it as a general-purpose hash for passwords, signatures or integrity checks. The HOTP and TOTP code paths do not use MD5.

Making the digest configurable or switching it would break interoperability without a security gain that the user could use. A pull request would be wrong, and an issue would only ask the maintainers to act on something they have already chosen on purpose. Nothing should be sent.

Reason: an external contract prevents the correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec saw `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in the `MD5` class (`app/src/main/java/org/cry/otp/MD5.java`, line 19). The call is on `java.security.MessageDigest` and the algorithm is a literal, so the report is real in the plain sense: MD5 is not in RVSec's list of expected algorithms. I am not calling it a false positive.

The class has no other use in the repository. I searched for `MD5` and `MessageDigest` across `app/src` and found three call sites. `mOTP.gen` (`mOTP.java`, lines 20 and 23) and the "show secret" dialog in `Profiles.java` (line 250) use it. Everything it hashes is part of the mOTP one-time-password scheme the app implements. `mOTP.java` links the scheme's description at https://motp.sourceforge.net/, and the app's info string lists "mOTP - http://motp.sf.net" as a reference.

That page says the one-time password is produced "by hashing the following data with MD5", then taking the first six characters. It says the server verifies the password because it knows the same time, secret and PIN. The page calls mOTP "a de facto standard" with more than 40 implementations. The page does not give a byte-level specification, so I could not check the exact concatenation order from it.

The server is a third party that the user operates or uses, and it computes MD5 over the same inputs. If the app switched to SHA-256, the six characters it shows would stop matching what the server expects, and every mOTP profile would fail to log in. Only an opt-in change that the mOTP servers also support could fix this, and nothing in this repository offers that. I did not invent such a setting.

I could not confirm a security impact. The code does not use MD5 for a choice the app made. Whether the secret derivation in `MD5(seed).substring(0, 16)` is required by the scheme or is this app's own step is not settled by the page. Even so, the derived secret feeds the same server-compared code. Changing it would also change the codes for every stored profile.

Searched: all of `app/src` (main and test), the build file and the string resources. There is no README or other design document. The only test (`app/src/test/java/TotpTests.java`) covers TOTP and does not touch `MD5`. I did not run the build because I made no change.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
The MD5 digest is applied to the app's package name to select a configuration value. It is not used to protect data or verify authenticity, so MD5's cryptographic weaknesses do not create the reported security risk here.

The digest is compared with existing constants, so changing the algorithm alone would alter behavior for package names that currently match. There is no reason to make that change solely in response to this finding.

cards.title: No action: MD5 is used as a package-name fingerprint
cards.text:
The access-point update hashes the app's own package name with MD5, reduces the digest to an integer with `contentHashCode`, and compares it with three fixed values. The result selects configuration that controls scan caching, signal-level calculations, and a version-display marker. It does not protect passwords, authenticate network peers, or verify the integrity of security-sensitive data.

This use does not require cryptographic collision resistance. The reported algorithm alone therefore does not establish a security defect that warrants a pull request or issue. Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 would change the fingerprints and stop the existing values from matching, altering behavior for recognized package names.

No source changes are proposed.

cards.title: Select access point cache behavior by package name
cards.text:
## Summary

I found that `AccessPointsAdapterData` hashes the app package name with Java `MessageDigest` and uses the result to select scan-cache behavior. RVSec reported the MD5 call. I replaced it with explicit checks for the release and debug package names because the hash is only used to select between those behaviors.

## What does this implement/fix?

The two package names declared by this project retain their current selection. Other package names use the smaller-cache path; I added tests for both declared names and another name.

## Does this close any issues?

None known.

## How was this tested?

The debug app build passed with `build_check`, and `:app:testDebugUnitTest --tests com.vrem.wifianalyzer.wifi.accesspoint.AccessPointsAdapterDataTest` passed. I used a writable `ANDROID_USER_HOME` for the build. I did not test on a device.

## Checklist (required before marking ready)

- [x] I added or updated unit tests
- I followed the project's coding style (ktlint) and formatting
- I ran lint and addressed or documented any warnings
- CI checks pass (unit tests, coverage, lint)
- [x] No sensitive data, keys, or secrets are included

## Additional context

The old selector includes a third integer whose package name I could not identify in this repository. Please check whether another distributed package relies on it. RVSec has not been rerun on this change.

## Reviewer notes

Please check the package-name mapping for any other supported builds.

cards.title: Question about the MessageDigest use in calculateChildType
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `AccessPointsAdapterData.calculateChildType` in `app/src/main/kotlin/com/vrem/wifianalyzer/wifi/accesspoint/AccessPointsAdapterData.kt`.

In `calculateChildType`, `MessageDigest.getInstance` is called with `MD5`, while RVSec expects SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512. The digest is folded into an integer compared with fixed TYPE constants, which are not recomputed by the same path. MD5 is not suitable where collision resistance is needed.

I didn't open a pull request because I could not find a change that keeps the current behaviour intact. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer, I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: No security change warranted for the package-name hash
cards.text:
The MD5 digest hashes the app's own package name, reduces the digest to a 32-bit integer, and compares it with fixed constants to select a configuration affecting scan caching and signal calculations. It does not protect secrets, verify data integrity, or authenticate TLS connections. The reported use does not establish a security vulnerability that warrants a report or patch.

Replacing MD5 with SHA-256 alone would break those comparisons. The release and debug package names currently match the constants selecting the larger configuration; their SHA-256 results would select the smaller configuration and change scan behavior without providing a security benefit here.

No source changes are proposed. No build or tests were run.

cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the use of MD5 in `AccessPointsAdapterData.calculateChildType` (the same pattern also appears in `GraphWrapper.calculateGraphType`). I looked at the code and I don't think the maintainers need to hear about it.

The digest is not used for anything security-related. The code hashes the app's package name, reduces the result to an `Int` with `contentHashCode`, and compares it against three fixed constants (`TYPE1`, `TYPE2`, `TYPE3`). If it matches, the list size is `SIZE_MAX`. Otherwise it is `SIZE_MIN`. No secret, signature, password or integrity guarantee depends on MD5, so collision or preimage weaknesses don't apply. It is only a cheap fingerprint of a public string.

Switching to SHA-256 would not be a drop-in fix. The three constants were precomputed from the current MD5-based value, so they would all have to be regenerated for every package name the project ships. That would change a mechanism the maintainers set up on purpose, and I can't tell from the repository what it is meant to cover. A mistake would silently cap the list size for legitimate builds. A cosmetic change to satisfy a scanner doesn't justify that risk, and I didn't build or test one.

Nothing here is a vulnerability, so I'm not sending a PR or an issue.

A runtime crypto-usage checker flagged `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` in `AccessPointsAdapterData.calculateChildType`, saying it expected a SHA-2 algorithm. I looked at the code and I don't think the maintainers need to hear about it.

**What the code does.** The method hashes the app's package name (`com.vrem.wifianalyzer`, plus the `.BETA` suffix for debug builds). The result only picks between `SIZE_MAX` and `SIZE_MIN` for a UI size setting. `GraphWrapper.calculateGraphType` does the same thing.

**Why MD5 is not a vulnerability here.**
- The input is a public, constant string, not user data, a password or a secret.
- Nothing is signed, authenticated or verified, and no integrity guarantee depends on collision resistance.
- An attacker gains nothing from MD5 weaknesses. Anyone can already read the package name and change the constants or the comparison by repackaging the APK.

Switching to SHA-256 would change the computed value, so it would never match the constants. Every build would then fall into the `SIZE_MIN` branch, which silently changes app behaviour. To keep behaviour the same, the constants would have to be recomputed and changed in the same patch, and that adds churn for no security benefit. It would also only quiet a warning.

**Conclusion.** The finding is a false positive for this usage. A PR would change behaviour or add churn for no gain, and an issue would only ask the maintainers to triage a non-problem. I made no code changes and am sending nothing.

Thanks for sending a pull request!

## Summary
- `AccessPointsAdapterData` hashed the app's package name with `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`, took `contentHashCode` of the result, and compared it with `TYPE1`/`TYPE2`/`TYPE3` to choose `SIZE_MAX` or `SIZE_MIN`. RVSec reported the MD5 call. The hash only picks a variant, so I replaced it with a direct package name check instead of a different algorithm.

## What does this implement/fix?

I worked out by hand that `TYPE1` and `TYPE3` are the MD5 hash codes of those two names. If the package name can't be read, it still falls back to `SIZE_MAX`.
- `AccessPointsAdapterDataTest.kt`: added tests for the release, BETA, other and unreadable cases.

## Does this close any issues?
- No.

## How was this tested?
- `assembleDebug` built successfully. I did not run the unit tests, ktlint or lint, and did not test on a device.

## Checklist
- [x] I added or updated unit tests (see `app/src/test/`)
- I followed the project's coding style (ktlint) and formatting
- I ran lint and addressed or documented any warnings
- CI checks pass (unit tests, coverage, lint)
- [x] No sensitive data, keys, or secrets are included

## Reviewer notes

- `GraphWrapper.calculateGraphType` has the same MD5 check. RVSec did not report it, so I left it and the `TYPE` constants alone.
- Decision for you: I put the package names directly in this class; the alternative is one shared list used here and in `GraphWrapper`.

cards.title: No change needed for package-name hashing
cards.text:
The reported MD5 operation hashes only the app's own package name, then reduces the digest to a 32-bit integer and compares it with fixed constants. The result selects configuration used for scan caching and signal-level handling. It does not protect secrets, authenticate peers, or verify external data, so this use does not require a cryptographically secure digest.

Replacing MD5 alone would invalidate the existing package fingerprints and change scanning behavior for the release and debug builds. The report does not establish a security defect that warrants a patch or issue.

No source files were changed, and no build or unit tests were run.

cards.title: Question about the MessageDigest use in calculateChildType
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `AccessPointsAdapterData.calculateChildType` in `app/src/main/kotlin/com/vrem/wifianalyzer/wifi/accesspoint/AccessPointsAdapterData.kt`.

MessageDigest.getInstance receives the literal MD5, outside the reported algorithm allow-list; the runtime measurement also recorded MD5.

I have not opened a pull request because I could not find a change that keeps the current behaviour intact. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

**What the code does (confirmed).** `AccessPointsAdapterData.calculateChildType` (app/src/main/kotlin/com/vrem/wifianalyzer/wifi/accesspoint/AccessPointsAdapterData.kt:66-76) calls `java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` (import at line 31), feeds it `MainContext.INSTANCE.mainActivity.packageName`, and reduces the digest to `digest.contentHashCode`. On any exception it falls back to `TYPE1`. So RVSec's message (MD5 found, SHA-2 family expected) matches the source literally. The class belongs to this repository's `app` module (`namespace = 'com.vrem.wifianalyzer'`, app/build.gradle:71); it is not copied code.

**What the value is used for (confirmed).** The only caller is `update` (line 42), which passes the result to `type` (line 77). `type` checks whether the value equals `TYPE1`, `TYPE2` or `TYPE3` (app/src/main/kotlin/com/vrem/wifianalyzer/wifi/graphutils/GraphConstants.kt:31-33). It returns `SIZE_MAX` on a match and `SIZE_MIN` otherwise. The result is stored in `Configuration.size` (Configuration.kt:29), which only drives `sizeAvailable`. That in turn picks the scan-cache depth and the signal-averaging branch (wifi/scanner/Cache.kt:73-86, 99) and the "S" suffix on the About version string (AboutFragment.kt:125). The hash is not stored, sent, or compared against anything secret. It is a runtime discriminator over the app's own package name, and the code matches the published "MD5 used only as a non-security key" shape. I found no suppression or comment saying the choice is deliberate. `GraphWrapper.calculateGraphType` (graphutils/GraphWrapper.kt:166-175) has an identical block, which RVSec did not report here.

**Why I am not sending a patch.** A digest that only tells variants apart should be replaced by explicit variant logic that keeps every known mapping, not by a different algorithm. The three accepted values `TYPE1`..`TYPE3` are one-way hashes. The repository states only one package name, `com.vrem.wifianalyzer` (app/build.gradle:80), plus the debug suffix `.BETA` (app/build.gradle:100). I searched the Gradle files, README, manifests and sources and found no other package name. I could not run a hash or script in this session, so I could not even confirm which of the three constants match those two names. The name behind at least one constant is not recoverable from the repository. Any patch I wrote would either drop a mapping, so that a build with that package name would silently drop to `SIZE_MIN`, or swap MD5 for SHA-256 and recompute constants I cannot derive. The second option only changes what RVSec sees and keeps the same hidden-hash design. I changed no files and ran no build.

**Impact.** Not established. A package-name hash selecting cache depth protects no user data or secret, so MD5's collision weakness has no role here.

**Open.** Which package names `TYPE2` and `TYPE3` stand for, and whether the hashed form is intentional obscurity, are maintainer knowledge. Only the maintainers could replace the hash with an explicit package-name comparison, and they would want to do it in both `AccessPointsAdapterData` and `GraphWrapper` together.

Changing the algorithm alone would invalidate the existing comparisons, affecting caching and signal-level calculations for recognized package names. No code change or issue is warranted for this report.

cards.title: Passphrase-protected SSH private keys use a weak home-grown key derivation
cards.text:
While running the app under a runtime crypto-usage checker, the AES key and IV used to protect generated SSH private keys were flagged as not coming from a recognised source of key material. I looked at the code and I think the warning points at a real, if modest, weakness. I have not changed anything because a fix affects the stored key format and needs a decision from you.

**Where**

The passphrase-encryption helper in `app/src/main/kotlin/io/treehouses/remote/ssh/` (the `encrypt` and `decrypt` functions), called from `PubKeyUtils.getEncodedPrivate` / `decodePrivate`. These are used when a user generates an SSH key with a passphrase (`BaseSSHKeyGen`, `KeyUtils`) and when such a key is loaded (`SSH.kt`).

**What it does today**

- The passphrase plus an 8-byte random salt is hashed with SHA-256, repeated 1000 times.
- The first 16 bytes of the result become the AES-128 key and the next 16 bytes become the CBC IV. Both are built directly from the SHA-256 output.
- There is no integrity check on the ciphertext. A wrong passphrase is only noticed if the padding or the key encoding happens to fail to parse.

**Why it matters**

- 1000 rounds of plain SHA-256 is a very cheap guess rate for an offline attacker who gets hold of the stored key blob (for example from a device backup). A password-based KDF such as PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a much higher iteration count, or a memory-hard KDF, would be a better fit. Android provides PBKDF2 through `SecretKeyFactory`.
- The IV is derived from the passphrase and salt rather than generated randomly and stored. The salt is random per key, so the IV does not repeat in practice, but it is not the usual construction.
- The code is copied from a 2008 helper (and, via ConnectBot, its key storage format), so this is inherited design rather than a recent regression.

**Why I did not send a patch**

Switching the KDF changes the derived key, so every key already saved with the old scheme would stop decrypting. A safe change needs a format version marker (or a try-new-then-fall-back-to-old read path), with re-encryption of existing keys on the next successful unlock. How to do that, and whether the migration is worth it for this app, is your call.

**Suggested direction**

1. Add a version byte to the stored blob.
2. For new keys, derive the key with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (or similar) with a high iteration count, use a random IV stored alongside the salt, and preferably switch to an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM.
3. Keep the current scheme for reading old blobs, and re-encrypt them in the new format once unlocked.

I am happy to prepare a patch along these lines if you would like one and agree on the migration approach.

cards.title: Protect newly stored SSH private keys with authenticated encryption
cards.text:
Use a random salt and nonce, PBKDF2, and AES-GCM when encrypting new password-protected SSH private keys. This makes password guessing more expensive and detects changes to encrypted key data.

Continue to read existing encrypted keys using the original format. Existing keys are not automatically re-encrypted, and older versions of the app cannot read keys written in the new format.

The debug build and private-key storage unit tests pass.

cards.title: Randomize IVs and derive keys for saved private keys
cards.text:
Today `Encryptor` derives the AES key and IV from a password and salt before encrypting encoded SSH private keys. RVSec reported the `SecretKeySpec` and `IvParameterSpec` calls without a usable message. I changed new encryption to derive the key with PBKDF2 and generate the IV with `SecureRandom`; Android recommends a random IV stored with the ciphertext.

Newly saved encrypted keys cannot be read by earlier app versions. Keys saved by earlier versions still use the existing decryption path; RVSec may still report its spec constructors when that path runs. The project builds, and the focused round-trip and legacy-reader tests pass.

Please check the new format on devices, against RVSec, and with any consumers of exported or older data. This code credits an earlier project, so the change may also belong upstream. I chose a versioned suffix and PBKDF2 for new records; another compatible format could be used instead.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the key and IV construction in `Encryptor.encrypt` (`app/src/main/kotlin/io/treehouses/remote/ssh/Encryptor.kt`). Both reports carry the message "unknown", so they give no concrete defect. I read the code to see whether either one points at a real problem.

`encrypt` makes a fresh random 8-byte salt on every call. It runs the password and salt through 1000 rounds of SHA-256. It then splits the 32-byte result into a 16-byte AES key and a 16-byte IV. Because the salt is random, the IV is not constant or hard-coded. It is different for each encryption. The key and IV arrays and the intermediate digests are zeroed after use. The checker most likely complains because the key and IV come from a hash instead of directly from a secure random generator. That is a heuristic mismatch, not a visible bug.

The only way to satisfy that heuristic would be to change how the key and IV are derived, for example by using PBKDF2 and a random IV stored next to the ciphertext. That would change the on-disk format of the stored private keys. Keys already encrypted by earlier versions of the app would no longer decrypt. A change like that needs a migration path and a decision from the maintainers. It is more than a small fix from an outside contributor, and the report gives no evidence of an actual vulnerability to justify it.

I did not change any code, and I am not sending a pull request or an issue. The key derivation is on the weak side (a fixed 1000 iterations, with the key and IV taken from one digest). If the maintainers ever want to improve it, they could do so as a deliberate format-versioning change.

cards.title: Strengthen protection of stored SSH private keys
cards.text:
Password-protected SSH private keys use a custom derivation with only 1,000 SHA-256 iterations and an 8-byte salt. Someone who obtains the stored ciphertext can test password guesses offline, and the low work factor makes those guesses relatively cheap.

The keys are encrypted with AES-CBC without authentication, so changes to the stored ciphertext cannot be reliably detected. Consider a versioned format using a standard password-based key derivation function with an appropriate work factor, a fresh random salt, and authenticated encryption. Existing encrypted keys need to remain readable and be migrated safely when the password is available.

cards.title: Use a random IV and PBKDF2 key when encrypting SSH private keys
cards.text:
When a password is set on a generated SSH key, `Encryptor.encrypt` encrypts the private key with AES/CBC. It builds the `SecretKeySpec` and the `IvParameterSpec` from a repeated SHA-256 digest of the password and salt, so the IV is not random. RVSec reported both constructor calls.

This change derives the key with PBKDF2 (`SecretKeyFactory`, `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1`, which exists on minSdk 23) and lets the cipher pick a random IV on `init`. The IV is stored in front of the ciphertext, and `Encryptor.decrypt` reads it back. The salt, the iteration count and the 16-byte key size are unchanged.

Newly saved encrypted keys use a format that earlier versions of the app cannot read. Keys saved by earlier versions still read: `PubKeyUtils.decodePrivate` tries the new format first and, if that fails, falls back to the old SHA-256 path, now `Encryptor.decryptLegacy`. That fallback still builds a `SecretKeySpec` and `IvParameterSpec`, and RVSec will still report it whenever an old key is unlocked. Old keys are not re-encrypted.

The project builds with this change. I did not run it on a device, and the repository has no unit tests for this code. Reviewers may want to unlock an old and a new encrypted key on a device. Whether RVSec accepts the PBKDF2 key is unverified.

cards.title: Passphrase-protected SSH private keys use a weak key derivation (1000 rounds of plain SHA-256)
cards.text:
When a user generates or imports an SSH key and sets a passphrase, the private key is encrypted by `Encryptor.encrypt` (called from `PubKeyUtils.getEncodedPrivate`). I found this while reviewing the AES key and IV setup in that method. I did not change any code, because a fix alters the stored format.

How the key and IV are derived today:

- The passphrase is concatenated with an 8-byte random salt and hashed with SHA-256, repeated `ITERATIONS = 1000` times (`PubKeyUtils.kt`).
- The first 16 bytes of the final digest become the AES-128 key and the next 16 bytes become the CBC IV.

Why this is worth a look:

- Plain iterated SHA-256 is cheap to brute-force on GPUs. 1000 rounds is far below what current guidance asks for with PBKDF2 or similar. Anyone who gets hold of the stored encrypted key (for example from a device backup or the app database) can guess weak passphrases quickly.
- There is no integrity check on the ciphertext. A wrong passphrase is only detected when PKCS5 padding or key decoding happens to fail.
- The IV comes from the same digest as the key, not from a separate random source. Because the salt is random for every encryption, the IV is not reused across keys, so I don't see a practical break from this alone. It would be cleaner to generate a random IV and store it with the salt.

Possible direction, if the maintainers agree:

- Derive the key with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (or similar) with a much higher iteration count, using `SecretKeyFactory`.
- Store a version marker and the KDF parameters together with the salt, and use a random IV.
- Keep the current `decrypt` path for existing data, and re-encrypt keys in the new format when they are next unlocked.

I held back from sending a patch because changing the derivation without a version marker and migration would make every already-saved passphrase-protected key undecryptable. How to handle that migration is a decision for the maintainers.

The code is adapted from ConnectBot's key handling, so the same format may also matter if keys are ever exchanged with other tools.

cards.text:
The encryption path fills a fresh eight-byte salt with a cryptographic random generator, hashes the password and salt for 1,000 iterations, and copies separate halves of the resulting SHA-256 digest into a 16-byte AES key and a 16-byte IV. The buffers are populated before use; their initial zero values are not used for encryption. The salt is stored with the ciphertext so decryption can reproduce the same values.

The reports provide no concrete violation in this construction, so they do not justify a code change or issue. This conclusion concerns these reports, rather than a general assessment of the stored-key encryption format. No source files were changed, and no build was run.

cards.title: Use a random IV when encrypting SSH private keys
cards.text:
When a key pair is saved with a passphrase, `Encryptor.encrypt` builds an `IvParameterSpec` for the AES/CBC cipher from the second half of the iterated SHA-256 digest of the passphrase and salt. RVSec reported that IV as not coming from a random source. It is now filled by `SecureRandom` and returned to the caller. The key derivation is unchanged, and I did not touch the `SecretKeySpec` call.

The IV has to be stored to decrypt later, so `PubKeyUtils.encrypt` now writes a version byte, the salt, the IV and the ciphertext. `PubKeyUtils.decrypt` still reads the old salt-plus-ciphertext layout, which `Encryptor.decrypt` handles as before. Old data is recognised by its length, which is always 8 bytes past a multiple of 16, and the new layout never has that length. Keys saved by this version cannot be read by older app versions.

I added a `decrypt` overload that takes the stored IV. The project builds with this change (`build_check` passed). I did not run the app or add a test, because the module has no unit-test source set. A reviewer may want to save a passphrase-protected key and connect with it, then do the same with a key saved by the previous version.
