cards.title: No action on the reported key and IV initialization
cards.text:
The reports do not establish an invalid, hardcoded, or zero key or IV. The private-key encryption path supplies an eight-byte salt buffer and 1,000 hashing iterations. Encryption fills the salt using a cryptographic random generator, then hashes the user-provided password with that salt. The resulting SHA-256 digest is split into a 16-byte AES key and a 16-byte CBC IV before either is used.

The zero-filled allocations are temporary buffers populated from the digest. Clearing those buffers after cipher initialization does not clear the parameter objects: both constructors copy their input bytes, as documented in the Android references for [key parameters](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/SecretKeySpec) and [IV parameters](https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/crypto/spec/IvParameterSpec). The salt is also copied into the stored encrypted data before its temporary buffer is cleared, allowing decryption to reproduce the same key and IV.

These findings do not justify changing the existing storage format or sending a defect report. This conclusion concerns the reported initialization calls, rather than the overall strength of the legacy password-based encryption format. No source files were changed and no build was run.

cards.title: Strengthen password protection for saved SSH private keys
cards.text:
Generating an SSH key with a nonempty password encrypts the private key using a custom derivation: SHA-256 of the UTF-8 password plus an eight-byte random salt, followed by repeated hashing with the same salt for 1,000 rounds total. The final digest is split into a 16-byte AES key and a 16-byte CBC initialization vector. Anyone who obtains the saved encrypted key can test password guesses offline, with each guess requiring only 1,000 SHA-256 operations and a decryption. This provides limited resistance to guessing weak passwords.

Please use a standard password-based key derivation function with a work factor calibrated for supported devices. [RFC 8018](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8018#section-5.2) specifies PBKDF2, and its [iteration-count guidance](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8018#section-4.2) calls for the highest cost acceptable to users.

The saved encrypted bytes contain only the salt followed by ciphertext, with no format version or derivation parameters. This needs a migration design before changing the encryption code: new records should identify their format and parameters, existing records should remain decryptable, and migration should happen after a successful unlock. Simply changing the hash loop or IV generation would prevent users from unlocking previously saved keys.

cards.title: Generate an independent IV for encrypted SSH keys
cards.text:
`Encryptor.encrypt` uses `SecretKeySpec` and `IvParameterSpec` with halves of a password-and-salt digest to encrypt an SSH private key. RVSec flagged both calls without a usable explanation. I now derive the key with `SecretKeyFactory` and generate a separate random IV, so the IV no longer depends on the password digest.

New encrypted keys use a versioned record. Earlier app versions cannot read these records; the updated app can still read older keys. The previous constructors remain in `Encryptor.decrypt` to read old records, and RVSec will still report them when that path runs.

The app builds and the unit tests pass. Please check older keys on Android, any readers outside this repository, and whether RVSec recognizes the new key derivation. The copied encryption code may also need an upstream change. I chose a new record format that retains the old reader instead of continuing to write the old format.

cards.title: Generate an IV and derive the private-key encryption key
cards.text:
Today `Encryptor.encrypt` splits a password-and-salt digest into the AES key and IV used to encrypt an encoded SSH private key. RVSec reported the `SecretKeySpec` and `IvParameterSpec` calls without usable details. I changed the key to use the platform's password-based key derivation and generate a fresh IV independently for each encryption.

I store the IV with the ciphertext and keep the old decryption path for existing keys. Older app versions cannot read newly encrypted keys. The old constructors remain in `Encryptor.decrypt` when reading older keys and may also be reported by RVSec.

The app build and focused unit tests pass. Please check on Android devices, with existing stored keys, and with RVSec; other consumers of these records may also need review. The encryption code was copied from another project, so this change may also belong upstream. I chose a new marked format; retaining the old format is the alternative.

cards.title: Use a cipher-generated IV when encrypting SSH private keys
cards.text:
When a key pair has a password, `Encryptor.encrypt` runs AES/CBC over the private key. It took the IV from the second half of an iterated SHA-256 digest of password and salt, and passed it to `IvParameterSpec`. RVSec reported that call because it saw no randomly generated IV there.

Now `encrypt` calls `Cipher.init` without an IV, so the cipher generates one. It returns that IV in front of the ciphertext. `PubKeyUtils` stores a one-byte format marker, the salt, then IV and ciphertext. The key derivation is unchanged.

Keys encrypted by this version cannot be read by older versions of the app. Keys saved earlier are salt plus ciphertext, so their length is 8 modulo 16. `PubKeyUtils.decrypt` sends those down the old path, which `Encryptor.decrypt` still serves unchanged. New data has the marker and a different length. The new reader is `Encryptor.decryptWithIv`.

The project builds with this change. I added no tests because the module has no unit-test source set. I did not try it on a device or with existing stored keys, so a reviewer should check unlocking an old key and a new one.

cards.title: Use a random IV when encrypting in Encryptor.encrypt
cards.text:
In `Encryptor.encrypt`, the `IvParameterSpec` passed to the AES/CBC `Cipher` was built from bytes 16..31 of the iterated SHA-256 digest of the password and salt. It was not random, and it was not read back from the data. RVSec reported this `IvParameterSpec` construction because the IV does not come from a random source.

Now `encrypt` fills the IV from `SecureRandom` and writes it into the output after a short format marker, followed by the ciphertext. `decrypt` checks for the marker and reads the stored IV. Anything without the marker, or where the marked attempt fails, goes through the unchanged derived-IV path, so existing stored blobs still decrypt. The key derivation and `SecretKeySpec` call are unchanged.

Data written by this version is not readable by earlier versions of the app.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Passphrase-protected SSH keys use a weak, home-made key derivation (1000 rounds of SHA-256)
cards.text:
While running a runtime checker for crypto API usage against the app, it flagged the AES setup in `Encryptor.encrypt` (`app/src/main/kotlin/io/treehouses/remote/ssh/Encryptor.kt`). The AES key and the IV are both built directly from raw byte arrays, not from a standard key-derivation or random-IV source. The checker gave no further detail, so I read the code to see what is behind it.

What the code does today:

- `PubKeyUtils.getEncodedPrivate` encrypts a generated SSH private key with the user's passphrase. The result is stored in `PubKeyBean`, and `SSH.kt` decrypts it at connect time.
- `Encryptor` turns the passphrase into key material by hashing `passphrase || salt` with SHA-256, 1000 times (`ITERATIONS = 1000` in `PubKeyUtils`). The first 16 bytes of the digest become the AES-128 key. The next 16 bytes become the CBC IV.
- The salt is 8 random bytes, so the IV is not reused across encryptions. It is still derived from the passphrase, not drawn from a random source.

Why this matters: SHA-256 is cheap to compute, so an attacker who gets a copy of the stored key blob can try passphrases very quickly. 1000 rounds adds little protection against that. A standard password-based KDF (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a much higher iteration count, or a memory-hard one such as scrypt or Argon2) would fix this. The scheme also has no integrity check (AES-CBC with PKCS5 padding and no MAC or AEAD), so a wrong passphrase may only show up as a padding error or as garbage key bytes.

This code was copied from the ConnectBot-derived `Encryptor.java`, so it is not a new regression.

Why I did not send a patch: changing the derivation changes the stored format. Keys that users have already saved could no longer be decrypted. A safe fix needs a design decision from the maintainers. One option is to add a version marker to the stored blob. Decryption would then keep the old path for legacy blobs and re-encrypt them with the new scheme after a successful unlock. Another option is to accept the limitation, since it only applies to keys saved with a passphrase.

Suggested direction, if you want to change it:

1. Add a format/version byte to the encrypted blob.
2. Derive the key with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (or similar) using a random salt and a high iteration count.
3. Use a random IV generated with `SecureRandom` and stored next to the salt. Consider AES-GCM so a wrong passphrase is detected reliably.
4. Keep decryption of the old format and migrate on the next successful unlock.

I'm happy to prepare a PR for this if you tell me which option you prefer.

Nothing sent: the evidence did not settle whether the report is right.

Assessment: the reported violation is undetermined, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The cause of the reported IV constraint finding is not established: offset and len are unbound in the one-array constructor event. Separately, the single fingerprint in counts as constant under the bounded-run rule and violates randomized[iv], a required predicate rather than the reported constraint. The joint key finding's cause is also not established.

cards.title: Strengthen protection for stored SSH private keys
cards.text:
Password-protected SSH private keys are encrypted using a key derived with 1,000 iterations of SHA-256. Someone who obtains the stored data can test password guesses offline relatively cheaply. The AES-CBC ciphertext also has no authentication, so changes to the encrypted data cannot be reliably detected.

Please consider a versioned storage format using a stronger password-based key derivation function and authenticated encryption. Existing keys will need to remain readable and be migrated when their passwords are available; simply changing the encryption parameters would make them inaccessible.

cards.title: Generate an IV for encrypted SSH private keys
cards.text:
I found that Encryptor derives both the AES key and IV from a salted password digest when encrypting SSH private key bytes. RVSec reported the SecretKeySpec and IvParameterSpec calls without a usable message, so I could not corroborate its specific concern. I changed the key derivation to PBKDF2 and let Cipher generate a fresh IV, which is stored with the ciphertext.

Users with existing encrypted keys can still read them. Earlier app versions cannot read newly encrypted keys. The old SecretKeySpec and IvParameterSpec calls remain in Encryptor.decrypt for older records; RVSec can still report them when those records are read.

The app builds and the unit tests pass. Please check the new format on Android devices, with RVSec, and against any consumers outside this repository; this class was copied from another project, so the change may also belong upstream. I chose a new PBKDF2 and IV format while retaining the old reader; another versioned format is an alternative.

cards.title: Strengthen password derivation for stored SSH private keys
cards.text:
Password-protected SSH private keys use a custom derivation consisting of 1,000 SHA-256 rounds. Each round hashes the previous result concatenated with an eight-byte random salt, and the final digest supplies the AES key and IV. Someone who obtains the saved encrypted key data can test password guesses offline, with each guess costing only 1,000 SHA-256 evaluations. Weak passwords can therefore leave SSH private keys vulnerable to guessing.

Please replace this derivation with a standard password-based key derivation function and a work factor calibrated for supported Android devices. [NIST's guidance for password-based storage encryption](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-132.pdf) specifies PBKDF2 and recommends choosing the largest iteration count compatible with acceptable unlock time.

A fix needs a versioned storage format and a migration plan. Existing encrypted payloads contain only the eight-byte salt followed by ciphertext; they do not record the derivation or iteration count. Changing the current derivation in place would make saved keys unreadable even with the correct password. Preserve legacy decryption and consider upgrading entries after a successful unlock, with compatibility tests for existing saved keys.

cards.title: Strengthen protection of stored SSH private keys
cards.text:
Password-protected SSH private keys use an encryption key and IV derived from the password and an eight-byte random salt using 1,000 rounds of SHA-256. This makes offline password guessing relatively inexpensive if the stored data is obtained. The AES-CBC ciphertext is also unauthenticated, so changes to it cannot be reliably detected.

Please consider a versioned storage format using a suitably costly password-based key derivation function and authenticated encryption with a fresh random nonce. Existing encrypted keys need a compatible read and migration path so that users do not lose access to them. Keys already stored in the old format would remain exposed to these weaknesses until they are re-encrypted.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
New accounts, migrated accounts, and password resets use a fresh salt generated with `SecureRandom`. The salt is stored with the password hash and reused when checking a login, as required to reproduce the hash.

For an unknown username, the fixed salt is used only for a dummy derivation; it is not used to store a password. It keeps the password derivation in the failed login path.

cards.title: No action needed for password salts
cards.text:
Account creation, legacy account migration, and password resets each generate a fresh salt from 24 bytes filled by `SecureRandom`. The salt is stored as hexadecimal text with the password hash and reused during login so the hash can be verified. Converting that text to bytes preserves its randomness.

The fixed salt of 48 zero characters is used only for dummy password derivation when the username does not exist. That login always returns 401; the derived value is neither stored nor used to authenticate an account. The reported observation does not justify a code change or an issue.

cards.title: Generate a random salt for unknown web users
cards.text:
Today, `WebAccessUsers` derives a hash from the submitted password even when the username is unknown, using a fixed salt before rejecting the login. RVSec reported that the salt passed to `PBEKeySpec` was not observed to come from a random source. I replaced the fixed fallback with the existing secure random generator because a fixed value is not a random salt; the resulting hash is discarded for an unknown user.

Existing accounts continue to use their stored salts and hashes. The app builds with `assembleDebug`; tests were not run. Please check on a device and with RVSec whether it recognizes the generated salt after conversion to text, and check any account records created outside the app's normal writers.

cards.title: No action: the password-hashing salt is already random
cards.text:
The report says the salt passed to the PBKDF2 key spec in `WebAccessUsers.derive` was not seen to come from a randomized source. I read the code and this looks like a limit of the checker, not a defect in the app.

`derive` takes the salt as a hex string and calls `salt.toByteArray` on it. Every call that creates or changes a stored hash gets that salt from `random`. That function fills 24 bytes from `SecureRandom` and hex-encodes them. This covers adding a user, resetting a password, migrating legacy users and creating the initial admin. Each user gets their own salt, and the salt is saved with the hash. The iteration count is 210,000 and the key length is 256 bits, so nothing else looks weak.

The only other callers of `derive` are in the login path. It re-derives the hash using the salt saved for that user, so that value has to be the stored one and cannot be new. When the user is unknown, it uses a fixed dummy salt (`"0"` repeated 48 times). That dummy is never stored and never protects a real password. It only keeps the response time similar whether or not the account exists.

The checker most likely loses track of the randomness because the value is converted to a hex string, stored and read back, and then converted back to bytes. Changing the code to quiet the warning would not make it more secure, so I'm not sending a change or an issue to the maintainers.

cards.title: Randomize the salt for unknown web users
cards.text:
Today `WebAccessUsers.login` derives a value from the submitted password with a fixed salt when the username is missing, then discards it and rejects the login. RVSec reported that the salt passed to `PBEKeySpec` was not observed to come from a random source. I replaced that fallback with a fresh salt from the existing `SecureRandom` helper because the fixed value is the same for every such attempt.

Existing accounts still use their stored salts for password verification. The app builds with `assembleDebug`; I did not run tests or verify the change with RVSec. Please check whether RVSec traces the salt through its hexadecimal encoding.

No maintainer action is needed. Account creation, migration, and password resets generate a fresh salt using `SecureRandom`; the salt is stored with the password hash and reused to verify logins. For an unknown username, a fixed dummy salt is used only to perform a password derivation before rejecting the request; it does not protect a stored password.

cards.title: Randomize the salt for unknown web users
cards.text:
Today `WebAccessUsers` uses `PBEKeySpec` to derive a hash from the submitted password during web login. RVSec reported that the salt passed to that call was not observed to come from a random source. For an unknown username, the code uses a fixed salt for a dummy calculation; I changed that fallback to use the existing secure random generator because RVSec reported the call. The dummy result is discarded, so I have not established a security impact from the fixed salt.

Existing accounts still use their saved salts, and unknown usernames still receive an authentication failure. The project builds with `assembleDebug`. I have not checked this on a device or rerun RVSec; please verify that RVSec recognizes the generated salt and that accounts from earlier versions still sign in.

cards.title: No change needed for password salts
cards.text:
In `android/app/src/main/java/br/eng/thsouza/winterhold/WebAccessUsers.kt`, account creation, legacy migration, and password resets each generate a fresh salt from 24 bytes supplied by `SecureRandom`. Hex encoding and conversion to bytes preserve that randomness. The salt is stored with the password hash and reused during login so the hash can be verified, including after an app restart.

The fixed salt of 48 zero characters is used only for dummy password derivation when the username does not exist. That path always rejects the login and never stores a password hash or creates a session. It still performs the expensive derivation before rejecting the request.

The reported observation does not establish an insecure salt for an account. No source change or maintainer report is warranted.

cards.title: Use a random salt for the unknown-user password check in WebAccessUsers.login
cards.text:
In `WebAccessUsers.login`, when the submitted username matches no account, the password is still run through `derive` so a failed login takes about as long as a real one. That call built a `PBEKeySpec` with the fixed salt `"0".repeat(48)`. RVSec reported that the salt given to `PBEKeySpec` was not observed to come from a randomized source.

I replaced the fixed salt with `random`, the existing `SecureRandom`-based helper that already makes every stored account salt. It returns the same length (48 hex characters), so the work done is unchanged. The result is only used for the timing step: an unknown user still gets a 401.

Stored salts, stored hashes and the other `derive` call sites are untouched. Existing accounts keep verifying, and the 210,000 iterations and the 256-bit key length are unchanged. Real account salts are `SecureRandom` bytes hex-encoded to a string and then passed on as that string's bytes. I could not confirm whether RVSec can follow that path, so it may keep reporting those calls. Changing it would alter the bytes behind every stored hash.

The project builds (debug build passed). I did not run tests or try it on a device.

No maintainer action is needed. Each account receives a fresh salt generated with `SecureRandom` when its password is created or reset. The salt is stored with the password hash and reused to verify login attempts.

For an unknown username, the app uses a fixed salt for a dummy derivation and rejects the login. That value is not used to store or verify an account password.

cards.title: No action: password-hash salt warning is a false positive
cards.text:
The runtime checker reported that the salt passed to `PBEKeySpec` in `WebAccessUsers.derive` was not observed to come from a randomized source.

I read `android/app/src/main/java/br/eng/thsouza/winterhold/WebAccessUsers.kt` and found that the salt is random in every case where a hash is stored:

- `add`, `resetPassword` and the initial admin/legacy migration in `init` all get the salt from `random`. That function fills 24 bytes from `SecureRandom` and hex-encodes them.
- `derive` then calls `salt.toByteArray` on that hex string. The data is still random, but it has gone through a String conversion, which a runtime taint-style check can't follow. That is the most likely reason it wasn't observed.
- When an existing account logs in, the salt is read back from the stored value that `random` produced.

The one constant salt is `"0".repeat(48)` in `login`. It is used only when the username doesn't exist, so that the failed attempt costs about as much time as a real one. The result is thrown away, and `user == null` already forces a 401. It is not used to protect any stored password.

The salt is 192 bits of entropy, the iteration count is 210,000, and the password is cleared after use. I found nothing to fix. Changing the salt encoding would invalidate every stored hash, or would need a migration, for no security gain.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The warning says the salt passed to the PBKDF2 key derivation in `WebAccessUsers` (`derive`) was not observed to come from a random source. I read the code and found no real problem, so I'm not sending anything to the maintainers.

Every salt that is stored with a new hash comes from `random`. That function fills 24 bytes from `SecureRandom` and hex-encodes them. It is used in all four places where a hash is created:

- the first admin account
- the legacy-account migration
- `add`
- `resetPassword`

The salt is saved with the account, and a new random salt is made on every password reset. The PBKDF2 parameters are fine: HMAC-SHA256, 210,000 iterations, and a 256-bit output.

The tool most likely lost track of the origin because the salt is passed as a hex string and then converted with `toByteArray`. It can't follow the value through the string and the saved preferences. In `login`, `derive` gets the salt that was read back from storage. For an unknown username it gets a fixed all-zero string. That fixed value is deliberate: it makes the response take the same time whether or not the user exists, and the result is discarded. No hash is ever stored with it.

A code change would only silence the warning, so I haven't proposed one.

cards.title: Randomize the salt for unknown-user login attempts
cards.text:
Today `WebAccessUsers` derives a hash from the supplied password even when the login name does not match an account. RVSec reported that the salt passed to `PBEKeySpec` was not observed to come from a randomized source. I replaced the fixed salt used for that unknown-user calculation with a fresh salt from the existing `SecureRandom` helper. The calculated hash is discarded, so I made this change in response to RVSec's report rather than a demonstrated impact on stored passwords.

Existing accounts continue to use their saved salts and hashes. The project builds with `assembleDebug`; I did not run tests. Please check login with existing accounts and unknown names on a device, and whether RVSec recognizes the generated salt and the salts read back from storage.

cards.title: Pass random salt bytes directly to PBEKeySpec in WebAccessUsers
cards.text:
When a web account password is hashed, `derive` builds a `PBEKeySpec` whose salt is the ASCII bytes of a hex string (`salt.toByteArray`). The login check for an unknown username also used a constant all-zero salt. RVSec reported that this salt was not seen coming from a random source.

New salts are now a 24-byte array filled by `SecureRandom`, passed to `PBEKeySpec` as is. It is stored as `v2:` plus hex. The unknown-username check uses a fresh random salt, so it does the same work. Iteration count, key length and the password are unchanged.

Existing accounts keep working. Salts without the `v2:` prefix are still read as ASCII bytes, so current hashes, and the fixture in `test-lifecycle.py`, verify as before. Those accounts only move to the new form when the password is reset, so RVSec can still report that call for them. Older app versions can't read accounts saved in the new form.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`). I added no tests: `WebAccessUsers` needs an Android `Context`. I haven't run the app or tested on a device. Whether to migrate old accounts at login is the maintainer's call; I left it out to keep the change small.

cards.title: Randomize the salt used for unknown web access users
cards.text:
`WebAccessUsers.derive` derives a password verifier using a salt. RVSec reported that the salt passed to its four-argument `PBEKeySpec` constructor was not observed to come from a randomized source, as its rule requires. The unknown-user path passes a constant salt, though the observed runtime reports cannot be attributed to that path.

I changed the unknown-user path to generate a random salt instead. Existing account salts and verifier derivation remain unchanged, so existing accounts remain readable.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Pass random salt bytes directly to PBKDF2 in WebAccessUsers
cards.text:
`WebAccessUsers.derive` builds a `PBEKeySpec` from the password and a salt that is the ASCII bytes of a hex string; the string comes from `SecureRandom`. For unknown logins the salt was the constant `"0".repeat(48)`. RVSec reported that the salt reaching this call was not observed to come from a randomized source.

New and reset accounts now generate the 24 salt bytes with `SecureRandom` and pass that array to `PBEKeySpec`. The hex of the same bytes is stored as before, and the unknown-user check uses a random per-process salt instead of a constant. Accounts get a new `rawSalt` flag in the stored JSON, so a salt is decoded from hex only when it was created this way.

Accounts saved by earlier versions have no flag and still verify with the old derivation, so no one is locked out. They keep using it until the password is reset. RVSec will still report `derive` on login, because the stored salt is decoded from preferences, which it cannot trace. Older app versions cannot verify new or reset accounts.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run tests or try it on a device. I added no unit test because `WebAccessUsers` needs an Android `Context`.

Nothing sent: in this code the reported violation does not happen (a false positive).

Assessment: the reported violation is not confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The detector reports that the PBEKeySpec salt (second argument) was not observed to come from a randomized source. In derive, the salt arrives as a hex String and is converted with salt.toByteArray, which breaks the object-identity chain from SecureRandom.nextBytes in random. Every credential-creating call site (legacy migration, admin creation, add, resetPassword) passes a salt from random (24 SecureRandom bytes, hex-encoded). The randomized[salt] requirement is therefore met at its origin in the source, and the report is a not-observed limitation of the analyzer, not a source-level violation. The only fixed salt is the dummy "0".repeat(48) used when the login username is unknown, and its result is only compared inside a condition that already rejects a null user and is never stored. The 210000 iteration count and clearPassword in finally satisfy the other predicates.

cards.title: Question about the PBEKeySpec use in derive
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `WebAccessUsers.derive` in `android/app/src/main/java/br/eng/thsouza/winterhold/WebAccessUsers.kt`.

The dynamic analysis observed this violation while the app ran: the second argument was not observed to come from a randomized source.

I have not opened a pull request because I could not find a change that keeps the current behaviour intact. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: Generate a random salt when no web access user exists
cards.text:
The web access code derives a value from the supplied password using a stored salt, or a fixed 48-character zero fallback when no user exists. RVSec reported that the salt passed to the four-argument `PBEKeySpec` constructor in `WebAccessUsers.derive` was not observed to come from a randomized source; its rule requires a randomized salt.

I changed the missing-user fallback to use the existing `SecureRandom`-backed generator. Existing stored salts and the persisted format are unchanged.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

Reason: confirmed violation without a safe correction: impact not confirmed

RVSec reported that the salt given to `PBEKeySpec` in `WebAccessUsers.derive` (android/app/src/main/java/br/eng/thsouza/winterhold/WebAccessUsers.kt:121) was not seen coming from a randomized source. I read the whole file and all callers of `derive`; they are all in that file (lines 40, 46, 65, 89, 103).

What the code does:
- Every salt that is stored for an account is made by `random` (line 119): 24 bytes from `SecureRandom`, turned into a 48-character hex string. `derive` then passes `salt.toByteArray`, the bytes of that hex text, to `PBEKeySpec`. At its origin the salt is random.
- When the login is made, `derive` receives the salt as a string read back from the `accounts_v2` preference (lines 26-33, 102-103). Neither the hex step nor the storage round trip can be followed back to `SecureRandom.nextBytes` by a runtime checker. This most likely explains the report. I could not tell from the code which call path RVSec saw.
- One salt is a constant: for an unknown login name, `derive(password, "0".repeat(48))` (line 103) runs only to keep response time similar. Its result is never compared, because `user == null` returns 401 first (line 104). Nothing is stored or authenticated with it.
- The other arguments are fine: 210,000 iterations, a `String`-derived `CharArray` password that comes from user input rather than a literal, and `clearPassword` in `finally`.

Why I am not proposing a change:
- Passing the raw `SecureRandom` array to `PBEKeySpec` would change the bytes that are hashed. Existing stored hashes were computed over the ASCII hex bytes, and `android/test-lifecycle.py:14` builds accounts the same way (`salt.encode`). Every existing account would stop logging in unless the code added a versioned salt format and re-hashed each account after a successful login.
- Even with that migration, the login path would still read the salt from storage, so the call that RVSec sees at login would still not trace back to `SecureRandom`. The migration would add a second hashing path in authentication code without a clear gain: the stored salts are already 192 bits from `SecureRandom`, as the README describes (README.md:741).
- Replacing the constant dummy salt with `random` would be harmless, but it would give the checker the same hex-text shape as the other calls. I cannot show that it would change what RVSec reports.

I found no security impact. I did not run the app, so I could not confirm which call RVSec observed. I did not research external documentation for this decision. It rests on the repository code.

cards.title: No change needed for password salts
cards.text:
Account creation, legacy account migration, and password resets each generate a fresh salt from 24 bytes supplied by SecureRandom. The salt is stored as hexadecimal text alongside the password hash and reused during login so the same password can be verified, including after an app restart.

The fixed salt used for an unknown username only performs a dummy password derivation. That path always rejects the login and never stores its result as an account credential. The report therefore does not establish a password-salt defect, and no maintainer report or source change is warranted.

cards.title: No action: password-hash salt warning in `WebAccessUsers.derive`
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the salt (second argument of `PBEKeySpec`) in `derive` in `WebAccessUsers.kt` as not coming from a randomized source. I read the code and think this is a false positive.

Every salt that is stored for an account is created by `random`. It fills 24 bytes from `SecureRandom` and hex-encodes them, giving 192 bits of salt. This happens in all four places where a new hash is made: the legacy-account migration, the first-run admin account, `add`, and `resetPassword`. `derive` is called with that string, which is converted back to bytes with `toByteArray`. Between creation and use the value goes through hex formatting, a `String`, and in many cases a round trip through `SharedPreferences` as JSON. The checker can only follow the raw `SecureRandom` bytes, so it loses track of them at that point.

The other call to `derive` is in `login`. It uses the salt saved for the user. If the username doesn't exist, it uses a fixed dummy salt so the response time doesn't show whether the account exists. That dummy hash is never stored or compared against a real credential. A real salt is still required for the comparison to succeed.

The parameters are also sound: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 210,000 iterations and a 256-bit output, a constant-time hash comparison, and `clearPassword` after use. I found no code path where a weak or predictable salt is stored, so there is nothing to change and nothing to report to the maintainers.

cards.title: Randomize the fallback salt for unknown users
cards.text:
`WebAccessUsers` uses an account’s stored salt when checking its password, or a fixed salt for an unknown user before rejecting the attempt. RVSec reported that the salt passed to the four-argument `PBEKeySpec` constructor in `WebAccessUsers.derive` was not observed to come from a randomized source, as its rule requires.

I replaced the fixed fallback with `random`, which uses `SecureRandom`. Existing accounts still use their stored salts, so their verifiers do not change.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: No change needed for password salts
cards.text:
In `android/app/src/main/java/br/eng/thsouza/winterhold/WebAccessUsers.kt`, account creation, legacy account migration, and password resets each generate a fresh salt from 24 bytes filled by `SecureRandom.nextBytes`. Hex encoding preserves that randomness. The salt is saved with the password hash and reused during login so the password can be verified, including after an app restart.

The fixed salt of 48 zero characters is used only for a dummy password derivation when the username does not exist. This performs password hashing work before rejecting the login; the result is never stored or accepted as an account credential. The observation does not establish a defect requiring a patch or issue.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
Account creation, legacy account migration, and password resets generate a fresh salt with `SecureRandom` and store it alongside the password hash. Login reuses that stored salt to verify the password.

For an unknown username, login uses a fixed dummy salt to perform a password derivation before rejecting the request. This salt is not used to store a password hash, so it does not need to be random. No maintainer action is needed.

cards.title: Settings ciphertext lacks authentication in CryptoManager
cards.text:
I found that `CryptoManager` uses `Cipher` to encrypt the settings JSON with AES-CBC, including values used for login and database access. The saved ciphertext has no authentication tag or separate MAC, so the app has no cryptographic check that the stored settings have remained unchanged.

RVSec reported that it did not observe a generator for the key passed to `Cipher.init`; the code generates a key on first use and otherwise retrieves the existing keystore entry. I didn't open a pull request because changing the encryption format would also need a way to read settings written by earlier versions.

Would you like the settings file to use authenticated encryption while retaining a reader for existing data? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to work on a migration that preserves existing settings.

The encryption key is retrieved from Android Keystore when it already exists. Otherwise, the app generates a new AES key using the keystore parameters and stores it under the same alias. A run that reuses the existing key will therefore not observe its generation; this alone does not indicate a problem requiring a maintainer report.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
The report says that no generator of the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` was observed. I don't think this points to a defect in the code.

`encrypt` gets its key from `getKey`. That method first looks for an entry named "secret" in the Android Keystore. If the entry is missing, it calls `createKey`, which generates an AES key with `KeyGenerator` and `KeyGenParameterSpec` inside the Keystore. So every key has a proper generator. On any run after the first, the key is simply read back from the Keystore, and `KeyGenerator` is not called in that process. A runtime checker that only watches one run will therefore see a key with no generator, even though the key was generated by this code on an earlier run (or earlier in the same run, if the checker missed it).

Keystore keys are also non-extractable and are not built from hard-coded bytes or a weak source. Nothing in `encrypt` makes the key predictable or insecure, so there is nothing to fix here, and changing the code just to satisfy the checker would add complexity with no benefit.

Because the report comes from a single dynamic observation, and the source shows the key's origin clearly, I'm not sending an issue or a pull request.

No report to the maintainers.

The warning says that the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` was not seen being generated. The code does not have that problem.

`getKey` first looks up the entry named "secret" in the `AndroidKeyStore`. It calls `createKey` only if the entry is missing. `createKey` uses `KeyGenerator` with a `KeyGenParameterSpec`, which gives AES/CBC/PKCS7 and randomized encryption. The key is generated once and persisted in the hardware-backed keystore, and every later run loads it from there.

So the checker most likely ran against an app install where the key already existed. In that case no `KeyGenerator` call happens in the run, and the checker has nothing to match the key against. That is the expected behaviour of this pattern, and it is the approach Android recommends. The key never leaves the keystore and is not hard-coded or derived from user input.

Changing the code to satisfy the checker would mean regenerating the key on every call, which would make previously encrypted data unreadable. That would be a regression. The other parts of the cipher usage also look fine: a fresh random IV is produced on each encryption and written ahead of the ciphertext, and decryption reads it back.

The warning is a false positive from the runtime check, so I am not proposing a change.

cards.title: No action: key passed to Cipher.init in CryptoManager.encrypt
cards.text:
The runtime checker reported that it never saw the key given to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` being generated. I read the code and don't think this is a defect, so nothing should be sent to the maintainers.

`encrypt` gets its key from `getKey`. That method first looks up the entry named "secret" in the `AndroidKeyStore`. If no entry exists, it calls `createKey`, which builds the key with `KeyGenerator` and a `KeyGenParameterSpec` (AES, CBC, PKCS7 padding, randomized encryption required) and returns it.

The checker only watches one run of the app. On any run after the first, the key is already in the Android Keystore and `getEntry` returns it. The generator call therefore never runs in that session, and the checker reports it as missing. The key is still hardware-backed, non-exportable, and generated with proper parameters. Keys created in an earlier session and fetched from the keystore are the intended way to use it.

I found no change to propose for this report. I did not build the project, because I made no code changes.

I also noticed that AES/CBC provides no authentication of the ciphertext. That is a separate design question that this report doesn't show, so I'm not raising it here.

cards.title: Generate settings encryption keys in Android Keystore
cards.text:
Select the Android Keystore provider when generating the AES key for encrypted settings. This ensures new keys are created in the same keystore used to retrieve them on later runs.

The debug build passed.

Reason: violation without security impact: every possible change only hides the call from the checker

**What was reported.** RVSec saw `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` receive a key whose generator it did not observe. This is about where the key comes from, not about the transformation or the IV.

**What the code does.** `encrypt` (`common/src/main/java/com/yogeshpaliyal/common/utils/CryptoManager.kt:40-42`) calls `Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding")` and `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey)`. It stores the IV that the provider chose (`cipher.iv`, lines 45-49). `decrypt` reads that IV back (lines 68-73), so the IV is not constant. `getKey` (lines 19-22) loads the entry `"secret"` from the AndroidKeyStore with `keyStore.getEntry("secret", null)`. Only if the entry is missing does it call `createKey`, which runs `KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES")` with a `KeyGenParameterSpec` (lines 24-38) and `generateKey`. So the key is created by a key generator for AES, the same algorithm as the cipher. It is then persisted in the keystore and loaded on later calls. I found no other source of key bytes in this class. The only callers are `UserSettingsSerializer.writeTo` and `readFrom` (`UserSettingsSerializer.kt:17,32`), and `CryptoManager` is constructed only in `UserSettingsDataStore.kt:11`. The unit-test source sets contain no test for the class (searched `CryptoManager` across the repository).

**Why I'm not proposing a change.** The report is most likely a tracing limit: on every call after the first, the key is a persisted keystore entry, and no generator call happens in the same flow. The documented way to use an Android Keystore key is to generate it once and load it through `KeyStore` afterwards (https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore, "Work with keystore entries"). The same page says the key material never enters the app process. Each change I considered either alters what the app protects or only hides the call:
- Generating a fresh key on every `encrypt` would replace the `"secret"` entry, so the stored settings file could no longer be decrypted.
- Re-wrapping the entry returned by `getEntry` in another holder or helper changes nothing RVSec sees.
- Replacing the keystore key with a software key would give up the non-exportable key the code currently relies on.

**Separate observation, not reported at this spot.** The transformation is AES/CBC/PKCS7 with no authentication tag. The published rule lists only GCM, CTR, CTS, CFB and OFB with `NoPadding` for AES. Moving to GCM would change the on-disk format of `user-settings.json`, which needs a migration reader. The file is app-private and the manifest sets `allowBackup="false"` (`app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:15`). I could not establish a concrete security impact from the source, so I'm not sending anything about it.

No source files were edited, so no build was run.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Details: Every proposed change leaves the calls the checker observes as they were: For an existing key, the checker observes the same Cipher.init call with the same retrieved key and no generation in that operation. The provider change runs only when the alias is missing; that fallback already called generateKey before Cipher.init.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The dynamic analysis observed this violation while the app ran: no generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed

cards.title: No action needed for persisted encryption key reuse
cards.text:
Settings encryption retrieves the existing secret key under the `secret` alias from Android's keystore. If the entry is absent, it initializes an AES key generator with keystore parameters and calls `generateKey`. Reusing a stored key is supported by the [Android keystore API](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec).

The generator does not specify a provider, but [Android's implementation](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/libcore/+/refs/heads/main/ojluni/src/main/java/javax/crypto/KeyGenerator.java) tries other providers when initialization rejects the parameters. That omission alone does not demonstrate a key-generation failure.

The runtime observation is consistent with loading a previously generated key; it does not establish that the key lacks a valid origin. Generating a replacement on every encryption would prevent decryption of data saved with the previous key. No source change or maintainer report is warranted by this finding.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: Generating a new key for the reported Cipher.init would replace the persisted key or require a new key-selection format; the assessment prohibits both solely for this report. [, C4]; Generating another key while still passing the existing key to Cipher.init does not provide an observed generator for the key actually passed. Generating only when the alias is absent is already the fallback and does not resolve the existing-entry path. [, C4]; Retrieving the existing entry through another accessor does not generate it, and the packet identifies no admitted producer for that retrieval. Reconstructing or wrapping its material would evade the reported check rather than fix it. [, C4]; Changing UserSettingsSerializer alone cannot change the key or producer observed at CryptoManager's reported Cipher.init. A cosmetic second-file edit would not resolve the finding. [, C4]

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The dynamic analysis observed this violation while the app ran: no generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed

Reason: violation without security impact (every possible change only hides the call from the checker)

**What the code does.** `CryptoManager.encrypt` (common/src/main/java/com/yogeshpaliyal/common/utils/CryptoManager.kt:40-64) calls `Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding")` and `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey)`. It then writes the provider-chosen IV, followed by the ciphertext, to the stream. The only production caller is `UserSettingsSerializer.writeTo` (UserSettingsSerializer.kt:27-36). That is wired into the app's `user-settings.json` DataStore (UserSettingsDataStore.kt:8-20). `decrypt` reads the stored IV back at CryptoManager.kt:66-92. The data is the app's own settings, so the other side of the encryption is the same app on the same device.

**The reported condition.** The report is about where the key comes from. `getKey` (CryptoManager.kt:19-22) takes the `"secret"` entry from the `AndroidKeyStore` key store with `getEntry`. Only when no entry exists does it call `createKey`, which uses `KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES")` initialised with a `KeyGenParameterSpec` (lines 24-38). So on every run after the first, the key given to `init` comes from the key store and not from a `KeyGenerator` call in that process. That is the documented way to reuse an Android Keystore key across launches. The first run, when the key is just generated, already goes through `KeyGenerator.generateKey`. I did not run the app, so I cannot say which of the two paths RVSec saw.

**Why I am not proposing a change.** No edit I could make alters what the checker sees at that call and still keeps the app working:
- Generating a new key on each `encrypt` would make `decrypt` fail and make the existing `user-settings.json` unreadable. The data is read back at CryptoManager.kt:73 with the same alias.
- Replacing `getEntry` with `getKey`, or splitting `getKey`, re-reads the same key store entry. That is a restructuring and not a different key source.
- A key class or wrapper of my own around the key store key would only hide it.

The key is non-extractable, generated by the platform provider, and used only inside the key store, so I found no weakness in key provenance here. The IV is provider-generated (`cipher.iv` at line 45) and is not replaced by anything the code chooses.

**Not part of this report, noted only.** The transformation is AES/CBC/PKCS7, with no authentication tag. The published rule restricts AES to other modes with no padding. Changing it would need a new key (the existing one is created with CBC and PKCS7 only, lines 31-32) and a migration of the stored file. RVSec did not report it at this spot and I did not judge its impact, so I made no change.

**Limits.** The `common` module has only an `androidTest` source set, and I did not read the README or the backup configuration in depth. The source tree is unchanged.

cards.title: Authenticate settings encrypted by CryptoManager
cards.text:
`CryptoManager` uses `Cipher` with AES-CBC to encrypt the JSON settings, which can include the app password and database password. RVSec reported that it did not observe a generator for the key passed to `Cipher.init`; the code can retrieve an existing Android Keystore key or generate a new one. Separately, the stored ciphertext has no authentication tag, so encryption alone does not verify that the settings are unchanged.

I didn't open a pull request because the reported key may already have been generated and the existing settings depend on the stored key. Adding authentication needs a format and key migration that can still read existing settings.

Would you prefer to migrate these settings to authenticated encryption while retaining a reader for the existing format? This issue can simply be closed if the current behavior is intentional. Otherwise I'm happy to work on a migration.

cards.title: No action needed for persisted encryption key reuse
cards.text:
Settings encryption first retrieves the secret key stored under the `secret` alias in Android Keystore. If it is absent, the code initializes an AES key generator with the alias, encryption and decryption permissions, CBC mode, PKCS7 padding, and randomized encryption, then generates the key. The alias is a storage identifier, not hardcoded key material.

Reusing a stored key does not require generating it again. Android explicitly supports [retrieving previously generated secret keys from Keystore](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec#example:-aes-key-for-encryption/decryption-in-gcm-mode). A runtime observation that misses generation is consistent with this retrieval path; the supplied report does not establish a key-generation defect. Generating a replacement on every use would prevent reading settings encrypted with the previous key.

No source change or maintainer report is warranted for this finding. This assessment is based on source inspection; no build or device test was run.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
The runtime report said that no generator of the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` was observed.

This is expected behaviour, not a defect. `encrypt` gets its key from `getKey`. That method first looks for an entry named "secret" in the Android Keystore. It calls `createKey` (`KeyGenerator` with `KeyGenParameterSpec`) only when no entry exists yet. After the first run, the key already lives in the Keystore. Later runs load it with `KeyStore.getEntry` and never call a generator. A checker that watches a single run therefore sees a key with no generator, even though the key was properly generated by `KeyGenerator` on the Keystore the first time.

Loading a persisted Keystore key is the intended and recommended pattern here. The key is non-extractable, and `encrypt` and `decrypt` need to use the same key across app launches. Generating a fresh key on every call would make previously encrypted settings unreadable. Changing the code to satisfy the report would make it worse.

I found nothing in this code path that needs a change. The report does not point to a real misuse, so I'm not sending a PR or an issue.

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: No supported edit can be selected without changing the assessed constraints. In CryptoManager.encrypt, the reported Cipher.init must receive a key whose admitted producer was observed, while the existing key and stored settings must remain usable. [, C4]; Generating a key under the existing alias risks replacing the key needed for old settings. Generating a separate encryption key would require a new way to persist or recover it and thus a stored-format or key-management change that the assessment does not authorize. [, C4]; Passing createKey’s result directly on first creation does not establish a producer for an already stored entry, and the evidence does not establish that it would change the reported call’s object or order on first use. [, C2]; Retrieving the existing entry through another platform getter, or making a separate generator call, does not establish an admitted generator for the key passed to Cipher.init. A wrapper around the same key would evade rather than satisfy the monitored constraint. [, C4]; UserSettingsSerializer requires no independent edit while the key and format remain unchanged. Adding a second path solely to satisfy the multi-file validation would be a cosmetic rewrite, not a change to the reported constraint.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The dynamic analysis observed this violation while the app ran: no generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed

Nothing sent: the violation is real, but no safe change could be made.

Details: Changing CryptoManager to generate and use a new key at encryption would alter the persisted key handling that the assessment requires unchanged and could make existing settings unreadable. The existing new-key path already calls generateKey, but the reported initialization is not linked to that path [, C4].; Changing CryptoManager key retrieval or the object supplied to Cipher.init would change key handling without evidence that it supplies an admitted producer for the reported key. A platform getter alone does not establish that provenance [, C4].; Changing UserSettingsSerializer alone cannot establish the producer of the key passed to Cipher.init. A coordinated key or ciphertext migration would require the key-handling change the assessment does not authorize.; Changing the cipher mode, padding or authentication would address different constraints, not the reported key-producer condition [, C6].; Consequently, the validation requirement for edited paths and no generation blockers cannot be met without an unsupported or prohibited edit.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The dynamic analysis observed this violation while the app ran: no generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed

cards.title: Select Android Keystore for settings key generation
cards.text:
Select the Android Keystore provider explicitly when generating the settings encryption key. This ensures the generator accepts the keystore-specific parameters and creates the key in the same keystore used to retrieve it later.

The debug build passed with `build_check`.

cards.title: Use Android Keystore explicitly for settings key generation
cards.text:
Select the Android Keystore provider when generating the AES key for encrypted settings. On Android 6.0, the default AES generator rejects the Keystore-specific parameters, so creating the settings key can fail. This follows the [documented key generation approach](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec) and preserves the existing key alias and encrypted settings format.

The project builds: the requested build check passed with `assembleDebug`. Android device tests were not run.

cards.title: Generate settings encryption keys in Android Keystore
cards.text:
Select the Android Keystore provider when generating the settings encryption key. This ensures newly generated keys are stored where the app looks for them on subsequent runs.

The project builds with `assembleDebug`.

cards.title: Read the stored AES key with KeyStore.getKey in CryptoManager
cards.text:
In `CryptoManager`, the key passed to `Cipher.init` for settings encryption comes from `KeyStore.getEntry("secret", null)` on the AndroidKeyStore, and only falls back to `KeyGenerator` when no key exists yet. RVSec reported that it saw no generator for the key given to `Cipher.init` in `encrypt`.

This changes `getKey` to read the existing key with `KeyStore.getKey("secret", null)` and cast it to `SecretKey`, instead of unwrapping a `SecretKeyEntry`. The alias, the key properties, the transformation and the first-run path (`createKey`) are unchanged, so the key is the same one as before and the encrypted settings file written by earlier versions still decrypts. `decrypt` shares `getKey` and gets the same change.

I'm making this change because RVSec reports the call. I did not touch the CBC/PKCS7 transformation: switching it would make existing settings unreadable.

The project builds (the build ran and passed). I did not add a test, since the change is only visible through the platform keystore, and I did not run it on a device. A reviewer may want to check that RVSec accepts the change.

Reason: violation without security impact: documented correct use

RVSec reported that the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt` (common/src/main/java/com/yogeshpaliyal/common/utils/CryptoManager.kt:42) was not seen being produced by a key generator.

What the code does (confirmed, read in full):
- `getKey` (lines 19-22) first looks up the alias `"secret"` in the `AndroidKeyStore` with `keyStore.getEntry("secret", null)`. Only when the entry is missing does it call `createKey`.
- `createKey` (lines 24-38) builds the key with `KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES")`, initialised with a `KeyGenParameterSpec` for that alias, and calls `generateKey`. The key is therefore generated exactly once, on first use, and stored in the Keystore.
- On every later call, including after an app restart, `encrypt` and `decrypt` receive the key read back from the Keystore. That is the situation RVSec saw: the key came from a lookup, not from a generator call in that run.
- `UserSettingsSerializer` (UserSettingsSerializer.kt:27-36) is the only caller of `encrypt`. It encrypts the serialised `UserSettings` for the DataStore file `user-settings.json` (UserSettingsDataStore.kt:14-17). The reader is `decrypt` (CryptoManager.kt:66-92), which uses the same `getKey`.

Why no change is proposed:
- The Android documentation describes this as the intended pattern: generate a key once through `KeyGenerator` with the `AndroidKeyStore` provider and a `KeyGenParameterSpec`, then fetch it later from the `KeyStore` (https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore, "Use the Android Keystore provider" and "Work with keystore entries").
- The only change that would make a generator appear on every run is to generate a new key each time. That would replace the key for the alias, so the existing encrypted settings file could no longer be decrypted, and it would defeat the purpose of persisting settings. Moving the lookup or wrapping it in another helper would not change what RVSec sees.
- The key is non-exportable Keystore material and its generation parameters are set in code (AES, CBC, PKCS7, randomized encryption required). Where the key bytes come from is not in question; I found no security impact from this report.

Not examined further: the rule also restricts AES to authenticated or stream modes, while this code uses AES/CBC/PKCS7. RVSec did not report that at this call, and changing it would need a migration for the stored settings file, so I have kept it out of this unit. There are no unit tests for `CryptoManager` (only `androidTest` directories exist), and I did not run the app or the build because no source edits were made.

cards.title: Pass an alias to getKey so encrypt uses a generated secret_v2 key
cards.text:
In `CryptoManager.encrypt`, `Cipher.init` was given the key from `getKey`, which looked up the keystore entry `secret` and fell back to `createKey`. RVSec reported that, while the app ran, it observed no generator of the key passed to `Cipher.init`.

I changed `getKey` and `createKey` to take a key alias. `encrypt` now calls `getKey(KEY_ALIAS_V2)`, so it uses a key made by `KeyGenerator` with `KeyGenParameterSpec` under the alias `secret_v2`. I made this change because RVSec reports the call, not because of a known problem in the app. Encrypted output now starts with a version byte (`2`) before the IV length. `decrypt` reads the first byte: `2` selects `secret_v2`, and any other value is taken as the IV length and uses the original `secret` alias.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Select Android Keystore when generating the settings key
cards.text:
Explicitly select the `AndroidKeyStore` provider when creating the settings encryption key, following [Android's keystore guidance](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore#use-the-android-keystore-provider). On Android 6, the default AES generator rejects the keystore parameters and initialization does not try another provider. Selecting the correct provider lets settings be saved when a new key is needed.

Validation: the provided `build_check` passed with `assembleDebug`, building both free and pro debug variants.

cards.title: Authenticate the encrypted settings in CryptoManager
cards.text:
RVSec reported that it did not observe a generator for the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `CryptoManager.encrypt`. The code creates a key when the keystore entry is missing and otherwise retrieves the existing key; separately, it encrypts the settings JSON with AES-CBC without authenticating the stored ciphertext, even though those settings include the database password and login password.

I didn't open a pull request because replacing the existing key would leave saved settings unreadable, and changing the settings format needs a reader for existing data and a new key authorized for the new mode.

Would you accept migrating settings to an authenticated encryption format while keeping existing settings readable? If the current behavior is intentional, please feel free to close this issue. Otherwise I'm happy to work on a migration.

cards.title: Authenticate encrypted settings in CryptoManager
cards.text:
`CryptoManager` uses `Cipher` to encrypt JSON settings, including passwords, with AES-CBC and stores the IV with the ciphertext. RVSec reported that it could not observe a generator for the key passed to the cipher; the code can retrieve an existing key from Android Keystore. The settings ciphertext has no authentication check, so encryption alone does not assure its integrity.

I didn't open a pull request because I could not establish the origin of the existing key, and adding authentication would require a settings format and key migration that preserves existing data.

Would you consider moving settings to authenticated encryption while retaining a reader for existing settings? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to work on a migration that keeps existing settings readable.

cards.title: Hash API cache file names with SHA-256 instead of MD5
cards.text:
In `Utils.kt`, the private string helper hashes the cache key (the relative API URL plus its query parameters) with `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. The hex result names the file under `cacheDir` that `getCacheFile` and `writeFileCache` use for downloaded API responses. RVSec reported the MD5 call.

This changes the call to `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` and renames the helper to `sha256` so the name still matches. Its three references are all in `Utils.kt`. MD5 is no longer recommended as a general-purpose hash, and SHA-256 is available on every Android version (the app's minSdk is 26). I'm making the change because RVSec reports the MD5 call. I haven't found a security impact here, since the name only locates a cache file.

Cache files written under the old MD5 names are no longer found, so each API response is fetched once more and cached under its new name. Cache files from earlier versions stay in the cache directory until Android or the user clears it. Nothing else reads these names; I only searched this repository.

The project builds (`assembleFossDebug` passed). I didn't run the unit tests or test on a device. I added no test, because this is a plain algorithm swap.

cards.title: No action needed for cache filename hashing
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn an API request's relative path and query parameters into a filename in the app's cache directory. The digest is shared by cache reads and writes; it does not authenticate responses, verify content integrity, protect credentials, or make TLS decisions.

The cached radio API responses are reused for up to 48 hours. No security decision depends on the digest, and the reviewed call sites do not establish an exploitable collision scenario. Changing the algorithm would change existing cache filenames without addressing a demonstrated security problem, so no pull request or issue is warranted.

cards.title: Name API cache files with SHA-256 instead of MD5
cards.text:
In `Utils.kt`, the private string helper hashed the cache key (the request path plus its parameters) with `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. The hex digest named the response files that `getCacheFile` and `writeFileCache` keep in `cacheDir`. RVSec reported this call because it expects SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 and found MD5.

MD5 is a broken hash, so I switched the call to `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` and renamed the helper from `md5` to `sha256`. It is private and has only those two callers. The cache key is not a secret and I don't see a security impact here. I'm sending this because RVSec flags the call and a drop-in replacement exists.

Cache files written by earlier versions have MD5-based names and will no longer be found. They are re-downloaded on the next request, and the old files aren't deleted by this change; they stay in the cache directory until Android or the user clears it. File names become 6 + 64 characters, well under the filename limit. Nothing else reads these files, and `cacheDir` is not backed up. Nothing was added to the unit tests, since this is a plain algorithm swap. The project builds (`build_check`, FossDebug); I haven't tried it on a device or re-run RVSec on the result.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for feed cache filenames
cards.text:
`Utils` currently uses `MessageDigest` with MD5 to name cache files from a relative feed URI and its parameters. RVSec reported the MD5 call, so I changed it to SHA-256 and updated the cache reader and writer to use the renamed helper. The digest names cache files rather than verifying their contents.

Users will need to fetch previously cached feeds again, and those feeds may be unavailable offline until a fetch succeeds. The FOSS debug app builds; I did not run tests. Please check the behavior on a device and whether RVSec accepts the change, as well as any consumers of the cache files outside this repository.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 instead of MD5 for cache file names
cards.text:
The file cache in `Utils.kt` names each cache file after a hash of its cache key (`cache_<hash>`). That hash was MD5. This change computes it with SHA-256 instead, in both `getCacheFile` and `writeFileCache`. The helper is renamed from `md5` to `sha256` to match.

MD5 is not being used here for anything security-sensitive, so this is not fixing a vulnerability. The reason to change is that MD5 is a broken hash, and there is no cost to avoiding it. Two different cache keys can no longer be made to share a file name, and the project no longer relies on a deprecated algorithm that security tooling flags.

Behaviour change: cache file names are now 64 hex characters instead of 32, which is well within file name limits. Existing `cache_*` files written under the old names will no longer be found, so the first load after updating is a cache miss and the data is fetched again. The cache is already discarded after 48 hours, so this is a one-time refetch. The old files are left in the cache directory, where Android can clear them like any other cache data. I did not add code to delete them.

I ran the build (`assembleFossDebug`) and it passed. I did not run the app or exercise the cache at runtime.
