cards.title: No action
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn API request keys into filenames in the app's private, temporary cache. It does not protect credentials or verify downloaded content. The cache can be repopulated from the API and entries expire after 48 hours.

Although MD5 is unsuitable where collision resistance is a security requirement, this use does not establish such a requirement. Changing the filename hash would invalidate existing cache entries without addressing a demonstrated security problem, so there is nothing to report to maintainers.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The report flags the MD5 digest in `Utils.md5` (app/src/main/kotlin/com/ounben/amaradio/Utils.kt). I don't think the maintainers need to hear about it.

MD5 is used only to turn a cache key (a feed URL plus parameters) into a file name for the on-disk response cache (`getCacheFile` and `writeFileCache`). The digest isn't used for authentication, integrity checks, signatures, password storage or anything an attacker could exploit. At worst, two keys that collide would share a cache file. Such a collision would be hard to produce, and the file would expire after 48 hours anyway. Nothing in the repository treats the hash as a security boundary.

Switching to SHA-256 would only silence the warning. It would also change every cache file name. Files written under the old names would be orphaned in the cache directory, because nothing deletes them until the system clears the cache. That makes the change slightly worse than leaving the code alone, with no security gain.

The one other digest in the code, in `CustomStationManager.kt`, already uses SHA-256.

I didn't change any code and I didn't run the build.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn request keys into filenames in the app's disposable cache. It does not protect passwords, verify data, or establish trust. The cache expires after 48 hours, and a cache miss causes the app to fetch the data again.

Changing the digest would invalidate existing cache entries without addressing a demonstrated security problem. No maintainer action is needed for this use.

cards.title: Question about the MessageDigest use in md5
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `Utils.md5` in `app/src/main/kotlin/com/ounben/amaradio/Utils.kt`.

Utils.md5 (Utils.kt:105) calls MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5"), a literal outside the allowed algorithm set {SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512}, which violates the rule's algorithm constraint. The digest is only a cache-file key: "cache_"+hex names a file under ctx.cacheDir, and both getCacheFile (read) and writeFileCache (write) derive it from the same method.

I have not opened a pull request because I could not find a change that keeps the current behaviour intact. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for cache filenames
cards.text:
In `Utils.kt`, cache reads and writes currently use an MD5 hash of the cache key in the filename. RVSec flagged the `MessageDigest.getInstance` call in `Utils.md5` for using MD5, which is unsuitable where collision resistance is required.

I changed the helper to use SHA-256 and updated both callers, keeping the byte conversion and lowercase hexadecimal formatting. Reads and writes still use matching filenames, but existing MD5-named cache files will no longer be found.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for response cache filenames
cards.text:
`Utils` uses `MessageDigest` to name cached responses from the relative request URI and its parameters. RVSec reported the MD5 call; I changed it to SHA-256, which Android recommends when the algorithm can be chosen freely. This change addresses the report; I did not find a security use for this cache digest.

Users will fetch previously cached responses again after updating, because their old cache filenames no longer match. The app build passed. Please check for any external consumers of these cache filenames and verify the change with RVSec on a device.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 to name the API cache files
cards.text:
I ran the app under RVSec, which reported the `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` call in `Utils.kt`. That call hashes the cache key (the request path plus its query parameters) to build the `cache_<hex>` file name that `getCacheFile` and `writeFileCache` use in the app's cache directory.

I changed the call to `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` and renamed the private helper from `md5` to `sha256`, so its name still matches what it does. MD5 is a broken hash. RVSec's message lists SHA-256 among the algorithms it expects. This is not a security fix: the hash only names cache files, and I did not find any security use of it.

Cache file names get longer, 64 hex characters instead of 32. Cache files written by earlier versions will no longer be found, so each request is fetched once more. Cached entries already expire after 48 hours, and old files are not deleted, so the system clears them when it needs space. Nothing else in the repository computes or reads these names.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run tests or try it on a device. I left the old CHANGELOG line about MD5-hashed caching as it was. If you would rather keep MD5 for a cache name, this can be closed.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for feed cache filenames
cards.text:
Today `Utils` hashes the relative feed URI and parameters with `MessageDigest` to name cached responses. RVSec reported the use of MD5 at that call. I switched the cache reader and writer to SHA-256 because Android recommends SHA-2; the digest is used for cache filenames rather than a security check.

Users will need to fetch previously cached feeds again after updating, and those feeds may be unavailable offline until fetched. Earlier app versions cannot use the new cache filenames. The foss debug app build passed; I did not run tests. Please check the cache behavior on a device and whether RVSec accepts the change.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for cache filenames
cards.text:
Today, `Utils.md5` hashes cache keys with MD5 to name cache files. RVSec reported its `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` call under its rule. MD5 is unsuitable where collision resistance is required.

I switched both cache reads and writes to SHA-256 and renamed the helper, preserving the input conversion and full hexadecimal encoding. Both paths still use the same filename derivation. Existing MD5-named cache files will no longer be found and may remain until cache cleanup.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 to name API cache files
cards.text:
`Utils.getCacheFile` and `Utils.writeFileCache` name each cached API response `cache_<hash>`, where the hash is computed in the private `String.md5` helper with `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` over the request path plus its query parameters. RVSec reported that MD5 call; SHA-256 is among the algorithms it expects.

MD5 has known collision attacks, so I replaced it with `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` and renamed the helper to `sha256` so its name matches what it does. Nothing else changed: the key, the `cache_` prefix, the 48-hour expiry and the hex encoding are the same. I'm not claiming a security impact here. The hash only names files in `cacheDir`, so this is done because RVSec reports the call.

Cache files written by earlier versions are named with the MD5 value and will no longer be found, so the first requests after the update go to the network. They sit in the app's cache directory, which Android may clear when space is needed, and I found no other code that reads these file names. I ran the build and it passed. I did not run the tests or try it on a device. A maintainer may prefer to leave this as is, since the hash is not a security control.

Today, `Utils.md5` hashes cache keys with MD5 to name cache files. RVSec flagged its `MessageDigest.getInstance` call under its SHA-2 rule. MD5 is unsuitable where collision resistance is required, though these digests are not an identified security control.

I switched cache lookups and writes to SHA-256 and renamed the helper. Existing MD5-named files become cache misses, but they are disposable entries; cache content and expiration are unchanged.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for cache-file keys
cards.text:
I found that `Utils.md5` hashes the cache key with MD5 to create a non-security cache-file name. RVSec reported its `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")` call under its rule. MD5 is unacceptable where collision resistance is required.

I changed the helper to use SHA-256 and updated both cache lookups and writes. They still use the same input and full hexadecimal digest, so the paths remain consistent. Existing MD5-named entries will become cache misses.

cards.title: No action
cards.text: MD5 is used only to turn a Radio Browser request key into a filename in the app's local cache. It is not used to authenticate data, verify integrity, or protect secrets. A collision could cause one cached response to be returned for another request, but the cache is temporary and requests can be refreshed. This use does not warrant a security change on its own.

cards.title: No action needed for cache filename hashing
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn an API request path and its parameters into a filename in the app's private cache directory. The cached responses are reused for up to 48 hours. The digest does not authenticate responses, verify their integrity, protect credentials, or participate in TLS.

This use does not require a cryptographically secure digest. Replacing MD5 would change cache filenames and cause existing entries to be missed without addressing a demonstrated security problem. No code change or issue is warranted for this finding.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 instead of MD5 for cache file names
cards.text:
The file cache in `Utils.kt` derives each cache file name from a hash of the cache key. It used MD5 for this. This change switches it to SHA-256 and renames the helper from `md5` to `sha256`.

MD5 isn't a security risk here, because the hash only names files in the app's private cache directory. But MD5 is deprecated and gets flagged by crypto-usage checkers. SHA-256 is already used elsewhere in the app (`CustomStationManager`), and the change is small, so this keeps the app on one digest.

Cache file names go from 32 to 64 hex characters, which is well within filesystem limits. Files already in the cache under their old MD5 names won't be found again. That only costs one re-fetch per entry, since cache entries expire after 48 hours anyway, and the cache directory is cleaned up by Android as needed.

I ran `:app:assembleFossDebug` and it built successfully. I didn't test the cache behaviour on a device.

cards.title: No action needed for cache filename hashing
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn a radio-directory request path and its query parameters into a fixed-length filename in the app's private cache directory. The cache stores downloaded responses and reuses them for up to 48 hours. The digest does not verify response integrity, protect credentials, authenticate requests, or make trust decisions.

This use does not require a cryptographically secure digest. The finding does not establish a security problem in this cache lookup, and changing the algorithm would make existing cache entries unreachable without a demonstrated security benefit. No source change or maintainer report is warranted.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 instead of MD5 for cache file names
cards.text:
The feed cache in `Utils.kt` names its files `cache_<hash of the cache key>`. The hash was MD5. This changes it to SHA-256.

MD5 is not a security problem here. The hash only turns a cache key (a URL plus parameters) into a safe file name, and nothing depends on it resisting collisions. I'm proposing the change anyway because MD5 is deprecated, security scanners flag it, and SHA-256 is just as easy to use. The helper is renamed from `md5` to `sha256` to match.

One side effect: cache files are now named differently, so existing cached feeds won't be found after the update. They are refetched on the next request. The old files stay in the cache directory until Android clears it. Cached entries expire after 48 hours anyway, so the impact is small. File names grow from 32 to 64 hex characters plus the `cache_` prefix, well within filename limits.

I ran the debug build (`:app:assembleFossDebug`) and it passed. I did not run the app or exercise the cache by hand.

cards.title: No action needed for cache filename hashing
cards.text:
MD5 is used only to turn a Radio Browser request path and its parameters into a filename prefixed with `cache_` in the app's private cache directory. Cache reads and writes use the same mapping, and reads discard entries that are at least 48 hours old.

The digest does not protect credentials, verify response integrity, or determine whether a server is trusted. This filename mapping does not rely on cryptographic collision resistance for a security decision. The reported use therefore does not warrant a code change or an issue.

cards.title: No action needed
cards.text: MD5 is used only to turn API request keys into filenames for temporary cached responses. It is not used to protect passwords, verify authenticity, or make security decisions. A collision could cause the wrong cached response to be returned, but this use does not establish a security boundary, and the cache is disposable. Replacing the digest solely for this report would invalidate existing cache entries without addressing a demonstrated problem.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 for response cache file names
cards.text:
The response cache currently uses `MessageDigest` with MD5 to name files from the relative request URI and parameters. RVSec reported the MD5 call; I changed it to SHA-256 because of that report and updated both cache reads and writes. The digest names cache files and is not used here to authenticate their contents.

Users will need to fetch previously cached responses again after updating; those responses may be unavailable offline until fetched. I built the foss debug app successfully. Please check the cache behaviour on a device, any consumers outside this repository, and whether RVSec accepts the change.

cards.title: Read the Android keystore key with KeyStore.getKey
cards.text:
In `SecretService.getAndroidSecretKey`, the code loads the AndroidKeyStore `KeyStore` with `load(null)`, calls `getEntry(androidKey.alias, null)`, and takes `secretKey` from the resulting `SecretKeyEntry`. If no key exists, it falls back to `initAndroidSecretKey`.

RVSec reported that this call sequence on `KeyStore` (`load`, then `getEntry` with no `getKey` after it) is not one its KeyStore rule accepts. I replaced the `getEntry` lookup with `androidKeyStore.getKey(androidKey.alias, null) as? SecretKey`, so the sequence is now `load`, `getKey`. The `initAndroidSecretKey` fallback is kept. This change is made only because RVSec reports the call.

It should be safe because both calls are read-only and return the same AndroidKeyStore key. The `SecretKeyHolder`, its callers and the stored and exported ciphertext are unchanged.

cards.title: No action: nothing to send to the maintainers
cards.text:
A runtime checker flagged the call order in `SecretService.getAndroidSecretKey`. I read the code and don't think it is a real defect, so I'm not proposing a change or opening an issue.

The method does what Android's documentation prescribes for the platform key store. It uses a `KeyStore` instance obtained with `KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore")` and calls `load(null)`. It then reads the entry with `getEntry(alias, null)`. If no entry exists, it generates a new AES key through the key store.

The AndroidKeyStore provider has no store file and no store password, so `load(null)` is the intended call. `getEntry` takes a null protection parameter because the key material never leaves the secure hardware. Generic key store usage rules expect a password-protected store loaded from a stream. They have no model for this provider, so they report the sequence even though it is correct on Android.

The code has no real misuse that I could point to. The key is created with GCM and no padding, it is never exported, and the lookup and creation paths are separate. Changing the sequence to satisfy the checker, for example by passing a dummy password, would add noise or break the lookup. The only oddity is that `load(null)` is repeated on every call, but that is harmless and is the common pattern on Android.

I made no code changes, so I did not run the build.

The project builds (`assembleDebug` passed). I did not run the tests or try it on a device. I did not touch the `load(null)` that runs on every call of this method, so RVSec may still report that part. Please check on a device that existing installs still find their keys.

cards.text:
In `SecretService.getAndroidSecretKey` the app loads the AndroidKeyStore `KeyStore` and reads the AES key for an alias with `getEntry(alias, null)`, then unwraps the `SecretKeyEntry`. The existing fallback to `initAndroidSecretKey` then runs exactly as before. The change is a different read call, not a new behaviour. Only the key read changes. Key generation, the alias names and what callers get back are the same, and nothing stored changes format.

The project builds (debug assembly passed). I did not run the tests or try it on a device. The reviewer might check on a device that existing installs still read their stored keys.

cards.title: No action: runtime checker warning on getAndroidSecretKey
cards.text:
A runtime checker for Java crypto API usage flagged `SecretService.getAndroidSecretKey` because the sequence of KeyStore calls it observed did not match the checker's expected pattern. I looked at the code and don't think the maintainers need to hear about it.

What the code does:

- `SecretService` keeps one `KeyStore` instance, created once with `KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore")` (line 54).
- `getAndroidSecretKey` calls `load(null)` on that instance and then `getEntry(alias, null)`.
- If there is no secret key entry, it creates a key with `KeyGenerator` on the same provider.

Why I think this is a false positive:

- The `getInstance` call happens in the object initializer, not in the method. A checker that looks at one method at a time sees `load` without `getInstance` before it. A checker that sees repeated `load` calls on a shared instance may also complain.
- For the `AndroidKeyStore` provider, `load(null)` takes no stream or password. It only marks the instance as initialized and is safe to call repeatedly. The `null` protection parameter to `getEntry` is the normal usage for this provider, because key material never leaves the secure hardware or keystore daemon.
- I found no wrong algorithm, no weak parameters, and no missing step. The key spec is AES/GCM/NoPadding and the code handles a missing entry.

I considered moving `getInstance` and `load` into the method so the call order is visible in one place. That would only quiet the warning. It would create a new `KeyStore` object on every key lookup for no functional benefit, and the other methods in the class use the shared instance the same way. A PR that only changes code to satisfy a checker, with no behavior change, would be noise for the maintainers.

I did not change any code or run the build.

I changed the code to read the key directly with `KeyStore.getKey`. It retains the fallback when the returned key is missing or is not a secret key.

cards.text:
The key-loading code initializes the Android keystore with `load(null)` before calling `getEntry(alias, null)`. This matches [Android's documented usage](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore#WorkingWithKeyStoreEntries). When no secret key is found, the app initializes an AES key generator with the alias and generates the key through the Android keystore provider. The provider automatically stores the generated key under that alias, as described in the [key generation documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec). No separate save operation is required.

The reported sequence does not establish an API misuse, so no source change or maintainer report is warranted. No build or device test was run.

I changed the read to use `getKey` with the AndroidKeyStore null password and a safe `SecretKey` cast. The existing alias, fallback initialization, and exception propagation remain in place.

cards.text:
The Android keystore is loaded before the app retrieves the entry. A null protection parameter is appropriate for retrieving an Android keystore key, and a missing entry causes the app to generate a key. The keystore is shared and may be loaded again on later calls; reloading is supported by the API.

The reported sequence alone does not show a defect that needs a maintainer report or a code change. See the [Android keystore documentation](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore) and the [KeyStore API documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore).

cards.title: Open a fresh, loaded Android key store per operation instead of re-loading a shared one
cards.text:
`SecretService` kept a single `KeyStore` instance for the whole process and called `load(null)` on it at the start of every operation (`getAndroidSecretKey`, `getServerPrivateKey`, `getServerPublicKey`, `removeAndroidSecretKey`, `generateRsaKeyPair`). The same object was therefore loaded over and over, and it was shared between threads, which call these methods concurrently.

The documented way to use a `KeyStore` is to create it with `getInstance`, call `load` once, and then read entries. A runtime check of the crypto API usage flagged `getAndroidSecretKey` for this reason: on the shared instance it saw `load` repeated, and `getEntry` after earlier calls, instead of that sequence.

This change replaces the shared field with a small private helper, `openAndroidKeyStore`, that creates a new `KeyStore`, loads it, and returns it. Each operation now uses its own instance, so each one follows the standard order, and there is no longer a shared mutable key store object. The keys themselves live in the Android Keystore, not in the Java object, so key lookup, creation and deletion behave as before.

One small side effect: `generateRsaKeyPair` used to call `load(null)` on the shared key store without using it afterwards. That call is dropped, because `KeyPairGenerator` for the `AndroidKeyStore` provider does not need it.

I ran the debug build (`assembleDebug`) and it passed. I have not run the app or the instrumented tests on a device, so the behaviour on real hardware is untested. The reported sequence is a runtime-check finding and I have not re-run that check against this change.

cards.title: Use a freshly loaded Android key store for each key store operation
cards.text:
`SecretService` kept a single `KeyStore` object for the whole process and called `load(null)` on it at the start of nearly every operation (`getAndroidSecretKey`, `getServerPrivateKey`, `getServerPublicKey`, `removeAndroidSecretKey`, `generateRsaKeyPair`). So the same instance was re-initialised many times, and from several threads, while other calls were using it. A runtime check of the key store API flagged this: the sequence it saw in `getAndroidSecretKey` (a repeated `load` on an already-loaded instance, followed by `getEntry`) is not the usual create, load, use sequence.

This change replaces the shared instance with a small private helper, `loadAndroidKeyStore`. It creates a new `KeyStore` for the "AndroidKeyStore" provider, loads it, and returns it. Each operation now gets its own loaded instance, so no object is reloaded or shared between threads. Which keys are read, created or deleted is unchanged.

In `generateRsaKeyPair` I removed the `load(null)` call. That function only uses the key pair generator, which talks to the provider directly, and it never read from the key store object.

I did not run the app on a device or emulator, so the new behaviour has not been exercised at runtime. I ran the project's debug build and it passed.

cards.title: No maintainer action needed
cards.text:
The key lookup uses AndroidKeyStore and calls `load(null)` before `getEntry(alias, null)`. It reuses an existing secret key or generates one through the same provider when no secret-key entry is found. The lookup is initialized before use.

Android's [Keystore guide](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore) documents this loading and retrieval sequence. The [Android implementation](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/prebuilts/fullsdk/sources/+/88c7ff1cd72d6305ec59f97aadc2198cc2dc3592/android-34/java/security/KeyStoreSpi.java) also explicitly allows a null protection parameter when retrieving secret keys. The reported sequence therefore does not establish an application defect, and no source change or maintainer report is warranted.

cards.title: Read Android keystore secret keys directly
cards.text:
Today `SecretService.getAndroidSecretKey` reads a `KeyStore` entry to obtain keys used to encrypt and decrypt the salt, master key and stored master password. RVSec reported the sequence of calls used for that read. I changed it to retrieve the secret key directly with `getKey`, keeping the same alias and key creation fallback. I made this change for the RVSec report; Android documents both ways of retrieving the key.

The app builds. I haven't checked this on a device or rerun RVSec; please verify first use and existing vault data, including biometric password storage and export/import paths.

cards.text:
The key lookup selects `AndroidKeyStore`, calls `load(null)` before `getEntry(alias, null)`, and reuses the stored secret key when present. This matches the sequence in the [Android keystore documentation](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore#WorkWithEntries). Loading with a null parameter initializes access to the system keystore; it does not erase stored keys.

Android explicitly supports retrieving secret-key entries with null protection parameters, as shown in its [entry retrieval implementation](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/libcore/+/refs/heads/android14-release/ojluni/src/main/java/java/security/KeyStoreSpi.java). Missing keys are generated through the Android keystore provider, which stores them without a separate save call. The reported call-sequence mismatch does not establish an API misuse here, so no source change or maintainer report is warranted.

cards.title: Use a random salt for the PBKDF2 key in HashUtils
cards.text:
RVSec reported that the salt given to `PBEKeySpec` in `HashUtils` never came from a randomized source. Today the salt is the build's `APP_SALT` plus the passphrase, so the same passphrase always yields the same AES key. The `Cipher.init` report is about the key that spec produced, and the same change addresses it.

`encode` now draws a 16-byte salt from `SecureRandom`, derives the key from it, and writes `salt + IV + ciphertext`. `APP_SALT` is still used: it is passed to the cipher as GCM associated data. `decode` tries the new layout first and falls back to the old one, so messages and history entries from earlier versions still decrypt. That fallback still builds the old fixed salt, so RVSec will report that call whenever an old message is decoded.

Messages encoded with this version can't be read by older versions of the app.

I built the debug APK and the build passed. I haven't run the app or any tests, and the project has no unit-test source set. Whether RVSec accepts the change is unverified.

Maintainer choice: I kept `APP_SALT` as associated data. The alternative is dropping it from new messages.

cards.title: Generate a fresh salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
Today `HashUtils` derives an AES key from the entered key and a salt built from that same input and a build value. RVSec reported that the salt passed to `PBEKeySpec` was not observed to come from a random source, and also reported the resulting key at `Cipher.init`. I generate a fresh salt for each new message and include it with the ciphertext; a repeated salt gives the same derived key for the same input. The build value remains part of the authentication.

Recipients using earlier app versions cannot read new messages; updated versions can still read earlier messages. The original derivation remains in the old-message read path, where RVSec will still report it. The app builds; tests were not run. Please check older messages, device behavior and RVSec's recognition of salts read from messages. I chose a versioned message prefix; another versioned format is an alternative.

cards.title: Generate a fresh salt for each encrypted message

RVSec reported that this salt was not observed to come from a random source and also flagged the resulting key at Cipher.init. Reusing the same entered key produces the same derivation salt. I generate a fresh salt for each entered message and include it with the encrypted data; the entered key and build-time value still contribute to the derived key.

People using older versions cannot read newly encrypted messages. This version can read earlier messages: the old derivation remains in the decode path, and RVSec still reports that derivation when an older message is decoded. I built the app; please check messages from older installations, device behavior, and RVSec's results. The new messages use a version prefix; an alternative would be a different versioned format.

+package com.vauth.salty.utils
+
+import android.test.AndroidTestCase

+import com.vauth.salty.BuildConfig
+import javax.crypto.Cipher
+import javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory
+import javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpec
+import javax.crypto.spec.PBEKeySpec
+import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec
+
+class HashUtilsTest : AndroidTestCase() {
+    fun testNewMessagesUseDifferentSaltsAndRoundTrip() {
+        val first = HashUtils.encode("hello", "shared key")
+        val second = HashUtils.encode("hello", "shared key")
+        val firstBytes = Base64.decode(first.removePrefix("salty:v1:"), Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        val secondBytes = Base64.decode(second.removePrefix("salty:v1:"), Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        assertFalse(firstBytes.copyOfRange(0, 16).contentEquals(secondBytes.copyOfRange(0, 16)))
+        assertEquals("hello", HashUtils.decode(first, "shared key"))
+        assertEquals("hello", HashUtils.decode(second, "shared key"))
+    }
+
+    fun testReadsLegacyMessage() {
+        val password = "shared key"
+        val salt = (BuildConfig.APP_SALT + password).toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
+        val spec = PBEKeySpec(password.toCharArray(), salt, 600000, 256)
+        val key = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256").generateSecret(spec).encoded
+        val iv = ByteArray(12) { it.toByte() }
+        val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
+        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, SecretKeySpec(key, "AES"), GCMParameterSpec(128, iv))
+        val legacy = Base64.encodeToString(iv + cipher.doFinal("old message".toByteArray()), Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        assertEquals("old message", HashUtils.decode(legacy, password))
+    }
+
+    fun testRejectsWrongKeyTamperingAndTruncation() {
+        val encoded = HashUtils.encode("hello", "shared key")
+        val bytes = Base64.decode(encoded.removePrefix("salty:v1:"), Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        bytes[0] = (bytes[0].toInt() xor 1).toByte()
+        val tampered = "salty:v1:" + Base64.encodeToString(bytes, Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        for ((message, key) in listOf(encoded to "wrong", tampered to "shared key", "salty:v1:AA==" to "shared key")) {
+            try {
+                HashUtils.decode(message, key)
+                fail("Expected decoding to fail")
+            } catch (_: DecodingException) {
+                // Expected.
+            }
+        }
+    }

cards.title: Key derivation uses a deterministic salt; consider a random per-message salt (format change)
cards.text:
While checking how the app uses the Java crypto APIs, I noticed something about key derivation in `app/src/main/java/com/vauth/salty/utils/HashUtils.kt`. I did not change any code, because the fix alters the stored message format and that is your decision.

The PBKDF2 salt is built as the build-time `APP_SALT` plus the text the user typed, and that same user text is also the PBKDF2 password. The salt is therefore fixed for a given passphrase and is not random. The same passphrase always gives the same AES key, on every device and for every message. The 12-byte GCM nonce is random for each message, so nonce reuse is not a concern.

In practice this makes the derived key somewhat cheaper to attack. An attacker can precompute keys for common passphrases against one known `APP_SALT`. The default `Salty@AES-256` is public in `app/build.gradle`, and it is used for every build that doesn't set the `APP_SALT` environment variable. The salt adds almost nothing beyond the passphrase itself. The 600,000 iterations help, but a random salt is the standard way to remove the precomputation advantage.

A possible change is to generate 16 random bytes per message and mix them into the PBKDF2 salt. They would be stored with the output, for example as `salt || iv || ciphertext`. Decoding would read them back from the front of the message. This has two costs:

- Messages encoded by earlier versions would no longer decode with the new format. You would need a version marker or a fallback path for the old layout.
- The encoded text gets 16 bytes longer.

Questions for the maintainers:

1. Is the deterministic derivation intentional, for example so that two people can exchange messages using only a shared passphrase? A random salt stored in the message would still allow that, because the salt travels with the ciphertext.
2. If you want the change, how should existing history entries and messages that are already encoded be handled?

I can send a patch once you say which way to go on compatibility.

No deliverable: correção gerada, sem PR (resolvido junto com encode; PR retido: leaves out an effect users will notice that the review recorded ("Older clients cannot decode them;"): state it as a fact in one short plain sentence of your own, with the people who notice it as the subject; do not copy the note's wording)

cards.title: Use a random PBKDF2 salt for each message in HashUtils
cards.text:
RVSec, a runtime checker for Java crypto API use, reported that the salt given to `PBEKeySpec` in `HashUtils` was not observed to come from a random source. Today the key for AES-GCM is derived from the passphrase the user types, with a salt made of the build's `APP_SALT` plus that same passphrase. The salt is therefore identical for every message encrypted with a given passphrase, and the same on every install. RVSec also reported the `Cipher` key in `encode`; that key comes from this derivation, so the change below addresses both.

`encode` now fills a 16-byte array from `SecureRandom`, uses it as the PBKDF2 salt, and writes it in front of the IV and ciphertext. `APP_SALT` is still used: it is now passed to `Cipher.updateAAD`, so messages remain tied to the build's value. `decode` reads the salt from the message. If that fails authentication, it falls back to the earlier layout (IV + ciphertext, salt = `APP_SALT` + passphrase), so messages made by earlier versions and stored in history still decode. That fallback still builds `PBEKeySpec` with the old fixed salt, so RVSec will still report it whenever an older message is decoded.

Messages encoded with this change are longer and use a layout that earlier app versions cannot decode, so anyone you send them to needs the updated app. Decoding an older message now costs one extra key derivation.

I built the debug APK with the project's build script and it succeeded. I did not run tests (the project has none) or try it on a device. For the reviewer: I kept `APP_SALT` as authenticated data rather than dropping it; dropping it would be simpler but would make messages portable across builds with different values.

cards.title: Use a fresh salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
In `HashUtils.encode`, I found that the code encrypts the message with a key derived from the supplied salt and stores the IV and ciphertext as Base64. RVSec flagged the `Cipher.init` call because its key comes from a key specification that RVSec had already reported.

I changed key derivation to use a fresh random salt along with length-delimited user key and app salt values, and store that salt with a version marker, IV and ciphertext. Decoding supports the new layout and falls back to the legacy layout for short marker matches or authentication failures, preserving access to older data.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Use a random salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
`PBEKeySpec` derives the message encryption key from the shared key and a build-time salt. RVSec reported that the salt was not observed to come from a random source, and also reported the resulting key at `Cipher.init`. I add a fresh random salt to each new message, giving repeated uses of the same shared key different derived keys.

People using older versions cannot decode new messages; this version can still decode older messages. The original derivation remains in `decode` for old messages and after a new-format decode fails; RVSec will still report it when that fallback runs. The app build passed; tests were not run. Please check devices, older messages, recipients and whether RVSec recognizes the new salt.

I chose a marked message format with the salt included; an alternative is a different versioned format.

cards.title: Key derivation uses a salt computed from the password, so identical passwords always give identical keys
cards.text:
While reviewing how the app uses the Java crypto APIs, I found something in the key derivation function in `app/src/main/java/com/vauth/salty/utils/HashUtils.kt` (`deriveKey`) that I think you should know about. I haven't changed any code, because the fix changes the encoded message format and that is your decision.

The user's "salt" (the shared secret typed in the app) is used as the PBKDF2 password. The PBKDF2 salt is built from `BuildConfig.APP_SALT` plus that same user string. `APP_SALT` is a build-time constant, and the default is `Salty@AES-256`. So the PBKDF2 salt is a pure function of the password and is not random. Anyone who uses the same shared secret gets the same AES key, on every message and in every install built with the same `APP_SALT`.

This has two practical effects:

- An attacker can precompute keys for common passwords once and reuse that work against every message from every user. A random per-message salt would rule this out.
- Two messages encrypted with the same shared secret use the same key. The IV is random per message (12 bytes from `SecureRandom`), which is good. But with a fixed key, the amount of data safely encrypted under it is limited by the GCM random-IV bound, and a per-message salt would remove that limit.

The 600,000 PBKDF2 iterations and the random IV are fine. The weak part is only the salt.

A possible fix is to generate a random 16-byte salt for each message in `encode`, derive the key from it, and write the output as `salt || iv || ciphertext`. `decode` would read the salt back from the front. `APP_SALT` could stay as extra input or be dropped.

The catch is compatibility. Messages already encoded, including the ones saved in the history database and any that users have sent to other people, use the current layout (`iv || ciphertext`) and the deterministic key. A new `decode` could not tell the two formats apart without a version byte or a fallback attempt. So the options I see are:

1. Add a format version marker, write new messages in the new format, and keep the old derivation in `decode` as a fallback.
2. Accept that old messages stop decoding.
3. Decide that this is acceptable for the app's threat model and document it.

Which of these do you prefer? I'm happy to send a PR for option 1 if you'd like it.

cards.title: Use a random derivation salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
The entered “Salt” acts as a password, but the derivation salt currently depends only on that password and a build-time constant. Generate a fresh 16-byte random salt for each encryption, following [NIST’s salt guidance](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-132.pdf), so repeated passwords produce independently derived keys.

Store the salt with the IV and ciphertext in a versioned message. Keep decoding support for existing messages and reject unsupported versions and truncated payloads. Older app releases will need an update to read new messages.

The debug APK build and all eight regression tests passed. Tests cover legacy compatibility, round trips, fresh salts and IVs, wrong passwords, tampering, and malformed messages.

cards.title: Use a fresh random salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
The derivation salt currently depends only on the build constant and the shared secret. Reusing a secret therefore reuses the encryption key and lets password-guessing work be shared across messages. This change generates a fresh 16-byte salt with SecureRandom for each encryption and stores it alongside the IV and authenticated ciphertext.

New messages use a `v2:` prefix followed by the Base64-encoded salt, IV, and ciphertext with its authentication tag. Decoding still supports existing messages with the original derivation and build salt. Older app versions cannot decode new messages. Format validation checks that both formats contain a complete IV and authentication tag.

All seven regression tests pass, covering round trips, independent derivation from the stored salt, fresh salts and IVs, legacy decoding, wrong passwords, tampering, and malformed input. The app builds successfully with `build_check`.

cards.title: Use a fresh salt to derive encryption keys
cards.text:
In `HashUtils.encode`, I encrypt the message with a key derived from the user-supplied key and `APP_SALT`. RVSec reports the `Cipher.init` call because its key comes from a `PBEKeySpec` already reported for constructing its salt from those inputs instead of random bytes.

I now generate a fresh 16-byte salt for each encryption and store it with the IV and ciphertext under a `=v2:` marker. This also resolves the non-random salt report in `deriveKey`, which `encode` calls. I updated decoding and validation to distinguish the layouts. The original `PBEKeySpec` remains in `deriveLegacyKey` when `decode` reads unmarked legacy ciphertext; RVSec still reports it whenever that legacy read runs.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Use a random salt when encrypting messages
cards.text:
`HashUtils.encode` encrypts the message with a key derived from the supplied salt and app salt. RVSec reports that the key passed to `Cipher.init` was already reported by the specification that produced it.

I changed encryption to use a fresh random salt and store it with the IV and ciphertext in a versioned envelope. The decoder tries the original layout and derivation if the new envelope cannot be used, and key derivation clears password material even on failure. Data written by this version is not readable by earlier versions of the app.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Key derivation uses a non-random salt (derived from the passphrase and a build-time constant)
cards.text:
`HashUtils.deriveKey` builds the PBKDF2 salt as `BuildConfig.APP_SALT + userSalt`. `userSalt` is also the PBKDF2 password. `APP_SALT` defaults to the public string `Salty@AES-256` unless the `APP_SALT` environment variable is set at build time. So the derived key depends only on the passphrase the user types. Nothing random goes into it.

This has a few consequences:

- Every message encrypted with the same passphrase uses the same AES key. Only the random 12-byte GCM IV differs. With AES-GCM, the more messages share a key, the more the random-IV collision limits matter.
- An attacker can precompute PBKDF2 results for common passphrases once and use them against anyone using the default build. The 600,000 iterations make this slower, but it is not the same as a per-message random salt.
- The README describes the passphrase as a shared "Salt (Key)". The word "salt" in the UI and code actually means the password. The real KDF salt is the thing that is missing.

I did not send a patch. The usual fix is to generate a random salt (for example 16 bytes from `SecureRandom`) in `encode`, derive the key from it, and store it with the output, e.g. `salt || iv || ciphertext`. That changes the encoded format. Messages produced by the current app version could no longer be decoded by a new version unless there is a fallback, and messages produced by a new version could not be decoded by older installs. Since people exchange these strings between devices, I think the maintainers should decide how to handle that.

Possible options:

1. Switch to the new format and add a fallback in `decode`. It would try the new layout first. If GCM authentication fails, it would retry with the old fixed-salt derivation. This keeps old messages and history readable. New messages would not be readable by old app versions.
2. Add an explicit version byte to the new format. This is cleaner, but the old format has no marker, so `decode` still needs the try-then-fall-back step for legacy input.
3. Keep the current format and document that the passphrase must be strong and that the key is deterministic per passphrase. This is the cheapest option but leaves the weakness above.

If the maintainers pick option 1 or 2, I can open a PR with it. If they want to keep the current behaviour, this issue can be closed.

In `encode`, the key passed to `Cipher.init` comes from that same derivation. Fixing the derivation covers it, so I don't think it needs separate work. The GCM IV in `encode` is already random per message.

This was found with an automated runtime checker on the built APK. I read the code to confirm it. I did not change any code or run the build.

cards.title: Randomize the key derivation salt for each message
cards.text:
Generate a fresh 16-byte salt for each encryption and store it with the IV and ciphertext. Previously, the salt depended only on the shared key and build constant, allowing password-guessing work to be reused across messages using the same key. This follows the [PBKDF2 salt guidance](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018.html#section-4.1). The shared key remains the password input, and the encryption IV is still generated independently.

New messages use a `v2:` prefix followed by the Base64-encoded salt, IV, and authenticated ciphertext. Existing unprefixed messages still decode using their original key derivation. Older app versions cannot read new messages, so recipients need to update. Format validation now checks both layouts, including the authentication tag length.

All six regression tests passed with `:app:testDebugUnitTest`, covering random salt and IV generation, salt-based decryption, Unicode and empty messages, legacy decoding, wrong passwords, tampering, and malformed input.

The debug APK build passed using `/home/antonow/comparison_20261113/bin/build_check` with a writable local Android user directory.

cards.title: Use a random salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
Generate a random salt for password-based key derivation for each new message and include it in the encoded output. This prevents messages using the same shared password from deriving the same key and makes precomputed password guesses less reusable.

The updated app can still decrypt existing messages. New messages use a different format, so recipients must update their app before decrypting them. Password strength remains important.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Details: At both reported calls, the monitor would observe the same values: PBEKeySpec receives the same deterministic salt, and Cipher.init receives the same derived key. Clearing the spec afterward does not change either call or the generated key.

Assessment: the reported violation is confirmed, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: The PBEKeySpec salt is deterministically derived from the app build value and the user-supplied key rather than a fresh randomized salt source. The reported Cipher key finding echoes that producer violation.

cards.title: Use a random salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
Generate a fresh random salt for password-based key derivation and include it in each new encrypted message. This prevents messages using the same shared value from deriving the same key and makes precomputed password attacks less reusable across messages.

Existing messages can still be decrypted with their original shared value and app build salt. Newly encrypted messages use a versioned format that older app versions cannot decrypt, so recipients need to update. The shared value should still be hard to guess.

The debug build passed. I also checked round trips, distinct salts, wrong passwords, tampering, and decryption of the previous message format using a local JVM harness.

cards.title: Key derivation uses a fixed, non-random salt; consider a per-message random salt (format change)
cards.text:
While running a runtime checker for Java crypto API usage against a build of the app, it flagged the PBKDF2 key derivation in `app/src/main/java/com/vauth/salty/utils/HashUtils.kt` (`deriveKey`).

The salt passed to PBKDF2 is `BuildConfig.APP_SALT + userSalt`. `APP_SALT` is a build-time constant (default `Salty@AES-256`, in `app/build.gradle`). `userSalt` is the shared secret the user types in, and the same string is also used as the PBKDF2 password. So nothing in the salt is random. The same secret always gives the same AES key, on every message and every device.

This is not an obvious bug. The code needs to derive the same key when decoding, and the ciphertext does not carry a salt. The IV is already random per message, and the AES-GCM output looks fine. The practical effect is that anyone who captures messages can attack the shared secret offline, and precomputed work carries across all users who share the same `APP_SALT` (the default is public in the repository). A per-message random salt would remove that sharing and also make every message use a different key.

A possible fix is to generate a random 16-byte salt in `encode`, derive the key from it (plus the app salt if you want to keep it), and write the output as `salt || iv || ciphertext`. `decode` would read the salt from the front. Old messages could still be read by trying the new layout first and falling back to the current one if the GCM tag check fails.

I have not sent a patch because it changes the message format. Messages encoded by a new version could not be decoded by older versions of the app, and that affects anyone exchanging messages between devices. The history database also stores the old-format strings. Whether that trade-off is acceptable is your decision, so I would like to know before writing it. I can send a PR if you want this.

The checker also flagged the `Cipher.init` call in `encode`, saying its key came from the derivation above. That is the same finding showing up again further down the code. The IV and GCM parameters there are fine, and I would not change anything for it separately.

I did not change any code or run the build.

cards.title: Use a fresh random derivation salt for each encrypted message
cards.text:
Encoding currently derives the encryption key from the shared password and a salt made from a build constant and that same password. Reusing a password therefore lets password-guessing work be reused across messages. Generate a fresh 16-byte random salt for each message, independently of the GCM IV, following [OWASP's guidance on salts](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html#salting).

New messages use `salty:v2:` followed by Base64 containing the salt, IV, and authenticated ciphertext. Decoding still accepts the original format and uses its original derivation. Older app versions cannot decode new messages, so recipients need to update. Validation checks the required salt, IV, and authentication-tag lengths and rejects unknown versions.

Regression tests cover independent salts and IVs, derivation from the stored salt, Unicode and empty messages, legacy decoding, wrong passwords, tampering, and malformed input. The debug APK build and all five tests passed.

+        val iv: ByteArray,
+        val encryptedBytes: ByteArray
+    )
+
+    private fun parseEncodedMessage(encodedMessage: String): EncryptedMessage {
+        // The colon-delimited prefix cannot occur in the original Base64 format.
+        val versioned = encodedMessage.startsWith(FORMAT_PREFIX)
+        if (encodedMessage.startsWith("salty:") && !versioned) {
+            throw DecodingException("Unsupported encoded message version")
+        }
+        val payload = if (versioned) encodedMessage.removePrefix(FORMAT_PREFIX) else encodedMessage
+        val combined = Base64.decode(payload, Base64.NO_WRAP)
+        val saltLength = if (versioned) DERIVATION_SALT_LENGTH else 0
+        val ciphertextOffset = saltLength + GCM_IV_LENGTH
+        if (combined.size < ciphertextOffset + GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS / 8) {
+            throw DecodingException("Encoded message is too short")
+        }
+        return EncryptedMessage(
+            derivationSalt = if (versioned) combined.copyOfRange(0, saltLength) else null,
+            iv = combined.copyOfRange(saltLength, ciphertextOffset),
+            encryptedBytes = combined.copyOfRange(ciphertextOffset, combined.size)
+        )
+    }
 }

+        }
+    }

+        val second = payload(HashUtils.encode(message, password))
+        assertFalse(first.copyOfRange(0, 16).contentEquals(second.copyOfRange(0, 16)))
+        assertFalse(first.copyOfRange(16, 28).contentEquals(second.copyOfRange(16, 28)))
+

+        assertEquals(message, HashUtils.decode(encoded, password))
+        assertThrows(DecodingException::class.java) { HashUtils.decode(encoded, "wrong key") }
+    }

+        val original = payload(encoded)

cards.title: Store a random PBKDF2 salt with each encoded message
cards.text:
`HashUtils.encode` derives its AES key with `PBEKeySpec` and `SecretKeyFactory`. The PBKDF2 salt is `BuildConfig.APP_SALT` plus the user's salt text, and the same user text is also the password, so the salt is the same for every message. RVSec reported that this salt does not come from a randomized source. It also reported the `Cipher.init` call in `encode`, which receives the key built from it.

`encode` now fills 16 bytes from `SecureRandom` and passes them directly to `PBEKeySpec` as the salt. The output layout is `salt || iv || ciphertext`. To keep `APP_SALT` mattering, I pass it to the cipher as GCM additional data. A message encoded by a build with a different `APP_SALT` still fails to decode, as before.

`decode` tries the new layout first. If authentication fails, or the message is too short for that layout, it falls back to the old layout and the old fixed-salt derivation, so history and messages from earlier versions still decode. That fallback keeps a `PBEKeySpec` call with the fixed salt, and RVSec will still report it whenever an old message is decoded.

Messages encoded after this change cannot be decoded by earlier versions of the app. Decoding an old message, or a wrong key, now runs the key derivation twice, so it takes a bit longer.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I haven't run it on a device, and the module has no unit-test source set, so I added no tests. Please check that RVSec accepts the change. `PBEKeySpec.clearPassword` is still not called, and I left that alone.

cards.title: Generate a fresh key derivation salt for each message
cards.text:
Generate a random salt for each new encrypted message and include it in a versioned message format. This prevents messages using the same shared key from always deriving the same encryption key and makes precomputed password guessing across messages less useful.

Continue to decrypt existing messages using the original derivation. Older app versions cannot decrypt newly encoded messages, so both parties need the updated app to exchange them.

cards.title: Generate a random salt for each encoded message
cards.text:
Today I see `PBEKeySpec` derive the encryption key from the entered key and a salt made from that same input and the app's build-time value. RVSec reported that the salt was not observed to come from a random source, and also reported the resulting key at `Cipher.init`. I added a random component for each new message; this avoids deriving the same key whenever the same input is used.

People using older versions cannot decode newly encoded messages. Earlier messages still decode: `HashUtils.decode` retains the old derivation when reading them, and RVSec will still report that derivation whenever it runs.

The app builds; I did not run tests. Please check older messages, shared messages on devices, and whether RVSec recognizes the new salt. I chose a marked message format with a legacy fallback; an alternative is a different versioned framing.

cards.title: No action: decryption correctly restores the saved IV
cards.text:
No code change or issue is warranted for this finding. Android encryption initializes AES-GCM without supplying an IV, obtains the provider-generated IV, and stores it as a prefix to the ciphertext. Both key-generation paths retain Android Keystore's default requirement for randomized encryption. This follows [Android's documented guidance](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder#setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(boolean)).

Decryption extracts the original 12-byte IV from that prefix and uses it with a 128-bit authentication tag. It must use the same IV that encrypted the data; generating a new random IV during decryption would cause authentication to fail and make stored secrets unreadable. Reading the IV from storage does not indicate that it was generated insecurely. The reported observation therefore does not establish a cryptographic defect.

No source code was changed. A standalone JVM check confirmed successful decryption with the saved IV and authentication failure with a changed IV. No Android device test or app build was run.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Details: Every IV spec this method builds reaches only decryptions, and commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt encrypts with Cipher.init(ENCRYPT_MODE, key) and no parameter spec, then keeps the IV the cipher returns: the provider generated that IV from its own random source, and the IV reaching the spec is that one, read back for decryption. What the detector's report means: NOT OBSERVED: the runtime monitor tracks the producers a rule requires by object identity within one process, and saw none for this object. No admitted producer was seen (e.g. SecureRandom for an IV, salt or seed; Key.getEncoded for key bytes). The monitor cannot tell innocent cases -- bytes read back from storage, an IV parsed from the ciphertext, a producer it does not see -- from the defective one: bytes that are constants compiled into the application or derived from constants. Where the bytes come from decides it.

Assessment: the reported violation is undetermined, with a security impact that was not established.

Cause: Unknown: decrypt reads the IV prefix from its input; the paired encryption path supplies a provider-generated IV, but the provenance of all reported inputs is not established.

Reason: violation without security impact: provider-generated IV

RVSec reported that the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` in `SecretEncryption.decrypt` was not observed to come from a randomized source. The Android implementation is `commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt`. This is the only `SecretEncryption` variant in the Android build. The desktop and JVM variants are not compiled into the APK.

What the code does (confirmed from source):
- `encrypt` (lines 152-167) calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey)` with no IV. It reads `cipher.iv` and returns `iv + encrypted`. The IV is therefore generated by the AndroidKeyStore provider, not chosen by the app.
- The key is created at lines 116-122 and 135-140 with `KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder` and no `setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(false)`. Android's default is therefore in force: caller-provided IVs are rejected when encrypting, "to ensure that only random IVs are used"
 (https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder).
 That page also recommends this exact pattern: init without an IV, then store `getIV` with the ciphertext.
- `decrypt` (lines 169-184) only slices the first 12 bytes of the stored ciphertext (`GCM_IV_LENGTH`) and passes them to `GCMParameterSpec(128, iv)`. The tag length of 128 is in the accepted set. Decryption has to supply a `GCMParameterSpec`, because the AndroidKeyStore cipher does not accept a plain IV spec (the code comment at lines 171-173 says the same).

The IV is random at its origin, and decryption just reads it back. RVSec cannot trace it across the store and load, which is why it reports no randomized producer. Any change that made the IV "app-chosen" would be refused by the key's own settings at encryption, and would replace the provider's IV, which the platform documentation advises against. A change that only restructured the decrypt call would not alter what RVSec sees. I therefore found no change worth proposing.

Not examined: the desktop `SecretEncryption.jvm.kt` and the KeyStoreEncryption helper in `commons/.../keystorage/`, which RVSec did not report. Callers of `decrypt` were not traced one by one, since the value comes from this class's own `encrypt` output.

Both key-generation paths retain Android's default requirement for randomized encryption. Encryption initializes the Android Keystore cipher without supplying an IV, then stores the cipher-generated IV alongside the ciphertext. Reason: violation without security impact (provider-generated IV)

RVSec reported that the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` in `SecretEncryption.decrypt` was not seen coming from a randomized source. The Android implementation I read is `commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt`. This is the one the APK compiles, not the desktop `.jvm.kt` one.

In `decrypt` (lines 174-177) the IV is the first 12 bytes of the input, and the tag length is the constant 128 bits. The constructor is `GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS, iv)`. The tag length is one of the accepted values. Nothing in `decrypt` produces an IV. It only reads back what `encrypt` stored.

`encrypt` (lines 155-159) calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey)` without an IV, then stores `cipher.iv` in front of the ciphertext. The IV is therefore generated by the AndroidKeyStore provider. The key is created through `KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder` (lines 116-122 and 136-140). Those builders never call `setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(false)`; I searched `commons/src` for it and found nothing. Randomized encryption is the Android default for such keys, so the provider supplies the IV on encryption and refuses a caller-chosen one.

The IV was therefore random when it was created. RVSec could not trace that origin across the store and the later read. Any change that made the code choose the IV itself would replace the provider's random IV. It would also make encryption fail with the existing keystore keys. Restructuring `decrypt` would not change what RVSec sees at that call.

Open points: I did not run the app. The same constructor pattern appears in `KeyStoreEncryption.kt:177`, which is outside this report.

Reason: violation without security impact

For data written by `SecretEncryption.encrypt`, the IV comes from the cipher after encryption is initialized without an IV; `decrypt` reads that IV from the ciphertext prefix ([source](commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt)). Android documents that this initialization generates a random IV and recommends supplying it with the ciphertext for decryption ([Android KeyGenParameterSpec documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder#setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(boolean))). Replacing the stored IV would prevent decryption, while supplying an IV at encryption conflicts with the default Android Keystore policy. The provenance of arbitrary or historical input was not established; the report does not establish a security impact in the app's own write-and-read path.

cards.title: No action needed for the stored decryption IV
cards.text:
The Android encryption path lets the Keystore cipher generate a fresh IV and prefixes it to the ciphertext. Both key-generation paths retain Android's default requirement for randomized encryption, which ensures random IVs for GCM. See the [Android Keystore documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder#setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(boolean)).

Decryption reads the original 12-byte IV from that prefix and uses it with a 128-bit authentication tag. It must reuse the IV from encryption; generating a new one during decryption would prevent authentication and recovery of the saved data. Reading an IV from storage does not indicate that encryption used a predictable IV.

The reported observation does not establish a defect, so no code change or maintainer issue is warranted. This assessment is based on source review and the documented API behavior; no build or device test was run.

Reason: violation without security impact

The current Android encryption path initializes the cipher without an IV, stores the IV returned by the cipher alongside the ciphertext, and uses that stored IV when decrypting ([SecretEncryption.android.kt](commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt)). Android documents that this encryption initialization generates a random IV and recommends retrieving it with `getIV` ([Android KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder documentation](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder#setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(boolean))). Supplying a newly chosen IV during decryption would prevent existing ciphertext from being read, and supplying one during encryption can be rejected by AndroidKeyStore.

The source does not establish the origin of every historical or malformed input, or identify the particular input seen by RVSec. This conclusion concerns the current writer's provider-generated IV path; it does not establish the provenance of every possible input.

Decryption must use the same IV as encryption; generating a new one there would prevent recovery of the data. No change is needed for this report.

cards.title: No action: the report is a false positive
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged `SecretEncryption.decrypt` because the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` was "not observed to come from a randomized source". I read the Android implementation (`SecretEncryption.android.kt`) and the desktop one (`SecretEncryption.jvm.kt`). I don't think this needs a code change.

`decrypt` is the inverse of `encrypt`. It has to use the IV that `encrypt` produced, so it reads the first 12 bytes of the stored blob and passes them to `GCMParameterSpec`. The IV is therefore never random at that point, and it should not be. Generating a new IV on decrypt would make every decryption fail the authentication check. The checker can only see that the bytes came from an array and not from a random generator, because the randomness was applied at encryption time, in an earlier call and possibly an earlier process.

The encrypt side is correct:

- On Android, `encrypt` calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` with no caller-supplied parameters. The AndroidKeyStore provider then generates a fresh random 12-byte IV for each operation. By default it rejects a caller-chosen IV for encryption, so a reused or predictable IV can't be introduced by accident. The code prefixes `cipher.iv` to the ciphertext.
- On desktop, `encrypt` also calls `init` without parameters. The JDK's AES/GCM implementation draws a fresh random IV from a `SecureRandom` on each call. The key is 32 bytes from `SecureRandom`.
- Both sides use the 12-byte IV length and a 128-bit tag, which are the recommended GCM values.

A change that only silenced the warning would add risk and no security benefit. Supplying our own IV on encrypt would replace the provider's guaranteed-random IV with code we would have to keep correct. Changing decrypt is not possible without breaking existing stored data.

I did not change any files, so I did not run the build.

cards.title: No action: the IV warning on the decrypt path is a false positive
cards.text:
The checker reported that the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` in `SecretEncryption.decrypt` was not seen coming from a randomized source.

I read both implementations: the Android one (`SecretEncryption.android.kt`) and the desktop one (`SecretEncryption.jvm.kt`). In both, `decrypt` has to take the IV from the stored data. It copies the first 12 bytes of the input, which are the prefix `encrypt` wrote, and passes them to `GCMParameterSpec`. A decrypting cipher must be given the exact IV used at encryption time. A fresh random value there would make every decryption fail, so the decrypt side can't be changed.

The IV is generated on the encrypt side. `encrypt` calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` without supplying an IV. The provider then generates a random one, and the code reads it back with `cipher.iv` and prepends it to the ciphertext. On Android the AndroidKeyStore key is built with its default setting that requires randomized encryption. That setting refuses caller-supplied IVs when encrypting. On desktop the JDK's AES/GCM provider also generates a random 12-byte IV when none is given. So no IV is ever reused or chosen by the app.

The checker most likely can't link the IV bytes it sees on decrypt to the random IV generated in an earlier encrypt call. They may even have been written by a previous process run. That is a limit of the runtime check, not a defect in the code.

Nothing needs to change, so I'm not sending a PR or an issue. I changed no source files and did not run the build.

Reason: violation without security impact

The Android encryption path initializes its cipher without supplying an IV, prefixes the cipher's IV to the ciphertext, and decryption reads that prefix back ([SecretEncryption.android.kt:152](commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt#L152), [decrypt:169](commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt#L169)). Android documents that the keystore's default randomized encryption generates a random IV in this situation and that it should accompany the ciphertext ([Android KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder#setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(boolean))).

The current round-trip therefore does not need a new IV for decryption. The report does not identify the particular stored record, so the origin of that record and of older data remains unverified. No source change or build was made.

Reason: violation without security impact (provider-generated IV)

RVSec flagged the `GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH_BITS, iv)` call in `SecretEncryption.decrypt` (`commons/src/androidMain/.../SecretEncryption.android.kt:177`) because it could not trace where `iv` was randomized. I read the class in full and followed the value.

- `encrypt` (lines 152-167) calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, getKey)` with no IV, reads `cipher.iv`, and stores it as the first 12 bytes of the output (`iv + encrypted`). The AndroidKeyStore provider therefore generates the IV, and it is random at its origin.
- The key is an AndroidKeyStore AES key built with `KeyGenParameterSpec` (lines 113-145). Neither builder calls `setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(false)`. The default is randomized encryption, so the keystore refuses a caller-chosen IV on encryption. A search for `setRandomizedEncryptionRequired` across the repository found no matches.
- `decrypt` only slices those 12 stored bytes (`copyOfRange(0, GCM_IV_LENGTH)`) and wraps them in `GCMParameterSpec`. The tag length is 128 bits, which is in the accepted set. The comment at lines 171-173 notes that the AndroidKeyStore cipher accepts only `GCMParameterSpec` for decryption.
- Every caller of `decrypt` that I found (`EncryptedDataStore`, `EncryptedMlsGroupStateStore`, `EncryptedKeyPackageBundleStore`, `EncryptedMarmotMessageStore`, `EncryptedPublishObligationStore`, `KeyStoreCordnBlobCipher`) passes bytes that `encrypt` produced. Search scope: `commons/src/jvmAndroid`, `commons/src/androidMain` and `amethyst/src/main`. I did not search the other modules.

The only way to change what RVSec sees at this call would be to make the code choose the IV itself. That would conflict with the keystore's randomized-encryption requirement and break every encryption. It would also replace a secure, provider-generated IV with a weaker one. Decryption has to rebuild the spec from the stored IV, so no change to this call can both satisfy the checker and keep the current behaviour. The message is a limit of what RVSec can trace, and there is no weakness to fix here. No change is proposed.

The build was not run, since no source was edited.

The encryption cipher generates an IV when initialized, and the app prefixes it to the ciphertext. Decryption reads that stored IV back because AES-GCM requires the same IV used for encryption. The IV does not need to be generated again during decryption, so this observation does not warrant a change or a maintainer report.

No report to the maintainers: the runtime checker's warning is a false positive.

The warning is about the decrypt path of the at-rest encryption helper in `commons`. It says the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` was not seen coming from a random source.

That is expected. Decryption has to use the same IV that encryption used. The encrypt path never sets an IV. It calls `cipher.init(ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` and lets the provider generate a fresh 12-byte random IV for each call. On Android the AndroidKeyStore requires randomized encryption by default, so it would reject a caller-supplied IV anyway. The helper then writes that IV in front of the ciphertext (`iv + encrypted`). Decrypt reads the first 12 bytes back and passes them to `GCMParameterSpec` with a 128-bit tag. The desktop version in `SecretEncryption.jvm.kt` does the same.

Decrypt does not choose an IV, so it cannot reuse a nonce. A random source cannot be observed at that call, because the value is read from stored data. A stored IV can only matter for nonce reuse on the encrypt side, and that side relies on provider-generated IVs.

I found nothing to change, so there is no code change and no issue to file.

cards.text:
The checker flagged `SecretEncryption.decrypt` (Android actual in `commons/src/androidMain/.../SecretEncryption.android.kt`) because the IV passed to `GCMParameterSpec` was not seen coming from a random source.

That is expected for decryption. GCM decryption has to use the same IV that was used to encrypt. `decrypt` reads it from the first 12 bytes of the stored blob, so it cannot be freshly random. A random IV there would make every decryption fail.

The randomness requirement applies to `encrypt`, and that path is fine. It calls `cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` without supplying an IV. The AndroidKeyStore provider then generates a fresh random 12-byte IV for each operation, and by default it refuses caller-supplied IVs for these keys. `encrypt` reads that IV back from `cipher.iv` and prefixes it to the ciphertext. The desktop actual works the same way with the standard JCE provider, which also generates a random IV when none is given.

The rest of the design is sound. The key is created without `setRandomizedEncryptionRequired(false)`, so the keystore keeps enforcing random IVs. The tag length is 128 bits, and each thread has its own `Cipher`.

Nothing sent: the code does not follow the rule, but without a security impact that a change would remove.

Details: Every IV spec this method builds reaches only decryptions, and commons/src/androidMain/kotlin/com/vitorpamplona/amethyst/commons/model/preferences/SecretEncryption.android.kt encrypts with Cipher.init(ENCRYPT_MODE, key) and no parameter spec, then keeps the IV the cipher returns: the provider generated that IV from its own random source, and the IV reaching the spec is that one, read back for decryption. No admitted producer was seen (e.g. SecureRandom for an IV, salt or seed; Key.getEncoded for key bytes). The monitor cannot tell innocent cases -- bytes read back from storage, an IV parsed from the ciphertext, a producer it does not see -- from the defective one: bytes that are constants compiled into the application or derived from constants. Where the bytes come from decides it.

The provider therefore generates the IV and the code only reads it back, so randomized[src] holds at its origin. The GCM tag length of 128 is in the allowed set. The IV content is read from the data being processed and is not a compiled constant. No edit would change what the rule protects.
