cards.title: Trust-all certificates in OkHttpClientModule.setupSsl
cards.text:
RVSec flagged the `SSLContext.init` call in `setupSsl`: its trust manager is an app-defined class whose checks do nothing, and `hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }` sits beside it. `cachingHttpClient` defaults `trustAllCerts = true` and no caller passes false, so every HTTPS connection, including the Fever, Google Reader and FreshRSS logins, accepts any certificate and host name. Android's TLS guide advises against a do-nothing `TrustManager`.

I didn't open a pull request because using the system trust manager (the existing `else` branch) would stop self-hosted servers with self-signed or private-CA certificates from connecting, and no setting would keep them working. The `@SuppressLint` suggests this is deliberate.

Is trusting every certificate intended for all users, or would you accept an opt-in setting or certificate pinning, with system trust as the default? If it is intentional, this issue can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to send a pull request for the option you prefer.

cards.title: Use certificate and hostname validation by default
cards.text:
In `setupSsl`, the default trust-all branch accepts server certificates without checking them and accepts every hostname. RVSec reports that `SSLContext.init` receives an app-defined trust manager not observed coming from a `TrustManagerFactory`.

I switch the default to the existing validating path, so the call no longer uses that trust-all manager by default. Explicit trust-all and client-certificate support remain available. Users can no longer connect by default to servers with untrusted certificates or mismatched hostnames.

Servers whose certificate the system does not trust (self-signed or from a private CA), accepted silently until now, are rejected. The added network security config lets their users install that CA on the device; without it Android ignores user-installed CAs for apps targeting API 24 or later.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`:app:assembleFdroidDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Certificates are never checked in OkHttpClient setupSsl
cards.text:
In `setupSsl` (OkHttpClientModule.kt), `cachingHttpClient` defaults to `trustAllCerts = true`. That default installs an `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing, plus a hostname verifier that accepts every host. So every HTTPS connection is accepted without validation, including account connections that send HTTP Basic credentials. RVSec flagged the `SSLContext.init` call because this trust manager is the app's own class and did not come from a `TrustManagerFactory`. The `platformTrustManager` branch already exists but is never reached.

I didn't open a pull request because switching the default to platform validation would stop connections to self-hosted servers with self-signed certificates. The code has a `@SuppressLint` on this manager and no user setting that controls it, so I can't tell whether it is intentional.

Is trusting all certificates intended for self-signed servers? If so, would you accept an opt-in per-account setting or certificate pinning in its place? The issue can simply be closed if the current behaviour is intentional.

Otherwise I'm happy to send a pull request for whichever option you prefer.

cards.text: Use normal server certificate and hostname verification for HTTP clients, including connections that use a client certificate. Previously, the default client accepted any certificate and hostname, allowing an attacker on the network to impersonate a server and intercept traffic. Servers with invalid or untrusted certificates will now fail to connect.

cards.title: Verify HTTPS server certificates and hostnames
cards.text:
Use the platform's certificate and hostname verification for HTTP clients, including when a client certificate is configured. Previously these clients accepted any server certificate and hostname, allowing an attacker to impersonate a server and intercept traffic, including account credentials.

cards.title: Validate server certificates and hostnames by default
cards.text:
The SSL setup in `setupSsl` currently accepts all server certificates and skips hostname verification by default. RVSec reports that `SSLContext.init` receives an app-defined trust manager instead of one from a `TrustManagerFactory`, as its rule requires.

I changed the default to use the factory’s trust managers and OkHttp’s hostname verifier, while retaining client certificate support and the explicit trust-all option. Users may no longer be able to connect to some previously reachable servers. I also added tests for the default and explicit hostname-verifier choices.

Servers whose certificate the system does not trust (self-signed or from a private CA), accepted silently until now, are rejected. The added network security config lets their users install that CA on the device; without it Android ignores user-installed CAs for apps targeting API 24 or later.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

I also added a test for it (`OkHttpClientModuleTest.kt`). The project builds with this change (`:app:testFdroidDebugUnitTest`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

+package me.ash.reader.infrastructure.di
+
+import android.content.Context
+import java.io.File

+import org.junit.Assert.assertSame

+import org.junit.Test
+import org.junit.rules.TemporaryFolder
+import org.mockito.Mockito
+
+class OkHttpClientModuleTest {
+    @get:Rule
+    val temporaryFolder = TemporaryFolder()
+
+    @Test
+    fun omittedSelectorUsesDefaultHostnameVerifier() {
+        assertSame(OkHttpClient().hostnameVerifier, client(null).hostnameVerifier)
+    }
+
+    @Test
+    fun falseSelectorUsesDefaultHostnameVerifier() {
+        assertSame(OkHttpClient().hostnameVerifier, client(false).hostnameVerifier)
+    }
+

+        val verifier = client(true).hostnameVerifier
+        val session = Mockito.mock(SSLSession::class.java)
+        assertTrue(verifier.verify("untrusted.invalid", session))
+    }
+
+    private fun client(trustAllCerts: Boolean?): OkHttpClient {
+        val owner = Class.forName("me.ash.reader.infrastructure.di.OkHttpClientModuleKt")
+        val method = owner.declaredMethods.single { it.name == "cachingHttpClient" }
+        val selectorIndex = method.parameterTypes.indices.single {
+            method.parameterTypes[it] == Boolean::class.javaPrimitiveType
+        }
+        val masks = IntArray((method.parameterCount + 31) / 32) { -1 }
+        if (trustAllCerts != null) {
+            val maskIndex = selectorIndex / 32
+            masks[maskIndex] = masks[maskIndex] and (1 shl (selectorIndex % 32)).inv()
+        }
+        val arguments = method.parameterTypes.mapIndexed { index, type ->

+        type == OkHttpClient.Builder::class.java -> OkHttpClient.Builder()
+        type == String::class.java || type.isArray -> null
+        type == java.lang.Boolean.TYPE -> false
+        type == java.lang.Byte.TYPE -> 0.toByte()
+        type == java.lang.Short.TYPE -> 0.toShort()
+        type == java.lang.Integer.TYPE -> 0
+        type == java.lang.Long.TYPE -> 0L
+        type == java.lang.Float.TYPE -> 0f
+        type == java.lang.Double.TYPE -> 0.0

cards.title: Question about the SSLContext use in setupSsl
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `setupSsl` in `app/src/main/java/me/ash/reader/infrastructure/di/OkHttpClientModule.kt`.

On the default trust-all path, SSLContext.init receives an array containing an application-defined accept-all trust manager rather than a factory-generated trust-manager array.

I have not opened a pull request because every version I wrote changed what the app does in a case it handles today; in the last one, a user loads a feed through the injected client whose certificate is untrusted or whose hostname does not match. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: Verify TLS certificates and hostnames
cards.text:
Use the platform's server certificate and hostname verification for HTTP clients. Previously, the default configuration accepted any certificate and hostname, allowing an attacker to impersonate a server and intercept traffic, including account credentials.

Keep client certificate authentication using the platform trust manager. Fail client setup if TLS configuration fails instead of silently dropping the client certificate. Servers with untrusted certificates will now need a trusted certificate.

The F-Droid debug build passes.

cards.title: Certificate checks are disabled in setupSsl
cards.text:
I found that `setupSsl` passes a trust manager with an empty server certificate check to `SSLContext.init`; RVSec reported that the manager was not obtained from a trust manager factory. The default clients also accept every hostname, so they do not verify the identity of HTTPS servers. I expect connections to verify the server certificate and hostname.

I didn't open a pull request because the code explicitly enables this behavior by default, and replacing it could prevent existing feeds or accounts from connecting to their servers.

Is accepting unverified certificates and hostnames intentional for these connections? The issue can simply be closed if the current behavior is intentional.

Otherwise I'm happy to help develop a change that verifies servers while providing a suitable way to support private certificates.

cards.title: Certificate checks are bypassed in setupSsl
cards.text:
The HTTP clients use `SSLContext.init` with a trust manager that accepts every certificate chain, and `setupSsl` also accepts every hostname. RVSec reported the custom trust manager passed to this call. These clients can send account credentials, so connections should verify the server's certificate and hostname.

I didn't open a pull request because the bypass is explicitly selected by default and changing it could prevent existing users from connecting to their configured servers.

Is the bypass intended to support servers with certificates Android does not trust? If this behavior is intentional, please feel free to close this issue.

Otherwise I'm happy to help add a way to trust the appropriate certificates while restoring verification.

cards.title: Certificate checks are bypassed in setupSsl
cards.text:
RVSec reported that `SSLContext.init` receives an app-defined trust manager in `setupSsl`. The default client accepts server certificates without checking them and also accepts any hostname. I think HTTPS connections should verify both, especially because service requests can carry account credentials.

I didn't open a pull request because the trust-all path is enabled by default and explicitly suppresses the warning, so changing it could affect existing server connections. I couldn't find a user setting that preserves that behavior selectively.

Should connections use normal certificate and hostname verification by default, with a way to support servers that need different trust settings? This issue can simply be closed if the current behavior is intentional.

Otherwise I'm happy to help implement the approach you prefer.

cards.title: Restore HTTPS certificate and hostname validation
cards.text:
The shared HTTP client currently accepts every server certificate and hostname by default. This lets an attacker impersonate feed or account servers and intercept credentials and content.

Remove the trust-all option and hostname bypass so ordinary connections use OkHttp's default TLS validation. Connections with a selected client certificate retain their key manager and use the platform trust manager. Servers with untrusted certificates or mismatched hostnames will now be rejected.

Add regression tests for certificate and hostname rejection, both with and without a selected client certificate.

The F-Droid debug build and all four TLS regression tests passed.

cards.title: HTTPS certificates and hostnames are not verified for any network request
cards.text:
While running the app through a runtime checker for TLS/crypto API usage, it flagged the SSL setup in `OkHttpClientModule.kt` (`OkHttpClient.Builder.setupSsl`). I looked at the code and I think the report is correct. It isn't a false positive.

`cachingHttpClient` has a parameter `trustAllCerts: Boolean = true`. Nothing in the repository passes a value for it, so the default always applies. This covers the shared client from `provideOkHttpClient` and the clients created in `ProviderAPI`, which the Fever, Google Reader and FreshRSS accounts use. With the default, `setupSsl` does two things:

- It installs an `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing and whose `getAcceptedIssuers` returns an empty array. It then passes that manager to `SSLContext.init` and `sslSocketFactory`.
- It sets `hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }`.

In practice every HTTPS connection the app makes accepts any certificate for any host. That includes expired, self-signed and wrong-host certificates. A network attacker could therefore read or alter feed traffic. They could also capture the credentials sent to self-hosted sync servers: the username and password, and the HTTP basic-auth details. This applies to users who set up a client certificate too. The `trustAllCerts = true` default also takes effect in the client-certificate (mTLS) path.

I did not send a patch because the right fix depends on a product decision. Changing the default to `false` would use the platform trust store and normal hostname checks. That is the safe behaviour, but it would stop working for people who run self-hosted servers with self-signed certificates and who may rely on the current behaviour.

Possible directions:

1. Default to `trustAllCerts = false`. Add an explicit opt-in per account (for example an "Allow untrusted certificates" switch next to the client certificate option) that is off by default and shows a warning.
2. Support pinning or trusting a user-chosen certificate for a given account, instead of trusting everything.
3. Keep today's behaviour but document it, if that is deliberate.

Two smaller points in the same function:

- `sslContext.init(arrayOf(clientKeyManager),...)` puts a possibly `null` key manager into the array when no client certificate alias is set. This only runs when trust-all is on, so it works today. If trust-all becomes opt-in, it should pass `null` for the key managers instead.
- `NoSuchAlgorithmException` and `KeyManagementException` are silently ignored. If SSL setup fails, the client carries on without the configured TLS settings and nobody is told.

I'm happy to prepare a PR for option 1 if the maintainers tell me which way they want to go.

cards.title: Verify HTTPS server certificates and hostnames
cards.text:
Remove the trust-all certificate manager and hostname verifier. HTTPS connections now use platform certificate validation and normal hostname verification, including when a client certificate is selected. This prevents an attacker on the network from impersonating a server and reading or changing traffic, including account credentials.

Servers with untrusted certificates or mismatched hostnames will need a valid, trusted certificate.

Build: `:app:assembleFdroidDebug` passed.

cards.title: Restore server verification in setupSsl
cards.text:
The default HTTP clients pass an app-defined trust manager to `SSLContext.init` that accepts every server certificate, and `setupSsl` also accepts every hostname. RVSec reported the trust manager passed to that call. Server certificates and hostnames should be verified so account credentials and feed requests are sent to the intended server.

I didn't open a pull request because the trust-all path is the default and explicitly suppresses the custom trust manager warning; removing it could change connections users rely on.

Is accepting servers without trusted certificates intended for these clients? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to help add certificate verification while accounting for the server configurations you want to support.

cards.title: Verify HTTPS server certificates and hostnames
cards.text:
The shared HTTP client currently accepts every server certificate and hostname. Feed downloads and account synchronization inherit this behavior, allowing a network attacker to impersonate an HTTPS server and intercept credentials or content.

Remove the certificate and hostname verification bypass. Ordinary clients now use OkHttp's TLS defaults, and clients configured with a client certificate use the platform trust manager. Servers with untrusted certificates or mismatched hostnames will fail validation.

Add local HTTPS regression tests for untrusted certificates, trusted certificates with mismatched hostnames, and trusted certificates with matching hostnames, both with and without a configured client certificate alias.

Validation: the provided build check passed for the F-Droid debug APK, and all six TLS regression tests passed.

cards.title: HTTPS certificates and host names are not verified for any network request
cards.text:
While reviewing how the app sets up TLS, I found that every HTTPS connection the app makes skips certificate validation and host name checking. This was found with an automated runtime checker and then confirmed by reading the code. I have not changed any code, because the fix involves a decision about behaviour for self-hosted users that I think belongs to the maintainers.

## What happens

In `app/src/main/java/me/ash/reader/infrastructure/di/OkHttpClientModule.kt`, `cachingHttpClient` has the parameter `trustAllCerts: Boolean = true`. Neither caller overrides it:

- `OkHttpClientModule.provideOkHttpClient` (the shared client used for local feeds and general fetching) calls it with the default.
- `ProviderAPI` (the base of the Fever and Google Reader / FreshRSS clients) calls it with only `clientCertificateAlias`.

Because the default is `true`, `setupSsl` always runs. It installs a hand-written `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing and whose `getAcceptedIssuers` returns an empty array. It also sets a host name verifier that always returns `true`.

The result is that any certificate is accepted for any host: expired, self-signed, issued for another domain, or forged. A person on the same network (public Wi-Fi, a hostile access point) can intercept or alter traffic. That includes feed content and, for Fever, Google Reader and FreshRSS accounts, the username and password sent to the sync server, and the API tokens returned.

The `trustAllCerts` option dates from the commit that added client certificate (mTLS) support, so it looks like it was meant for users with self-signed servers, but it is currently on for everyone and there is no setting to turn it off.

## Why I did not send a patch

Simply changing the default to `false` would close the hole. In that case the platform trust store would be used (OkHttp's defaults, or `platformTrustManager` when a client certificate is set). But it would also stop working for anyone who currently syncs with a self-signed or private-CA server and relies on the present behaviour. Doing it properly probably needs one of these, and I would like to know which you prefer:

1. Default to normal certificate validation, and add an opt-in per-account setting such as "Allow untrusted certificates", clearly labelled as unsafe.
2. Default to normal validation and let users trust their own CA through the Android user certificate store (no code needed for that, but it needs documenting).
3. Offer certificate pinning or "trust this certificate on first use" for self-hosted servers.

In any of these, the always-true host name verifier should go away unless the user has explicitly opted in. The trust-all manager should only be created in that opt-in path.

## Suggested next step

Let me know which option you want, and I'm happy to send a pull request for it.

cards.title: HTTP client accepts every TLS certificate and hostname by default, including for account sync
cards.text:
While running the app under a runtime checker for TLS and cryptography API use, I found that the HTTP client trusts any certificate. The checker flagged the trust manager passed to the TLS context in `setupSsl` (`app/src/main/java/me/ash/reader/infrastructure/di/OkHttpClientModule.kt`). That trust manager is a class defined in the app, not one obtained from the platform's trust manager factory.

## What the code does

`cachingHttpClient` has a parameter `trustAllCerts: Boolean = true`. No caller overrides it, so it is always on. This covers:

- the shared client from `provideOkHttpClient`
- the clients built in `ProviderAPI` for the Google Reader, FreshRSS and Fever accounts

When the flag is on, `setupSsl` does two things:

- It installs a hostname verifier that returns `true` for every host.
- It installs an `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` and `checkClientTrusted` do nothing.

Certificate chain validation and hostname checks are therefore both disabled for every HTTPS connection the app makes.

## Why it matters

Anyone on the network path, such as a hostile Wi-Fi network or a malicious proxy, can present any certificate and the app will accept it. For the sync accounts this exposes the server URL, the username and password, and the HTTP basic-auth credentials. An attacker could also tamper with the feed content the app shows.

As far as I can tell, this also applies when a client certificate (mTLS) is configured. The client certificate is presented, but the server's certificate is still not checked.

## Why I did not send a patch

The obvious fix is to default `trustAllCerts` to `false`, so the platform trust manager is used. That is already what the `else` branch does. It would stop self-hosted servers with self-signed certificates from connecting. There is currently no setting for those users, so this is a product decision for the maintainers. I did not want to break their sync without agreement.

## Suggested direction

- Default to the platform trust manager and platform hostname verification.
- If self-signed servers need to keep working, make the bypass an explicit per-account option. It should be off by default and carry a clear warning. A better alternative is to let the user pin or import the server's certificate.
- Keep the key manager (client certificate) setup separate from the trust decision, so that adding a client certificate does not turn off server validation.

Separately, `sslContext.init(arrayOf(clientKeyManager),...)` passes an array holding `null` when no client certificate is set. It would be cleaner to pass `null` or an empty array in that case.

I haven't changed any code and haven't built the project for this report. I'm happy to send a patch once you've decided which behavior you want.

cards.title: HTTPS certificates and hostnames are not verified by default
cards.text:
`cachingHttpClient` in `app/src/main/java/me/ash/reader/infrastructure/di/OkHttpClientModule.kt` has the parameter `trustAllCerts: Boolean = true`. No caller overrides it. This means every OkHttp client the app builds goes through `setupSsl` with trust-all enabled. That covers the shared client from `OkHttpClientModule.provideOkHttpClient`, which is used for feed fetching, and the client in `ProviderAPI`, which is used for the Fever, FreshRSS and Google Reader sync APIs.

With `trustAllCerts = true`, `setupSsl` does two things:

- It installs an `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing, so any certificate is accepted, including expired, self-signed or forged ones.
- It calls `hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }`, so the certificate does not even have to match the host.

Anyone who can intercept traffic can therefore impersonate any HTTPS server the app talks to. This includes someone on the same public Wi-Fi network. For the sync providers this exposes the server password, the HTTP basic-auth credentials and the session token. It also lets an attacker alter feed content or article data. HTTPS gives no protection in this configuration. The client certificate (mTLS) option does not help, because it only affects what the client presents, not how the server is checked.

I did not send a patch, because the obvious fix changes behaviour for some users. The trust-all setting is probably there so people with self-hosted servers using self-signed certificates can connect. If the default becomes `false`, the platform trust manager is used (the `else` branch already exists), and those users would have to install their CA on the device or be given another way to opt in. I think that is a decision for the maintainers.

Some options:

1. Default `trustAllCerts` to `false` everywhere and drop the trust-all path. Self-hosted users would need to install their CA certificate on the device.
2. Keep trust-all, but only as an explicit per-account opt-in. It would be off by default, with a warning in the account settings. The flag would be stored with the account's security key, like `clientCertificateAlias`, and passed into `ProviderAPI`.
3. Let the user pin a specific server certificate or fingerprint instead of trusting everything.

Whichever option is chosen, the hostname verifier should only be relaxed together with the trust setting. The shared client used for ordinary feed and image fetching should not need the override at all.

A smaller point: when no client certificate is configured, `setupSsl` calls `sslContext.init(arrayOf(clientKeyManager),...)` with an array holding a `null` element. Passing `null` for the key managers would be cleaner.

I'm happy to prepare a pull request for whichever option you prefer.

cards.title: HTTP client accepts any TLS certificate in setupSsl
cards.text:
RVSec reported that the `TrustManager` passed to `SSLContext.init` in `setupSsl` (OkHttpClientModule.kt) holds an app-defined manager that did not come from a `TrustManagerFactory`. That manager is a `X509TrustManager` whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing, and the hostname verifier is set to `hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }`. `cachingHttpClient` defaults `trustAllCerts` to `true`, and no caller passes `false`. So the shared client and the Fever, Google Reader and FreshRSS clients never validate server certificates. The Google Reader login sends the account password over these connections.

I didn't open a pull request because using the platform trust manager would stop connections to servers with self-signed certificates. The code looks deliberate (`@SuppressLint("CustomX509TrustManager")`), and I couldn't tell from the repository whether users depend on it.

Is accepting every certificate intentional, for example for self-hosted servers? If so, this can simply be closed. Otherwise I'm happy to send a patch that validates certificates by default, with an opt-in setting for self-signed servers if you want one.

cards.title: Validate server certificates by default in cachingHttpClient
cards.text:
`cachingHttpClient` in `OkHttpClientModule.kt` defaulted `trustAllCerts` to `true`. Callers that omit it (ProviderAPI, provideOkHttpClient) reached `setupSsl`, which passes an app-defined X509TrustManager with an empty `checkServerTrusted` to `SSLContext.init`, plus an accept-all hostname verifier. RVSec reported that the `TrustManager` given to `SSLContext.init` holds an app-defined manager and was not observed coming from a `TrustManagerFactory`. On the default path, no certificate validation happened.

I changed the default to `trustAllCerts: Boolean = false`, so the existing validating branch (`Platform.get.platformTrustManager`) is used. Accept-all is still reachable only by passing `trustAllCerts = true` explicitly.

Users of servers with self-signed or private-CA certificates will no longer connect unless that CA is installed on the device.

Servers whose certificate the system does not trust (self-signed or from a private CA), accepted silently until now, are rejected. The added network security config lets their users install that CA on the device; without it Android ignores user-installed CAs for apps targeting API 24 or later.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`:app:assembleFdroidDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: HTTPS clients accept any server certificate in setupSsl
cards.text:
I noticed that `setupSsl` in `OkHttpClientModule.kt` initialises an `SSLContext` with a trust manager the app defines, whose `checkServerTrusted` does nothing, plus a hostname verifier that returns true. `cachingHttpClient` defaults to `trustAllCerts = true` and no caller or setting changes it, so every client, including the Fever, Google Reader and FreshRSS ones that send passwords, accepts any certificate. RVSec reported that this manager did not come from a `TrustManagerFactory`. I'd expect the platform trust manager, which the existing `else` branch already uses.

I didn't open a pull request because defaulting to platform validation would stop users with self-signed or private-CA servers from connecting, and keeping them working needs an opt-in setting or pinning, which is your design decision.

Is trust-all intended for self-hosted servers? If so, this can simply be closed.

Otherwise I'm happy to send a pull request that validates by default and adds an opt-in override per account.

cards.title: Restore HTTPS certificate and hostname validation
cards.text:
The shared HTTP client currently accepts every server certificate and hostname, including for account synchronization. This lets an attacker impersonate an HTTPS server and read or alter traffic, including account credentials.

Remove the certificate and hostname verification bypass. Ordinary connections use OkHttp's default TLS configuration, and connections using a client certificate use the platform trust manager. Servers with untrusted certificates or mismatched hostnames will now fail validation.

Add regression tests for rejecting untrusted certificates and mismatched hostnames, both with and without a client certificate configured.

Validation: the provided build check passed for `:app:assembleFdroidDebug`. All four new tests passed with `testGithubReleaseUnitTest` on Java 17.

cards.title: Restore HTTPS certificate and hostname validation
cards.text:
The shared HTTP client currently accepts every server certificate and hostname by default. This lets an attacker impersonate HTTPS servers and intercept feed contents or account credentials.

Remove the trust-all option and permissive hostname verifier. Requests use OkHttp's normal TLS validation, including when a client certificate is configured through Android KeyChain. Servers with certificates that the device does not trust will now fail validation.

Add regression tests for rejecting an untrusted server certificate and a mismatched hostname, both with and without a client certificate configured.

The app builds successfully with the supplied build check (`:app:assembleFdroidDebug`). Both TLS regression tests pass.

cards.title: Use a fresh KeyGenerator for each key-spec tier in the vault
cards.text:
In `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey` I found that one `KeyGenerator` (AES, AndroidKeyStore) is created up front. The tier loop then calls `init(spec)` on it again for every fallback tier. A tier that fails (for example StrongBox being unavailable) therefore leaves the same generator being initialised a second time before `generateKey`. RVSec reported that call sequence.

The change moves `KeyGenerator.getInstance(...)` inside the loop, so each tier gets its own generator and runs one `init(spec)` and one `generateKey`. The specs, the tier order, the alias, and the error handling are unchanged, and `getInstance` stays outside the `try`, as before. Existing keys and sealed data are not touched.

I haven't checked whether RVSec's report on `seal` changes. That key may also come from the Keystore lookup rather than from a generator. The project builds (`assembleDebug` passed). I didn't run tests or try it on a device. A tier fallback needs a device without StrongBox to exercise.

cards.title: Use a fresh key generator for each key-spec fallback attempt
cards.text:
When the vault creates its AES key, it tries up to three key specs, strictest first (StrongBox plus unlocked-device-required, then without StrongBox, then minimal). Until now it created one `KeyGenerator` before the loop and called `init` on it again for every attempt.

On a device where the first attempt is rejected, which is any device without StrongBox, that one generator was used after it had already thrown. Android doesn't promise that a generator is usable after a failed `init` or `generateKey`, and a runtime check of the Java crypto API calls flagged the repeated `init` as an unexpected call sequence.

This change moves `KeyGenerator.getInstance` inside the loop, so each attempt starts with a new generator. The key specs, their order, the fallback behaviour, the logging and the error thrown when every attempt fails are all unchanged. Nothing is stored differently, and existing keys and sealed data are unaffected.

I'm not proposing a change to `seal`. The same check also reported that the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `seal` had no observed generator. I believe that's a false positive: when the key already exists, it's loaded from the Android Keystore rather than generated in that process. The cipher also leaves IV generation to the Keystore, which is what you want for AES-GCM, so I left it alone.

I haven't run this on a device with a failing first tier. I only confirmed that the reasoning above fits the code. `assembleDebug` builds and passes. I didn't run the unit tests, and I didn't add a new one, since the behaviour needs a real Keystore.

cards.title: Use a fresh KeyGenerator for each Keystore fallback
cards.text:
In `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey`, the code shares a `KeyGenerator` across AES key generation attempts at different fallback tiers. RVSec reported that the `KeyGenerator` call sequence is not accepted by its rule.

I create a fresh generator for each attempt while keeping the alias, AES parameters and fallback order unchanged. Provider lookup failures still propagate.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: No action: both runtime-checker reports describe correct use of the Android Keystore
cards.text:
I read the vault class (`androidApp/.../storage/KeystoreSecretVault.kt`) against both reports. I didn't change any code and didn't run the build, because nothing was edited.

## "No generator of the key given to Cipher.init was observed" (in `seal`)

`seal` gets its key from `getOrCreateKey`. After the first run, that call just loads the existing key from the `AndroidKeyStore` provider. The key was generated in an earlier process, so the checker can't have seen a generator for it. Keys held in the Keystore are meant to be used this way: the key material never leaves secure hardware, and the app only ever holds a handle to it.

The `Cipher.init(ENCRYPT_MODE, key)` call with no IV is also correct. A Keystore AES-GCM key refuses a caller-supplied IV by default, because it generates a fresh random one. The code then reads that IV back and checks that it is 12 bytes. Passing our own IV would be the less safe choice.

This looks like a limit of the checker. It can only trace keys generated within the observed run, not keys loaded from persistent storage. I don't see a code change that would be an improvement here.

## "Observed call sequence is not accepted" (in `getOrCreateKey`)

The method creates one key generator and then walks through the fallback tiers, calling `init` and `generateKey` on that same instance for each attempt. If a tier fails, the next one re-initialises the same generator. That is legal for the JCA, and the Keystore generator keeps no state between attempts that would matter here. The failed attempts are the intended fallback behaviour, documented in the method comment.

Creating a new generator for each tier would probably make the checker's sequence look cleaner. I couldn't confirm that, because I have no device or runtime checker. It would also change security-sensitive code on the strength of a tool's output alone, and `CONTRIBUTING.md` says unsolicited changes that aren't fixes for real bugs aren't wanted. So I'm not proposing it.

## Out of scope: possible race on first use

While reading the code I noticed a possible issue that neither report mentions. Several `KeystoreSecretVault` instances are created (in the service and the view model), and `getOrCreateKey` has no lock around its "load, else generate" step. If two first-time `seal` calls overlapped, both could generate a key under the same alias. I haven't reproduced this or checked how the callers are ordered. Because it is unconfirmed and was not reported, I'm not filing it. If a maintainer already knows the first seal always runs before any concurrent use, there is nothing to do.

cards.text:
In `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey`, the vault returns an existing AES key or tries to create one using three Keystore tiers. RVSec reported that the `KeyGenerator` call sequence does not follow its rule for using generators; a failed attempt can be followed by another initialization of the same generator.

I use a fresh generator for each attempt, while keeping provider lookup outside the retry catch and preserving the tier settings, order, and final exception. I added tests for the retry tiers, total failure, round-trip and existing-key behavior, including a generator that rejects reuse.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

I also added a test for it (`KeystoreSecretVaultRetryTest.kt`). The project builds with this change (`:androidApp:testDebugUnitTest`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Use a fresh KeyGenerator for each key-spec tier
cards.text:
In `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey` I noticed that a single `KeyGenerator` (AES, AndroidKeyStore) is created once and then `init`-ed again with each fallback `KeyGenParameterSpec` tier. When an earlier tier is rejected (for example StrongBox on a device without it), the same generator gets a second or third `init` before `generateKey`. RVSec reported that call sequence on this generator.

This change moves `KeyGenerator.getInstance` inside the tier loop, so every attempt is its own `getInstance`, `init`, `generateKey` sequence on a new generator. The specs, the tier order, the logging and the failure path (`KeystoreUnavailableException` after the last tier) are unchanged. The key alias, algorithm and wire format are untouched, so existing sealed data still reads.

Notes for review:
- RVSec also flagged `seal` because no generator of the key passed to `Cipher.init` was observed. I haven't confirmed whether this change affects that report. A key loaded from the Keystore on later runs, rather than generated in-process, is not touched.
- No unit test added: the code only runs against the AndroidKeyStore provider.
- `./gradlew` debug build via the build check passed. I haven't run it on a device or run the tests.

cards.text:
The vault uses `KeyGenerator` to create the Android Keystore key that encrypts stored secrets and the database passphrase. RVSec reported an unexpected call sequence when the generator is reused across fallback attempts. I create a fresh generator for each attempt so a retry does not initialize the same generator again. This change addresses the reported call sequence; I have not established a security impact from the existing sequence.

The vault still retrieves an existing key from Android Keystore and keeps the same ciphertext format. RVSec also reported that it could not find a generator for the key passed to `Cipher.init`; the existing-key path remains unchanged, so that report may persist.

The key creation path uses the Android Keystore provider and initializes the generator with a parameter spec before generating a key. Every fallback attempt supplies the alias, encryption and decryption purposes, 256-bit key size, GCM mode, and no padding. Retrying with fewer device-specific constraints does not skip initialization. An unexpected observed sequence alone does not establish incorrect API use.

The encryption path either uses the newly generated key or loads the existing key from Android Keystore. A persisted key does not need to be generated again in the current process before use. Android's [documented AES-GCM example](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec#example:-aes-key-for-encryption/decryption-in-gcm-mode) shows both parameter-spec initialization and retrieval of an existing secret key with `KeyStore.getKey`. The absence of an observed generator for a loaded key does not establish that the key is invalid or insecure.

These reports do not justify a source change or a maintainer report. No source files were changed, and no build was run.

Android's [documented AES-GCM example](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyGenParameterSpec#example:-aes-key-for-encryption/decryption-in-gcm-mode) shows both parameter-based initialization and later retrieval of the saved key.

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
I looked at both runtime-checker reports against the secret vault (`KeystoreSecretVault.kt`) and concluded that neither points to a defect worth sending to the maintainers. I changed no source files.

**Report about `seal` ("no generator of the key given to `Cipher.init` was observed").** This is a false positive. In the normal case `seal` gets its key from the Android Keystore by alias, because the key was created on an earlier run, and the checker only sees keys created through a key generator in the same process. The cipher usage is correct for the Keystore. It is AES-256-GCM, and the caller does not supply an IV, so the Keystore generates a fresh random one for each encryption. That is the mode the Keystore requires, since it rejects caller-chosen IVs when a key is used for encryption. `seal` also checks the IV length and writes it into the sealed blob. Nothing here needs fixing.

**Report about `getOrCreateKey` (unexpected call sequence).** The method creates one key generator and calls `init` and `generateKey` on it once per fallback tier. If a tier fails, the same generator is re-initialised with the next, looser spec. The checker flags this because the sequence is not the plain "create, init, generate" order. I found no functional problem in it. Re-initialising a Keystore key generator resets its spec, and a failed attempt leaves no alias behind. The code's comments say a Samsung A42 falls back to the minimal tier and works.

I considered creating a fresh generator for each tier so the sequence is always the plain one. That would change no behaviour and fix no bug, and it would only quiet the checker. `CONTRIBUTING.md` says the maintainers want security reports and bug reports for shipped features, and that other unsolicited PRs are closed. The project also treats this vault as sensitive code that should change rarely. A behaviour-neutral edit to it, made to satisfy a tool, is not something they asked for. Opening an issue would also add noise, because nothing is broken.

I did not run the build, because I made no code change.

cards.title: Create a new KeyGenerator for each key-generation attempt
cards.text:
In `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey`, the code created one `KeyGenerator` for AES and reused it across the tier fallback loop. When a tier's `init` failed, the same instance was initialised again with the next spec before `generateKey`.

RVSec reported that the call sequence on this `KeyGenerator` is not one it accepts. The sequence it expects is `getInstance`, then `init`, then `generateKey`, once per instance. I moved `KeyGenerator.getInstance` inside the `try` in each tier attempt, so every instance gets exactly one `init` and one `generateKey`, and a failed `init` is never retried on the same object.

The alias, the AES/GCM/NoPadding key parameters and the tier fallback order are unchanged. Keys already in the Keystore and existing sealed blobs stay readable.

I found this while running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs.

The project builds with this change (`assembleDebug`).

Happy to adjust this to the project's conventions.

cards.title: Create a fresh key generator for each vault retry
cards.text:
Today `KeystoreSecretVault` uses a `KeyGenerator` to create the Android Keystore key that encrypts stored passwords, channel keys, identity seeds and the database passphrase. RVSec reported an unexpected call sequence on the generator. I create a fresh generator for each fallback attempt so a retry does not initialize the same instance again. I made this change because of the RVSec report; I have not established a security impact from the existing retry sequence.

The app builds with `assembleDebug`; I did not run tests. Please check the fallback on affected Android devices and whether RVSec accepts the new sequence, including when an existing Keystore key is loaded. Please also verify previously stored secrets on a device.

cards.title: Use a fresh key generator for each vault fallback
cards.text:
The vault uses Java's `KeyGenerator` to create the Android Keystore key that encrypts passwords, channel keys, identity seeds and the database passphrase. RVSec reported an unexpected call sequence: the fallback loop can initialize the same generator again after an attempt fails. I create a fresh generator for each attempt in response to the report, while keeping the existing fallback tiers and stored data format.

The project builds with `assembleDebug`. I could not verify the fallback on a device or check whether RVSec accepts the new sequence; those checks would be useful on devices that need a less restrictive tier.

cards.title: Create a new KeyGenerator for each key-spec tier
cards.text:
When the vault creates its AES key, it makes one `KeyGenerator` for the Android Keystore and then calls `init(spec)` on it once per fallback tier. If a tier's `init` throws (for example StrongBox is unavailable), the same generator is initialised again with the next spec before `generateKey`. RVSec, a runtime checker for Java crypto API use, reported that call sequence on `KeyGenerator`.

This change moves `KeyGenerator.getInstance` inside the tier loop, so each tier gets its own generator that goes through `getInstance`, `init`, `generateKey`. The spec for each tier, the tier order and the error handling are unchanged. A failure in `getInstance` still propagates as before, outside the `try`.

RVSec also reported that the key passed to `Cipher.init` in `seal` had no observed generator. On a fresh install that key comes from this method, so I expect this change to resolve it. When the key is loaded with `KeyStore.getKey` instead, no generator runs in that process, and I haven't changed that path.

The project builds (`assembleDebug` passed). I didn't run the tests, a device, or RVSec again, so please check whether RVSec now accepts it.

cards.title: Create a fresh key generator for each Keystore spec tier
cards.text:
When the vault key is first created, the code tries up to three key specs, from strictest to most relaxed. Until now it created one `KeyGenerator` and called `init` on it once per tier. After a rejected spec, the next tier re-initialised the same object.

This PR creates a new `KeyGenerator` inside each attempt. The sequence per attempt is now get instance, `init(spec)`, `generateKey`. A generator whose `init` just threw is never reused.

Nothing else changes. The tiers, the key spec, the alias, the logging, the final `KeystoreUnavailableException` and the sealed-blob format are all the same. The change is a few lines in `KeystoreSecretVault.getOrCreateKey`.

I'm not aware of a failure this fixes. Re-initialising a generator is permitted, and the Android Keystore provider resets itself after a failed `init`. The motivation is robustness. This code path runs on devices with vendor-specific Keystore quirks (see the A42 note in the comment above it), and it is cheap to stop depending on how each vendor's provider behaves after a failed `init`. I found it because a runtime checker for crypto API usage flagged the repeated `init` calls on one generator.

The same checker also flagged `seal`, saying it never saw the key being generated. I did not change anything for that, because it looks like a false positive. `getOrCreateKey` first loads the existing key from the Keystore, so on any run after the first the key was generated in an earlier process, where the checker cannot see it.

I have not tested this on a device. That includes the fallback path, which needs a device that rejects the strict spec. The change does not touch the successful path, which still ends in `generateKey` after one `init(spec)`.

The project builds: `assembleDebug` passed. I did not run the unit test suites.

The vault first looks for an existing Android Keystore key and generates one only if it is absent. A key used for encryption may therefore have been created in an earlier run, outside the observed call sequence.

When creation is needed, the vault initializes the generator with an AES-GCM configuration before generating the key. If a device rejects a configuration, it retries with a less restrictive configuration while retaining AES-GCM and a 256-bit key. Encryption uses a provider-generated IV. The reported observations do not establish a cryptographic misuse or a need for a code change.

cards.title: Require at least 2048-bit RSA for certificate enrollment
cards.text:
Remove the 1024-bit option from the key-size selector and reject sizes below 2048 bits before starting a certificate request, including requests from managed configuration. This prevents new enrollments from generating RSA keys below the [minimum recommended for signature generation](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-131ar2.pdf).

Checked that undersized values are rejected, sizes of 2048 bits and above pass validation, and the selector retains 2048, 4096 and 8192 bits with a 4096-bit default. The Google debug build passed using the provided build check with a temporary writable Android settings directory for the debug signing key.

cards.title: Stop offering 1024-bit RSA keys for SCEP requests
cards.text:
In `ScepClient.CertReq` I generate the RSA key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.initialize(isKeyLen)`. That key signs the self-signed certificate and the CSR. The size comes from the key size spinner (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192), a saved setting, or the `rsa-key-length` MDM value, and nothing checks it. RVSec reported an invalid RSA key size at this call. It didn't tell me which value it saw.

This change drops 1024 from the spinner list and makes `CertReq` use at least 2048 bits, so an old saved setting or an MDM value of 1024 no longer produces a 1024-bit key. Those users get 2048-bit keys instead, and a saved 1024 selection falls back to the first list entry.

The project builds with this change (build_check passed). I haven't tested it on a device or against a SCEP server.

Open points: 2048 and 8192 stay selectable and RVSec may still report them, since it expects 3072 or 4096. Whether to also drop 2048, or add 3072, is your call. I couldn't read NIST SP 800-131A's key-size table, so the 1024 reasoning rests on general guidance toward larger keys.

cards.title: Require RSA keys of at least 2048 bits for enrollment
cards.text:
Remove the 1024-bit option from the enrollment screen and reject key lengths below 2048 bits when generating an enrollment key. This also prevents automatic enrollment from generating weak keys when a smaller length is supplied through managed configuration. Managed configurations using a smaller length must be updated for automatic enrollment to succeed.

The Google debug build passed using the supplied build check.

cards.title: Question about the KeyPairGenerator use in CertReq
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `ScepClient.CertReq` in `app/src/main/java/systems/sieber/droid_scep/ScepClient.java`.

The RSA KeyPairGenerator is initialized with a measured 8192-bit argument, outside the rule's permitted 3072- and 4096-bit values. The same constraint also excludes selectable 1024- and 2048-bit values. The reported Get → Init → Gen order is satisfied.

I have not opened a pull request because every version I wrote changed what the app does in a case it handles today; in the last one, a manual-enrollment user wants to select a previously offered 2048- or 8192-bit RSA key: after the change, neither size is offered; a saved selection is displayed as unavailable. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: RSA key sizes in SCEP enrollment
cards.text:
I found that SCEP enrollment uses `KeyPairGenerator` with the key size selected by the user or supplied through MDM. RVSec reported an invalid RSA key size at this call but did not specify the size. The available choices include 1024 bits, which is below the minimum in [NIST's guidance for RSA signature generation](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-131ar2.pdf); the generated key signs the request and its self-signed certificate.

I didn't open a pull request because restricting sizes to 3072 and 4096 would also change the existing 2048- and 8192-bit choices, and I don't know which size RVSec observed.

Would you prefer to remove the 1024-bit choice while retaining the larger choices? If the current behavior is intentional, this issue can simply be closed. Otherwise I'm happy to work on the agreed change.

cards.title: Fall back to the default RSA key length when the managed configuration value is unsupported
cards.text:
The auto-enrollment worker reads `rsa-key-length` from the managed configuration as a plain integer and passes it straight to the RSA key generator. Nothing checks it. A value such as 0, 512 or 3000 makes key generation fail with an invalid key size error. The exception is caught and logged, so the certificate is never requested. The only trace is a log line, and the enrollment fails again on every run.

The interactive screen avoids this because it only offers the lengths in the `rsa_lens` list (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). This change applies the same list to the managed configuration value. If the configured length is not in the list, the worker logs a warning and uses the default length (4096), so enrollment still goes ahead.

The change is confined to `CertInstaller.java`. The lengths offered in the UI and the default length are unchanged. 1024 is still accepted because the UI offers it. Whether to drop it is a separate decision for the maintainers.

I ran the project's build check (debug build). It passed. I did not run the app or test auto-enrollment on a device with a managed configuration.

cards.title: Key size choices in ScepClient.CertReq beyond 3072/4096
cards.text:
`ScepClient.CertReq` calls `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA")` and `keyGen.initialize(isKeyLen)`. The size comes from the key size spinner (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192; default 4096) or from the MDM `rsa-key-length` setting, which takes any integer. RVSec flagged this call as an invalid RSA key size without saying which value it saw. It expects 3072 or 4096.

I didn't open a pull request because every change that satisfies it removes 2048 or 8192, which aren't weak, and users or their MDM may rely on them. I also can't tell what sizes your SCEP servers expect.

Is the current list intentional, or would you prefer only 3072 and 4096, or just dropping 1024? You can simply close this if the current behaviour is intended. Otherwise I'm happy to send a pull request for the list you choose, including how saved and MDM values are mapped.

While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `ScepClient.CertReq` in `app/src/main/java/systems/sieber/droid_scep/ScepClient.java`.

In the run, `KeyPairGenerator.initialize(int)` received 8192 bits for RSA, which RVSec reported as an invalid key size. The shared method does not validate the size supplied by the caller, and the manual selector offers sizes other than 3072 and 4096 bits.

I didn't open a pull request because every version I wrote changed behavior the app supports today. My last version limited the manual selector to 3072 and 4096 bits; even if 8192 were restored, a user who switched away could not select it again. Is there a constraint I'm missing, and would you be open to a change here?

cards.title: RSA key length: 1024 is offered, and the managed "rsa-key-length" value is not validated
cards.text:
A runtime check of the app flagged the RSA key generation in `ScepClient.CertReq` with "invalid key size for algorithm RSA". I could not tell from the report which size was used, so this is based on reading the code. I have not changed anything.

The key length reaches `keyGen.initialize(isKeyLen)` in `ScepClient.CertReq` from two places:

1. The "Key Size" spinner in `ScepFragment`. Its entries (`rsa_lens` in `strings.xml`) are 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192. The default is 4096.
2. The managed configuration key `rsa-key-length` (an integer), read in `CertInstaller` for auto-enroll. It is passed on as-is. `ScepFragment` only checks that the value is greater than 0.

Two things follow from this:

- 1024-bit RSA is below what current guidance considers acceptable (2048 is the usual minimum), and it is one tap away in the UI.
- An MDM admin can set `rsa-key-length` to any integer, such as 0, a negative number, or a value the provider rejects. `KeyPairGenerator.initialize` then throws an unchecked `InvalidParameterException`. `CertInstaller.requestScep` doesn't catch it, so the scheduled enrollment work would likely fail with a crash instead of a logged error. I haven't run this case.

I didn't send a patch because the right fix depends on how you want to handle compatibility. Some SCEP servers may still need 1024-bit keys, and removing that option would be a product decision.

Possible options:

- Remove 1024 from `rsa_lens`, or keep it but label it as insecure.
- In `CertInstaller` and `ScepFragment`, check the managed value against the allowed sizes. If it isn't one of them, log a warning and use `default_rsa_len`.
- Catch the invalid-size case in `requestScep` so a bad value is logged instead of crashing the worker.

I can turn any of these into a PR if you tell me which you prefer.

cards.title: Question about the KeyPairGenerator use in CertReq
cards.text:
While running the app under RVSec, a runtime checker for how apps use the Java crypto and TLS APIs, it flagged `ScepClient.CertReq` in `app/src/main/java/systems/sieber/droid_scep/ScepClient.java`.

The RSA KeyPairGenerator receives the caller-supplied integer size without validation; 8192 reached initialize in a run, outside the rule’s {3072, 4096} constraint.

I have not opened a pull request because every version I wrote changed what the app does in a case it handles today; in the last one, a user selects 2048 or 8192 bits, or an existing managed configuration supplies either size, for a new certificate request: after the change, CertReq throws IllegalArgumentException before initializing the generator, so the request cannot proceed. Is there a constraint on this code I may be missing, and would you be open to a change here?

With your answer I can prepare a change and send it for review.

Thanks!

cards.title: No action
cards.text:
The runtime report says that `ScepClient.CertReq` called RSA key generation with a key size the provider rejected. I read every path that reaches that call. I did not find a way for normal use of the app to trigger it, so I don't think the maintainers need to hear about it.

How the key size reaches the call:

- In the interactive screen, the size comes from a spinner. Its entries are 1024, 2048, 4096 and 8192 (`rsa_lens` in `strings.xml`). All four are ordinary RSA sizes. The default is 4096.
- In automatic enrollment, `CertInstaller` reads the managed-configuration integer `rsa-key-length`. If it is unset, it uses 4096. The only way to get a rejected size here is for an administrator to configure a nonsensical number, such as 0 or a negative value. In that case the provider throws and the existing `catch (Exception)` in `requestScep` logs the message. The worker does not crash. Rejecting a bad configuration value and logging it is reasonable behaviour.
- In the interactive screen with a managed value, `setSpinnerDefault` only selects a spinner entry that matches the configured value. A value not in the list is ignored, so the spinner never hands an invalid size to the key generator.

The report gives no key size, so I can't tell which value triggered it. The most likely explanation is that the checker drove `CertReq` with a synthetic size, or ran on a device whose provider does not support one of the larger sizes. That would be a limitation of that environment, not something the app's own inputs produce.

I did not change any code. Adding validation would only turn one logged error into another, and a check against a fixed list of sizes could reject valid administrator choices such as 3072. I did not run the app or the build, since there is no code change to verify.

cards.title: Fall back to the default RSA key length when the managed config value is unsupported
cards.text:
## What this changes

For automatic enrollment, `CertInstaller` reads `rsa-key-length` from the managed configuration and passes it straight to `ScepClient.CertReq`, which hands it to `KeyPairGenerator.initialize`. The restriction is a free integer, so a value such as `0`, a negative number or `1000` makes key generation throw an `InvalidParameterException` ("invalid key size for algorithm RSA"). The worker catches it and only writes a line to the log, so auto enrollment and renewal silently never happen.

This change checks the value against the key lengths the app already offers (the `rsa_lens` array: 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). If the value is not in that list, the worker logs a warning and uses `default_rsa_len` (4096) instead. The manual enrollment screen is unchanged, since its spinner only offers those values.

I did not change the list of offered sizes. 1024-bit keys are still selectable, which you may want to revisit separately.

## Why

A typo or unsupported value in the MDM configuration should not disable certificate enrollment without any visible sign. Falling back to the default keeps enrollment working and leaves a warning in the log.

## Testing

I ran the debug build (`assembleGoogleDebug`) and it passed. I did not run the app or test enrollment against a SCEP server, so the fallback path is untested at runtime.

The size comes from the key-size spinner (1024, 2048, 4096, 8192) or from the `rsa-key-length` MDM setting. RVSec reported an invalid RSA key size at this call.

NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 lists 1024-bit RSA as disallowed, so I removed 1024 from the spinner and made `CertReq` raise any smaller size (for example from MDM) to 2048. A stored 1024 setting now falls back to 2048 in the spinner. The app builds (`assembleGoogleDebug` passed); I added no tests, as the module has none.

I left 2048 and 8192 as they were, because I found nothing showing they are weak, and lowering 8192 would reduce strength. RVSec may still report those sizes, and I couldn't tell which size it saw. Whether to also restrict choices to 3072 and 4096 is the maintainers' call. I didn't check how SCEP servers react to the change.

cards.title: Replace the 1024-bit RSA option with 3072 in the key size list
cards.text:
`ScepClient.CertReq` calls `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA")` and `initialize(isKeyLen)`, where the size comes straight from the key size spinner (`rsa_lens` in `strings.xml`) or from the MDM `rsa-key-length` setting. RVSec reported that the size reaching this call was not one it accepts for RSA (it accepts 3072 and 4096). The default (4096) is fine, but the list also offered 1024-bit keys, which are no longer considered safe for RSA.

This replaces the 1024 entry with 3072 and keeps the list sorted (2048, 3072, 4096, 8192). `ScepClient` itself is unchanged. A saved or MDM-pushed 1024 no longer matches a spinner entry, so the manual screen falls back to the first entry (2048). The automatic enrollment in `CertInstaller` still passes the MDM value to `CertReq` unchanged.

The project builds with this change (`build_check` passed). I haven't tested it on a device, and there is no unit-test source set.

Open point: 2048 and 8192 are still selectable and RVSec would likely still report them if chosen. I left them because they are not weak and some SCEP servers may expect 2048. Whether to drop them, or to clamp MDM-supplied values in `CertReq`, is your call.

cards.title: RSA key sizes in SCEP enrollment
cards.text:
When requesting a certificate, `ScepClient.CertReq` passes the selected or managed key size to Java's `KeyPairGenerator` and uses the key to sign the request. RVSec reported an invalid RSA key size at this call without giving the size. The app offers 1024-bit keys, which are too short for signature generation under NIST guidance.

I didn't open a pull request because restricting all requests to the sizes checked by RVSec would also change the existing 8192-bit choice and managed configurations.

Would you prefer to remove the 1024-bit option while retaining the other existing sizes, even though RVSec may still report some of them? If the current behavior is intentional, please feel free to close this issue.

Otherwise I'm happy to work on a change that preserves the sizes you want to support.

The Android Keystore instance is loaded before it is used to look up the key. The lookup uses a null protection parameter, which Android documents for retrieving a keystore key. If the alias is absent, the app generates an AES key in the Android Keystore.

The reported observation does not identify a misuse that warrants a change or a report to the maintainers. See the [Android Keystore documentation](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore) and [key protection reference](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/keystore/KeyProtection).

cards.title: Read the credential key directly from Android Keystore
cards.text:
Today `CryptoManager` reads a `KeyStore` entry to obtain the key used to encrypt MQTT credentials and the OpenCelliD API key. RVSec reported the sequence ending with that entry read. I changed it to read the secret key directly from the same alias; this addresses the reported sequence without changing the key or the stored ciphertext format. The existing read is not known to weaken the protection of these credentials.

The CDR debug app build passes. Please check key creation and credentials saved by an earlier version on a device, and confirm that RVSec accepts the new sequence.

cards.title: No maintainer action needed
cards.text:
The credential encryption code obtains an Android Keystore instance and calls `load(null)` inside its lazy initializer before any `getEntry` lookup. Later lookups reuse that initialized instance. If initialization throws, the lookup is not reached. An existing secret key is reused; a missing key is generated with the Android Keystore provider.

This follows Android's documented usage: its [keystore guide](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/keystore#UsingAndroidKeyStore) shows `load(null)` followed by `getEntry(alias, null)`. The [API reference](https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyStore#getEntry(java.lang.String,%20java.security.KeyStore.ProtectionParameter)) permits a null protection parameter and returns null for a missing alias. The reported call sequence does not establish an application defect, so no source change or maintainer issue is warranted.

cards.title: Read the Keystore master key with KeyStore.getKey
cards.text:
`CryptoManager.getOrCreateKey` looks up the AES key that encrypts the stored MQTT and OpenCelliD credentials by calling `KeyStore.getEntry(alias, null)` on the `AndroidKeyStore` and casting the result to `SecretKeyEntry`. RVSec, a runtime checker for Java crypto API usage, reported this call sequence on the `KeyStore` object, because it expects keys to be read with `getKey` after `load`.

This change reads the key with `keyStore.getKey(KEY_ALIAS, null) as? SecretKey` and falls back to `createKey` when nothing is there, as before. It returns the same Keystore-backed key for the same alias, so existing encrypted values still decrypt and nothing stored changes. The change was made because RVSec reports the call; I found no weakness in the old code.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run the app or any tests, and have not checked whether RVSec accepts the new sequence. `NsAnalyticsCryptoManager` has the same `getEntry` pattern but was not reported, so I left it alone; the same one-line change would apply there if you want it.

cards.title: No action: runtime checker warning on the key lookup in the credential encryption helper
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the private `getOrCreateKey` method in `CryptoManager.kt`. It said the observed sequence of keystore calls is not an accepted one. I looked at the code and at the rule it was checked against. I concluded this is a false positive and that no change should go to the maintainers.

What the code does:
- It opens the `AndroidKeyStore` provider and calls `load(null)`.
- It looks the key up with `getEntry(alias, null)`.
- If the key is missing, it creates an AES-256-GCM key through `KeyGenerator` with a `KeyGenParameterSpec`.

This is the pattern the Android documentation describes for Keystore-backed secret keys.

Why the rule doesn't fit:
- The rule models the generic desktop keystore types (JKS, JCEKS, PKCS12 and similar). It requires one of those type names, but `AndroidKeyStore` is not among them.
- It expects a `getKey` call after `load`, with a password that is neither a `String` nor hard-coded. Android Keystore entries have no password. Their protection comes from the hardware or system keystore.
- The code reads the entry with `getEntry` and passes a null protection parameter. That is correct for Android Keystore, and the rule doesn't allow it.

I found no real weakness in the code:
- The key is non-exportable and bound to the keystore.
- GCM with a random IV is required.
- There are no hard-coded secrets.
- `NsAnalyticsCryptoManager.kt` is identical apart from the key alias, so it would produce the same warning for the same reason.

Rewriting the lookup to use `getKey` to satisfy the rule would change working code to fit a rule that doesn't model Android. It would risk behavior regressions for no security benefit. I did not change any code, so I did not run the build.

cards.title: Read the Android keystore AES key with KeyStore.getKey
cards.text:
In `CryptoManager.getOrCreateKey` the app looks up its existing AES key in the `AndroidKeyStore` with `KeyStore.getEntry(alias, null)`, casts the result to `KeyStore.SecretKeyEntry` and takes its `secretKey`. RVSec, a runtime checker for Java crypto API usage, reported this call sequence on the `KeyStore` object.

This change reads the key with `KeyStore.getKey(alias, null) as? SecretKey` instead. It returns the same stored key, and the existing fallback to `createKey` when no secret key is stored is unchanged. The alias, key generation, cipher and the stored `base64(iv):base64(ciphertext)` format are untouched, so credentials encrypted by earlier versions still decrypt. I don't think this has a security impact. I changed it because RVSec reports the call.

`NsAnalyticsCryptoManager` has the same lookup. RVSec didn't report it, so I left it alone.

The project builds (`build_check` passed). I did not run tests or try it on a device, so someone should check on a device that an existing install still decrypts its stored MQTT and OpenCelliD credentials. I also can't tell whether RVSec accepts the new sequence.

cards.title: No action: runtime checker warning on the key lookup helper
cards.text:
A runtime checker for Java crypto API usage flagged the private `getOrCreateKey` helper in `CryptoManager.kt`. It said the observed sequence of keystore calls was not one its usage model accepts. It did not say which call it objected to.

I read the code. I could not find a defect, and I don't think a change should be sent to the maintainers.

The helper does the following:

- It gets the `AndroidKeyStore` instance and calls `load(null)`. This is the documented initialisation for that provider.
- It calls `getEntry(alias, null)` and casts the result to a secret key entry. The null protection parameter is correct, because Android keystore keys are not password protected.
- If no entry exists, it generates an AES-256 GCM key through the keystore-backed key generator. The key purposes, block mode, padding and randomized-encryption requirement are all set, and the key never leaves the keystore.

This matches the pattern in the Android developer documentation. The calls are in the expected order, and a missing alias is handled by the null fallback.

The most likely cause is that the checker's model of the keystore API is stricter than the Android provider needs. It may expect an alias-existence check before the entry lookup, or a particular `load` overload. Adding an alias check would only add a second call and a small race window between the check and the lookup. It would not make anything more secure.

The same code appears in `NsAnalyticsCryptoManager.kt`, so the warning applies to both and the reasoning is the same.

I made no code changes and did not run the build, since nothing was modified.

cards.title: No action: key store warning in CryptoManager.getOrCreateKey
cards.text:
The runtime checker reported that the call sequence in `CryptoManager.getOrCreateKey` is not accepted by its key store rule. I read the code and I don't think it points to a real problem, so I'm not sending a pull request or an issue.

What the code does: it opens the `AndroidKeyStore` provider with `KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore")` followed by `load(null)`. It then calls `getEntry(alias, null)`. If no key exists, it creates an AES-256 GCM key with `KeyGenerator` and `KeyGenParameterSpec`. The key is hardware-backed where available and never leaves the key store. The cipher uses `AES/GCM/NoPadding`, the IV is generated by the provider on encrypt (randomized encryption is required), and the 128-bit tag is passed explicitly on decrypt.

This is the sequence Android's documentation prescribes for the Android key store. The generic key store rule assumes a file-based store. It expects a password-bearing `load` and a protection parameter on `getEntry`. The Android key store has no passwords: `load(null)` is the only supported form, and a protection parameter for a key that is not password-protected is not used. Changing the calls to satisfy the rule would add a meaningless password or parameter without improving security. A rule written for desktop key stores doesn't fit this provider, so the report is a false positive.

I found no other issue in this method. The lookup-then-create path is correct, and failures are caught and logged by `encrypt` and `decrypt`. `NsAnalyticsCryptoManager` has identical code and would give the same report for the same reason.

I made no code changes and did not run the build.

This change addresses the reported sequence; I have not established a security impact from the original lookup.

cards.title: No action: key-store usage in CryptoManager is correct
cards.text:
The runtime checker flagged the sequence of key-store calls made from `CryptoManager.getOrCreateKey`. I read the code and found nothing to change, so I'm not sending an issue or a PR.

The code does this:

1. It opens the `AndroidKeyStore` provider with `KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore")` and calls `load(null)`.
2. It looks up the alias with `getEntry(KEY_ALIAS, null)`.
3. If no entry exists, it generates an AES-256 GCM key with `KeyGenerator` and `KeyGenParameterSpec`. The key is created inside the keystore and its purposes are limited to encrypt and decrypt.
4. Encryption lets the keystore pick a random IV. Decryption passes the stored IV in a `GCMParameterSpec`.

This is the pattern Android's documentation prescribes for the hardware-backed keystore. In this pattern `load(null)` and the `null` protection parameter are required. The `AndroidKeyStore` provider has no password or file, and the key material never leaves the secure environment.

I think the checker's generic key-store model assumes a file-based store such as JKS or PKCS12, with a stream and a password. The call order here is fine for that provider. The report is most likely a mismatch with that model and not a flaw in the app.

The only way to satisfy such a model would be to switch to a password-protected software keystore. That would store the master key less securely, so it would be a regression.

I did not run the build, because no source file was changed.
No valid deliverable: correction not generated.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 instead of MD5 to verify exported backup ZIPs
cards.text:
After a backup ZIP is written to the target location, `exportAsZip` re-reads both the local temporary file and the exported file and compares their hashes to detect a corrupted or truncated write. That comparison used MD5.

This change switches the comparison to SHA-256. The helpers are renamed from `md5Hash` to `sha256Hash`, and the log and exception messages now say SHA-256.

This is not a vulnerability fix. The hash is only used to compare two copies of the same file, so MD5 was functionally adequate there. I made the change because MD5 is a deprecated algorithm that static and runtime crypto checkers flag, and SHA-256 is a drop-in replacement that is available on every supported Android version. The hash value is never stored or persisted, so there are no compatibility concerns with existing backups. The cost is slightly more CPU time when verifying large backups.

There is no behaviour change otherwise: the retry-on-mismatch logic is untouched.

I ran the project's build check (compile plus debug unit tests) and it passed. I did not test an actual export on a device.

cards.title: Use SHA-256 to verify exported backup ZIPs
cards.text:
After exporting a backup, `exportAsZip` in `ExportExtensions.kt` hashes the temporary ZIP and the file just written to the chosen location, then compares the two to check the copy is intact. The hashing helpers in `IOExtensions.kt` call `MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")`. RVSec reported that call, and it expects SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 there.

I changed the helper to use `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`. I also renamed the three helpers from `md5Hash` to `sha256Hash`, renamed their two local variables and updated the log and exception messages, so no name still says MD5. The only callers are in `exportAsZip`.

The digest is computed in the same process on both sides and compared right away. It isn't stored, exported or compared with any earlier value, so backups made by older versions are unaffected. I don't claim a security impact here. I made the change because RVSec flagged the call. If you would rather keep MD5 for a plain integrity check, feel free to close this.

The project builds, and the unit tests that run with the build passed. I did not run an export on a device.

Both digests are computed during that export; a mismatch or unreadable file triggers a retry or failure. The digests are neither stored in the backup nor used during restore, password processing, or authentication.

This is an accidental corruption check, with no cryptographic authenticity guarantee. [RFC 6151](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6151.html#section-1) permits MD5 checksums used solely for error detection. The current use does not require collision resistance, so this finding does not justify a pull request or issue.
